Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-01/outputs/architecture.md

Greenhouse vent controller — proposed architecture

Status: textual design proposal tied to requirements.md. No live model or hardware has been changed. Source needs N-01–N-04 and decisions D-01–D-07 retain their meanings.

Boundary and functional allocation

The system includes temperature sensing, controller logic, local stop/reset and fault indication, motor actuation, travel sensing and a remote dashboard interface. The operator, weather, greenhouse thermal dynamics and external network infrastructure influence behavior. Plant-temperature control performance and weather safety cannot be inferred from threshold logic alone.

Function Transformation Candidate responsibility Requirement allocation
F-01 Accept/reject readings; detect freshness loss C-01 sensor and C-02 MCU R-06,R-12
F-02 Qualify temperature dwell; produce open/close requests C-02 MCU R-01–R-03,R-11,R-12
F-03 Arbitrate stop/fault/travel interlocks; inhibit motor C-02 MCU, C-03 local stop, C-04 driver/motor R-04–R-06,R-08,R-10
F-04 Expose local fault/mode and dashboard status C-02 MCU, C-06 proposed local indicator R-07
F-05 Serve scoped remote access with command/status checks C-05 dashboard and network endpoint R-09; constrained by R-04,R-08,R-10
F-06 Validate explicit recovery request and clear only eligible latches C-02 MCU, C-07 operator/reset interface R-05,R-08,R-11
F-07 Report and act on end-of-travel feedback C-08 end switches, C-02,C-04 Supporting design proposal for N-01; travel limits under D-06

C-01 → C-02 carries temperature over the candidate shared network. C-02 → C-04 carries mutually exclusive open/close/disable requests. C-08 → C-02 carries end-switch states. Proposed additional path: C-03 directly inhibits C-04 independently of successful network communication, with C-03 status also read by C-02 to latch the stopped mode. C-06 makes the N-03 fault visible when C-05 is unreachable. This path and indicator are design proposals beyond the original component list.

Behavior and precedence

Maintain independent stop/fault causes rather than one flag that a later event can overwrite. Priority is local stop or latched data fault, then travel interlocks, then eligible automatic requests. Remote commands never override an active inhibit. Simultaneous open/close requests are rejected with motion inhibited as a proposed arbitration policy.

State/event Proposed response Trace/status
Automatic, fresh valid T ≥ 32 °C Start/continue opening dwell; at elapsed 30 s request open if all inhibits are clear N-01,R-01; D-01 timing semantics
A valid dip to T < 32 °C before opening qualification completes Clear opening dwell; later high readings start at zero N-01,R-02
Automatic, fresh valid T < 28 °C Start/continue closing dwell; at elapsed 60 s request close N-01,R-03; reset on T ≥ 28 °C is proposal
28 °C ≤ T < 32 °C No new temperature-triggered move; clear dwell eligibility Hysteresis proposal; whether an ongoing stroke completes is D-06
Local stop actuated in any mode Direct inhibit, latch manual-stop cause, clear dwell timers, show mode N-02,N-04,R-04,R-05,R-10,R-11
Fresh valid data absent for 5 s Inhibit, latch data-fault cause, indicate fault; do not wait for a network acknowledgment N-03,R-06–R-08; D-02,D-03
Data returns or stop is released Update status only; retain corresponding recovery latch N-02,N-03,R-05,R-08
Explicit authorized resume with stop released, current valid data and other inhibits clear Clear eligible recovery causes, enter automatic idle, begin new dwell qualification Proposal under D-04,R-11; never replay buffered motion commands
End switch reached in direction of motion Remove drive in that direction Proposed travel protection; stuck/conflicting switches and maximum run time need D-06
Power return/startup Start inhibited until validity and explicit recovery policy are satisfied Conservative proposal, not supplied obligation; D-02,D-04

The requested response to missing data is stopping, not automatic movement to a presumed safe open or closed position. If the stopped position is unsafe in wind/rain, D-06 must reconcile that requirement with N-03 before a design is accepted.

Interface contracts to complete

ID Direction/item Required semantics and open limits
I-01 C-01 → C-02 temperature °C, sensor identity, validity, unique sequence, acquisition age/timestamp. Nominal 1 s period only; jitter, transport delay, skew and invalid-value limits unknown. C-02 owns freshness decision; reception time alone may accept buffered stale data.
I-02 C-03 → C-04 inhibit; C-03 → C-02 stop state Local actuation must dominate motion irrespective of network service. Electrical polarity, broken-wire behavior, bounce, driver response and physical stopping measurements require design/verification. No safety rating is claimed.
I-03 C-02 → C-04 motion; C-04 → C-02 status if available Open/close/disable, exclusive directions, reset/boot default disable proposed. Driver latency, coast/holding behavior, stall sensing and feedback availability unknown.
I-04 C-08 → C-02 travel state Open/closed limits and invalid combination; switch polarity, debounce and action on failure under D-06. End switches do not themselves establish all intermediate positions.
I-05 C-05 ↔ C-02 remote commands/status Mode, fault causes, current value, age and acknowledgment; identify command origin and freshness. Missing connection cannot bypass C-03. Remote privileges and timeout/expiry are D-05.
I-06 C-02 ↔ C-06,C-07 indication/recovery Local data-fault visibility and explicit operator resume request, with clear eligibility/denial feedback. Means and responsible operator require D-04.

Timing and failure reasoning

Opening response comprises sample observation delay + transport delay + 30 s qualification from the chosen reference + scheduling/arbitration + driver response + mechanical travel. Closing uses 60 s. Only the dwell values are supplied; neither a full-travel deadline nor a worst-case overall response is established.

Missing-data response comprises the adopted 5 s age threshold + bounded timeout-task dispatch + disable propagation + mechanical stopping. Local-stop response bypasses the data path but still depends on electrical inhibition and mechanical stopping. Until these terms are measured/bounded and D-03 resolved, neither path has a defensible universal 50 ms guarantee.

Alternatives worth assessing: retain network sensing with explicit freshness metadata; move sensing onto a local link to remove network-loss dependence; implement stop solely in MCU logic versus direct driver inhibition plus a latched controller state. The direct local path is proposed because N-04 requires network-independent stop availability. It does not establish processor-fault tolerance, power independence or a safety integrity level. Shared supply, a single driver, MCU, software and mechanical assembly remain dependencies. Greenhouse vent controller — proposed requirements baseline

Status: review draft. Source: ../request.md, supplied packet HO-01, case version 1.0. No design approval, implementation, executed test, or reliability estimate is implied. Source IDs are retained below; new R-, F-, C-, I-, D-, and V-IDs identify draft records and their links.

Source register

  • N-01 Owner: Open the vent when a valid inside-temperature reading stays at or above 32 deg C for 30 s. A brief dip below 32 resets the interval. Close below 28 deg C after 60 s.
  • N-02 Technician: A local manual stop overrides motion; resuming automatic mode requires an explicit action.
  • N-03 Maintenance: If data is missing for 5 s, stop motion and show a fault; do not automatically resume motion after data returns.
  • N-04 Owner: We want remote access, but the local stop must work during network failure.

The candidate parts and nominal 1 s sampling rate are proposals, not source obligations. The manager's 50 ms deadline has no supplied rationale and is not adopted. It remains D-03, distinct from the sourced 5 s missing-data interval.

Draft requirements

Acceptance below refers to commanded behavior unless a physical response is explicitly stated. Final timing tolerances and measurement reference points remain open in D-01 through D-03.

ID Statement and acceptance intent Basis/type Allocation; verification Status
R-01 In automatic mode with motion permitted, the controller shall request opening when valid inside-temperature readings have satisfied T ≥ 32 °C for a continuous 30 s qualification interval. It shall not request opening earlier on that interval. N-01; source-derived F-02/C-02; V-01 Draft; sampled continuity and request latency need D-01
R-02 The controller shall reset the opening qualification interval when an accepted valid reading is below 32 °C, including a single brief sampled dip. A subsequent qualifying reading shall begin a new interval. N-01; source-derived F-02/C-02; V-01 Draft
R-03 In automatic mode with motion permitted, the controller shall request closing after valid inside-temperature readings are below 28 °C for 60 s. A reading of exactly 28 °C shall not qualify as below 28 °C. N-01; source-derived; continuous low interval interpretation proposed F-02/C-02; V-02 Draft; reset and observation semantics in D-01
R-04 Actuation of the local manual stop shall override automatic and remote motion requests and stop vent motion. N-02, N-04; source-derived F-03/C-03,C-04; V-03,V-06 Draft; physical stopping time needs D-03
R-05 Following a local manual stop, the controller shall remain inhibited until an explicit operator action requests resumption of automatic mode; releasing the stop alone shall not resume motion. N-02; source-derived F-03,F-06/C-02,C-03,C-07; V-03,V-05 Draft; authority/action definition in D-04
R-06 If temperature data is missing for 5 s, the controller shall stop motion. N-03; source-derived F-01,F-03/C-02,C-04; V-04 Draft; missing-data age and physical response defined by D-02,D-03
R-07 On detection of the R-06 condition, the controller shall show a data fault. N-03; source-derived F-04/C-02,C-06; V-04 Draft; indication location/latency in D-02,D-04
R-08 Return of temperature data alone shall not resume vent motion after an R-06 stop. N-03; source-derived F-03,F-06/C-02,C-07; V-05 Draft; authorized reset policy in D-04

Derivation proposal from N-01–N-03: avoid stale timer completing immediately after recovery F-02,F-06/C-02; V-05 Proposed, requires D-04 decision
R-12 Invalid, duplicate, or stale readings shall not advance a temperature qualification interval or silently clear a missing-data fault. Derivation proposal from valid-reading condition in N-01 and missing data in N-03 F-01,F-02/C-02; V-04,V-05 Proposed; validity/freshness limits in D-02

N-01 is covered by R-01–R-03; N-02 by R-04–R-05; N-03 by R-06–R-08; N-04 by R-09–R-10. R-11–R-12 carry explicit derivation rationales and are not accepted additions. No requirement claims the candidate architecture already satisfies it.

Decisions needed for a final baseline

ID Decision and proposed owner Why it changes the design; evidence needed
D-01 Owner + control engineer: define sampled continuity, timer start, jitter tolerance, threshold accuracy, and opening/closing output deadlines. Nominal 1 s sampling cannot establish physical continuity between samples. Proposed timer starts at first accepted qualifying sample, uses elapsed monotonic time, and resets on disqualifying or invalid/gapped data; 30 samples alone do not equal 30 s. Need sensor accuracy, sample/transport jitter measurements and owner agreement. Confirm closing interval reset on T ≥ 28 °C.
D-02 Controls + maintenance: define validity, stale data, startup with no samples, age reference, clock synchronization and fault indication. Proposed timeout at age ≥ 5 s since last genuinely fresh valid sample; first-sample wait begins at startup. Replayed packets must not reset freshness. Source timestamps with bounded skew or sequence/age protocol are needed if network buffering can hide stale readings. Need transport behavior and sensor failure modes.
D-03 Mechanical/control lead + owner: define safe stopping response, its reference points, and allowable time. The sourced 5 s absence trigger is separate from detection scheduling, driver disable and mechanical stopping. Measure travel/coast/load and assess injury/overtravel/weather consequences. A universal 50 ms deadline is unsupported; accept, revise or reject it only with a hazard/performance basis.
D-04 Owner + maintenance: define reset authority and explicit action, local fault visibility, operator response, startup/power-return behavior, and behavior when several stop causes overlap. Proposed acknowledged reset only after stop released and data healthy, with new timers; clearing one cause must not clear another. Operator response cannot be assumed fast enough to protect plants or people. Need operational walkthrough and power-loss review.
D-05 Owner + network lead: define remote-access functions, authorization, unavailable/stale dashboard behavior and command expiration. Monitoring and remote motion control impose different risks. No remote request may bypass local inhibit or clear a fault without an approved explicit recovery action. Need intended users and command semantics.
D-06 Owner + mechanical/environment lead: define operating envelope, wind/rain behavior, safe position, travel limits and actuator holding. Stopping mid-travel is a sourced motion response, not proof of an environmentally safe position. Need vent/load data and outdoor conditions; opening, closing or holding can have different consequences.
D-07 Reliability/maintenance lead: establish required availability, fault handling and diagnostic coverage if quantitative claims are wanted. One MCU, shared network, power and motor driver are common dependencies. No failure probabilities or supplier reliability data were supplied; no reliability total or independence claim is supportable.

ID Claim and method Stimulus, observations and acceptance Planned result; proposed reviewer

Exercise below/at/above 32 °C, crossing with varied sample phase/jitter, just before/at/after 30 s, a single valid sub-32 dip near completion and repeated brief dips. Observe accepted samples, elapsed timer and open command. No early command; dip resets rather than pauses; subsequent opening needs a new 30 s interval. Evaluate command lateness against D-01 once set. Include an unsampled physical dip to expose the limit of any sampled-continuity claim. evidence/V-01-report not created; controls reviewer

V-03 R-04,R-05; loaded actuator test and interlock inspection Actuate local stop during opening, closing, idle and concurrent remote commands. Measure contact action, driver disable, motion cessation and restart behavior. Motion stops within the D-03 bound once established. Release alone causes no restart; explicit eligible resume follows the approved D-04 sequence. Do not substitute driver-output observation for physical stop evidence. evidence/V-03-report not created; mechanical/control reviewers

Repeat in both travel directions, startup with no samples, invalid streams, duplicated/reordered or delayed old messages, high jitter, and source-clock discontinuity. Observe true freshness reference, timeout dispatch, inhibit, physical stop and local indication with dashboard unavailable. At 5 s condition, fault/stop response follows agreed D-02,D-03 timing. Invalid/stale packets must not advance dwell or conceal age loss. evidence/V-04-report not created; controls + maintenance reviewers
V-05 R-05,R-08,R-11,R-12; recovery sequence test Restore valid data while manual stop is active and while it is released; clear causes in either order. Repeat explicit resume with data still stale, stale queued commands, held reset, partial timer progress, and restart/power return. V-06 R-09,R-10 and N-04; interface inspection and fault-injection demonstration Disconnect or saturate the shared network during motion, remove dashboard service, send concurrent/replayed motion commands, then actuate local stop. Observe errors, recovery authority, response time and plant-use consequences under an agreed use envelope. Agree success conditions with stakeholders; logic tests alone cannot establish usefulness or safe operation. evidence/V-08-report not created; owner/operator representatives

ID / statement reviewed Correction and consequence Evidence still needed / proposed owner
MD-01: “FDA Class III/PMA under 21 CFR 876.5820” Wrong device regulation. Section 876.5820 identifies a hemodialysis system. Section 880.5725 identifies a healthcare-facility infusion pump and specifies Class II. Use the latter as the provisional starting point for this external large-volume IV pump. Current eCFR, 880.5725(a)–(b), 876.5820(a). Regulatory lead: controlled intended-use and device/system boundary, product-code assessment, technological characteristics, predicate and substantial-equivalence assessment. A Class II starting point is not a completed 510(k) determination.
MD-02: “EU IIb under Rule 11” IIb is a plausible conclusion with the wrong principal rationale. Rule 12 addresses active administration/removal of substances: potentially hazardous administration leads to IIb; the current guidance lists infusion pumps. Rule 11 concerns software. Software driving/influencing the pump also requires consideration of Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3. MDCG 2021-24 Rev.1, April 2026, printed pp. 47–48. Regulatory lead: justify hazardous administration from intended substances, IV route, patient population and mode of application; assess all applicable rules and system/software boundaries, including any separately marketed software. Record the manufacturer's rationale and applicable conformity-assessment review.
MD-03: “IEC 62304 C because FDA Class III” Invalid mapping. Product class and software safety class are separate decisions. Class C may be supportable if the software-related hazardous situations can lead to death or serious injury under the applicable classification method, but no such risk analysis was supplied. Software safety/risk leads: identify software contributions to excessive, inadequate or unintended delivery and loss of protective functions; evaluate resulting harms, external risk controls, architecture/segregation, and the adopted edition's classification method. Record a justified software class independently of FDA class.

Two boundaries matter. FDA's infusion-pump guidance explicitly recognizes pumps submitted as part of a Class III system as a PMA case; nothing supplied establishes that system context here. Its current cover notice also distinguishes FDA software submission Documentation Level, generally Enhanced for infusion pumps, from device classification. Neither fixes the IEC software class. FDA, Infusion Pumps Total Product Life Cycle, 2014, section 3 and current cover notice.

For EU Rule 22, local feedback maintaining a clinician-set flow is not, by itself, an incorporated diagnostic function significantly determining patient management. The supplied absence of physiological diagnostic control gives no affirmative basis for Rule 22 Class III. Reopen that assessment if the device uses patient measurements to adapt therapy. MDCG 2021-24 Rev.1, printed p. 59.

The colleague's two blanket statements are incorrect. Criterion 3 permits an error to escape detection; it does not mean “no effect” or exemption from qualification. A Criterion 1 tool used for Level B software maps to TQL-2, not TQL-1. The log processor's final criterion remains open because “removing manual checking” does not identify which process credit is claimed.

Qualification starts with the intended use: which required activity is automated, reduced or eliminated, whether tool error could introduce or conceal a software error, and which effective checks remain on its output. Independently verifying the relevant output can change the need for qualification; a nominal review or spot check is not evidence that all credited error-detection work remains covered. FAA identifies DO-178C section 12.2 and DO-330 as its acceptable qualification method. FAA AC 20-115D, 21 July 2017, paragraph 10.

The decision boundaries are:

Criterion Impact/use boundary Application to the proposed workflow
1 Output becomes part of the airborne software and can introduce error. A generated executable/configuration may qualify; producing a test report alone does not establish this boundary.
2 Verification automation can miss error, and its output justifies reducing/eliminating other verification processes or development processes affecting the airborne software. Candidate if the report is used to waive additional testing, reviews or development work beyond the log-analysis activity it performs.
3 Within intended use, the tool can fail to detect error, without the Criterion 2 additional credit. Candidate if it replaces only the manual evaluation of those test logs, while the other applicable processes remain. Qualification can still be needed.

These distinctions are paraphrased from NASA/CR–2017-219371, Formal Methods Tool Qualification, February 2017, section 3.3.1, printed p. 11, Table 2. This is an accessible NASA-sponsored research report, not a substitute for the adopted standards or an authority decision.

Software level Criterion 1 Criterion 2 Criterion 3
A TQL-1 TQL-4 TQL-5
B TQL-2 TQL-4 TQL-5
C TQL-3 TQL-5 TQL-5
D TQL-4 TQL-5 TQL-5

The mapping is visible in FAA AC 20-115D, Table 2, printed p. 11. Its context is correlation/transition of legacy DO-178B tools. For a new use, confirm the decision against DO-178C section 12.2 and Table 12-1, and the applicable DO-330 objectives. A generator's name does not prove Criterion 1 qualification is required: examine whether its generated output enters the airborne product, the credit claimed, and output verification. Conversely, an applicable Criterion 1 generator for Level A maps to TQL-1 and for Level B to TQL-2.

Before choosing between Level A TQL-4 and TQL-5 for this processor, obtain this minimum decision package:

  1. Credit ledger: each existing manual check and associated objective; exactly what the tool automates; any additional activities to be removed; remaining reviewers/checkers and their detection scope. Show the before/after workflow, including raw-log retention.
  2. Use and configuration: executable/version, parser and comparison rules, expected input formats, operating environment, configuration, users, interfaces, supported and excluded cases. Identify whether it only summarizes or also decides pass/fail, filters evidence, computes coverage, or creates loadable data.
  3. Failure/escape analysis: missing/truncated/reordered logs, wrong test IDs or build, unit/rounding and timestamp errors, silently ignored failures, unexpected records, and a falsely successful report. For each, identify which independent check detects it and which software error could otherwise escape.
  4. Program basis: authority, accepted software level and DO-178/DO-330 editions, legacy/new use, tool operational requirements, qualification plan/data and any supplier limitations. Qualification is tied to this use and configuration; possessing a tool certificate or another project's evidence is insufficient alone.

Proposed next step: retain the current manual checking while the project decides the credited workflow. If qualification is required, scope its objectives and operational requirements to that workflow and establish evidence for normal, malformed and error-containing logs, independently known expected results, configuration control and problem handling. Alternatively, retain adequate independent output verification and document what credit is no longer claimed. No tool execution, qualification result or authorization to remove checking is established here.

Sources were accessed 2026-11-13. Full licensed DO-178C and DO-330 texts were not available/read; no new licensed clause content is asserted. Six cases shared one participant context, so this assessment is not a separately isolated participant run.

REQ-7 timing change — impact and evidence review

The 200 ms baseline is not verified by the supplied information. Preserve REQ-7's ID and its 500 ms revision history, but reopen its verification and timing allocation. The reported 460 ms result passed the former 500 ms criterion; it does not pass a comparable 200 ms criterion. A planned report path with no file supplies no result. This review uses the facts in ../request.md; the original test report, design, logs, timing specification and new report are not present for inspection.

Timing consequence

For a serial dependency from interface processing through detection to actuation, the supplied upper bounds sum to:

150 ms + 80 ms + 30 ms = 260 ms

That budget exceeds 200 ms by 60 ms, before any unallocated sensing, queues, scheduling, communications, output rendering or physical alert delay. This shows the stated serial budget cannot substantiate a 200 ms worst-case guarantee. It does not prove that every run takes 260 ms or that all stage maxima occur simultaneously; dependencies and conditions need inspection. Conversely, a typical faster run would not repair the missing worst-case argument.

The old observed 460 ms had 40 ms margin against 500 ms and would exceed 200 ms by 260 ms if its reference events and conditions are comparable. Its being 200 ms longer than the 260 ms stage sum is an unresolved discrepancy, not proof of a particular 200 ms overhead. Possible causes include omitted work, different configurations, time origins or incomparable definitions. Inspect the actual report and timeline before allocating that difference.

Located findings and impacts

ID Locator and observed fact Consequence Concrete repair; proposed owner/status
F-01 REQ-7 verification claim: reused reported PASS at 460 ms after limit changed 500 → 200 ms Current verification claim is unsupported; if the recorded observation applies to the same claim, it contradicts the new limit Retain old result and historical verdict; record its 500 ms scope. Set current REQ-7 verification to open/unverified. Retrieve report and perform explicit applicability review. Verification lead; open, blocks a supported verification claim
F-02 Interface 150 ms, detector 80 ms, actuator 30 ms allocations Serial upper-bound total is 260 ms with negative margin. Locally conforming elements can still miss the system deadline Establish end-to-end path and overhead; redistribute or redesign timing allocations, then obtain analysis and measurement. Architecture/performance lead; open
F-03 Planned new report path is reported absent Trace points to intended evidence, not an executed artifact Mark activity planned, outcome unset, artifact absent. Execute approved procedure on the revised configuration and attach actual report/raw logs. Verification lead; open
F-04 No trigger/alert definitions, baseline identifiers, operating envelope or timing uncertainty supplied Neither evidence reuse nor a precise pass decision can be assessed Define timing endpoints, inclusive ≤ 200 ms criterion, loads and alert visibility; identify exact design/test versions and measurement uncertainty. Requirement owner + test lead; open question, not an invented defect in unseen files

Affected work includes REQ-7's acceptance procedure and trace coverage; every stage and shared resource on its critical path; interfaces whose latency/rate/queue contracts change; scheduling, priority and buffering; resource contention with other functions; alert semantics and any safety/operational analysis relying on alert timing. Revisit suppliers only where their components carry changed allocations. No hazards, supplier commitments, certification requirements or particular alert technology were supplied, so their actual impacts remain to be assessed rather than asserted.

Evidence disposition

Record Lifecycle/outcome Configuration applicability Review/acceptance
Old report, reported 460 ms against 500 ms Reported executed PASS for old criterion; actual artifact/logs not examined Historical evidence for the former requirement if identity and conditions are confirmed. Not positive evidence of ≤ 200 ms. Potentially reusable for unchanged functions or method only after a scoped argument Prior review/acceptance unknown; no current acceptance inferred
New planned report Planned; no execution outcome; reported file absent No executed configuration exists in the supplied evidence No review or acceptance
This 260 ms arithmetic Desk analysis of supplied stage bounds under stated serial assumption Conditional; no deployed-controller timing measured Shows an allocation gap, not an executed system failure

A linked requirement, component, test and report is a navigation chain. It establishes neither that the report exists nor that the procedure exercises the current deadline under the intended conditions.

Repair options

  1. Keep 200 ms and reduce the serial path. After accounting for all overhead H, allocations must satisfy I + D + A + H ≤ 200 ms. With detector and actuator unchanged, interface allowance is at most 90 ms − H, a reduction of at least 60 ms even if H were zero. Investigate queue delay, transport, scheduling and avoidable processing before selecting changes. No such reduction is yet demonstrated.
  2. Introduce genuine parallelism or a shorter alert path. If interface processing and detection can validly run concurrently on the required fresh input, max(150,80) + 30 = 180 ms, leaving at most 20 ms for every other delay and uncertainty. This is a conditional architecture candidate, not a validated budget. If detection depends on interface completion, this arithmetic is invalid. A local earlier alert path might help only if it preserves the required alert meaning and conditions; an early acknowledgment is not automatically an alert.
  3. Change components, algorithms or partitioning. Use an independently scheduled critical path or faster stages if measurements identify the limiting mechanism. Reassess shared queues, false/missed alerts, ordering and interference after any optimization. Faster component specifications alone do not verify the system.
  4. Reconsider the requirement through its authorized owner. If no feasible architecture meets 200 ms within constraints, present the timing need, consequences and cost/scope trade. A justified alternate deadline or phased objective is a change decision, not a verification waiver disguised as a pass. Do not silently restore 500 ms or rewrite the old verdict to fit the new requirement.

Verification work and next decision

First obtain a timestamped end-to-end trace for the actual critical path and resolve the 460 ms versus stage-budget discrepancy. In parallel, the requirement owner must define the initiating event and the observable alert completion; revisions and loads must be comparable before subtracting timings.

Prepare V-7-REV against the final REQ-7 revision and frozen implementation: stimulate the specified event, measure from its defined time origin to observable alert, and collect stage timestamps on a common or demonstrably aligned clock. Exercise specified worst-load and queue conditions, event/sample phase boundaries, contention and relevant degraded/recovery modes. Determine the needed run set and analysis coverage from the actual timing model; do not invent a sample count or percentile for a hard deadline.

Acceptance requires ≤ 200 ms for the applicable conditions with documented measurement uncertainty and a justified bound on unobserved worst cases. A conservative observation criterion is measured elapsed time plus its uncertainty ≤ 200 ms; the adopted uncertainty treatment must be explicit. Record any > 200 ms result as a failure for that tested configuration, preserve the logs and identify repair. Regression checks must cover unchanged alert semantics and neighboring functions affected by changed scheduling/interfaces.

The resulting report must include exact requirement/design/firmware/configuration hashes, procedure and instruments, environment/load, trigger/end definitions, raw values and maxima, uncertainty, deviations and limits. Then perform applicability review and a separate authorized acceptance decision. Until that work exists, retain the new requirement as unverified, with an unresolved timing budget. No system test was run in preparing this review.

Neither completeness claim is supported. The strongest defensible statement is that the reported run exercised all counted RTL lines and found no reported violation within its stated bound and assumptions. Even that statement awaits the actual reports and configuration; only the team's assertions were supplied.

Finding Why it changes the decision Required correction
EL-01: 100% RTL line coverage “proves all requirements” A wrong implementation can execute every line. Line execution does not demonstrate correct values, sequencing, timing, modes, interfaces, error handling or requirements omitted from RTL. The coverage denominator may also exclude code. Retain the structural result with its scope. Establish requirements-based evidence and functional/property coverage separately; review exclusions and unverified requirements.
EL-02: depth 20 “proves eventual service for all executions” A 20-step search does not establish progress over arbitrary executions. A request near the boundary can remain unresolved; starvation can appear after the explored prefix. A proof using induction/completeness may use a depth internally, so the actual engine result matters. Distinguish a bounded check from an unbounded proof, and a response deadline from unbounded eventuality. Supply any induction, invariant, termination/completeness argument or liveness result. No such argument is supplied.
EL-03: environment assumes grant always high This removes the stated shared-arbitration behavior. It can exclude waiting, competition and starvation, or collapse progress to a trivial case. Even a correct proof under this assumption is conditional on an environment that has not been shown to exist. Replace the assumption with an agreed interface contract supported by the arbiter implementation/system evidence. Preserve the old result as a restricted result, not deployment evidence.

The logical distinction is reflected in the tool author's SBY reference, Options section, which distinguishes bounded safety checking, unbounded safety proof, unbounded liveness checking and reachability coverage. This source illustrates result types; it does not establish which tool or algorithm the team used.

Please supply these minimum meaningful artifacts, limited to the request/service thread initially:

  1. The requirement IDs and exact definitions of request, acceptance, grant and served; request persistence/cancellation, outstanding transactions, reset semantics and required response time or eventuality. Identify the applicable assurance basis rather than assuming avionics rules.
  2. The versioned RTL and relevant arbiter/interface model; clocks/reset, parameters and abstraction boundary; build/configuration hashes. Include any black boxes, cutpoints or abstracted state affecting service.
  3. The exact assertions and assumptions, their requirement links, initialization/clock semantics, and reasons each environmental assumption holds in deployment. Include reachability/antecedent and vacuity checks.
  4. Reproducible proof scripts, tool/solver versions and options, engine/mode, depth meaning, logs, status for each property, any proof certificate/invariants, counterexamples and timeouts. “PASS” without its semantics is insufficient.
  5. Requirement-to-test/property results and the line-coverage report: build, stimulus/seeds, covered/excluded lines and rationale, checkers/oracles, unresolved failures and waived/unreachable bins.

Proposed evidence plan:

Stage Discriminating activity and expected artifact Decision it supports
1. Define the service contract System/arbiter owners decide whether a persistent accepted request must be served within a justified bound B, or eventually under explicit conditions. Define reset/cancel exceptions and completion identity. Gives a testable property and prevents a timeout from being mistaken for service. B is unresolved, not assumed to be 20.
2. Challenge the environment Permit grant low, simultaneous competitors and realistic backpressure; cover accepted requests, waiting and service. Review each assumption for satisfiability and antecedent reachability; remove assumptions one at a time where practical. Detects overconstraint or vacuity. Covers show scenarios are reachable, not that they are safe.
3. Establish progress Prove the arbiter contract and use it compositionally, or include it in the model. For bounded service, verify the deadline from acceptance across all relevant states. For eventual service, seek an unbounded liveness argument with explicit fairness/availability assumptions, or a valid completeness argument. Retain inconclusive results. Supports only the proved property under discharged assumptions. Fairness cannot be introduced merely to make the result pass.
4. Attempt counterexamples Exercise sustained contention, grant denied beyond 20 cycles, request arrival at/after cycle 20, back-to-back requests, queue-full boundaries, reset/cancel while pending, and grant recovery. Include request duplication/loss checks and independent transaction tracking. A request held pending while another client is continually served is a concrete starvation candidate. Its legality depends on the agreed contract.
5. Connect to implementation Reconcile properties and tests against the requirement baseline; inspect functional/structural gaps. Check the applicable RTL-to-implementation chain, clock/reset crossings and timing, then use target observations for assumptions the RTL abstraction cannot establish. Limits extrapolation from ideal logic to delivered hardware.

If the real environment can deny service forever, unconditional eventual service is unsatisfiable. The design/operations owner must supply a justified resource guarantee or revise the requested behavior, perhaps to a bounded reported failure; a failure indication is a different requirement from successful service. No probability, assurance class or standard-clause mandate is inferred.

All activities above are proposed. No RTL, formal tool run, simulation or hardware test was provided or executed. The SBY primary documentation was accessed 2026-11-13. A primary paper on completeness thresholds was also attempted, but its extracted text was unreadable and it was not relied upon. Six cases shared this participant context; there was no per-case fresh-session isolation.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-05/request.md

A hardware team says 100% RTL line coverage proves all requirements and a bounded proof to depth 20 proves a request is eventually served for all executions. The formal environment assumes grant is always high, while deployed arbitration is shared. Ask for the minimum meaningful artifacts, review these claims, and propose an evidence plan. Do not manufacture licensed clause numbers.

Medication-container transport — operational scenario draft

Status: proposed operational agreement, not an approved policy or implemented robot design. Source is ../request.md (HO-07). The supplied facts are: a service robot hands a medication transport container to authorized staff; medication selection and dosing are outside the boundary; unavailable recipients, connectivity loss and recovery need coverage. All scenario and decision IDs below are newly assigned draft IDs.

The intended outcome is delivery of the identified container to a staff member authorized for that handoff, with an accountable custody record and a controlled disposition when delivery cannot complete. Delivery speed alone is insufficient. No current workflow, staffing plan, authorization technology, lock, local storage capability, clinical handling limit or timing target was supplied.

Boundary, roles and authority

Inside the operational boundary are mission assignment, transport, recipient contact, authorization checking, container identification, physical handoff, custody acknowledgment, exception management and recovery. Medication selection, dose determination, administration and judgment about medication suitability stay with the responsible clinical service outside this boundary. Transport staff may identify a handling concern and refer it; the robot does not infer suitability.

These are proposed responsibilities to confirm with the service owner, not claims that the roles are staffed today:

Actor Decision or responsibility Limit
Dispatching staff/custodian Identify the container and destination, establish the initial custody record, accept an authorized return Dispatch does not establish dosing correctness within this transport system
Receiving staff Establish identity and current authority for this container/handoff; accept or decline receipt; acknowledge physical possession Proximity, a uniform or knowing the destination does not establish authority
Duty transport supervisor Own exceptions; authorize wait, reassignment, assisted collection, return or mission cancellation within policy; reconcile uncertain custody Cannot create clinical authority or waive handling limits without the responsible service
Robot/transport system Execute an authorized mission, present status, support verification and record transport/handoff events; retain control pending an allowed transfer Does not choose a substitute recipient, waive authorization or assign medication decisions
Authorization service/policy owner Define who may receive which deliveries and how that authority is checked, including expiry and revocation Connectivity restoration alone does not reauthorize a recipient
Maintenance/recovery staff Restore transport capability under supervisor direction Maintenance access does not itself confer authority to take the container

Distinguish physical possession from accountability. While a robot carries the container, the service must name an accountable dispatch/transport custodian; a machine is not assumed to hold human accountability. The custody record links container ID, mission ID, prior custodian, receiving identity, authorization basis, transfer event and exception state. Minimize content to what transport needs; no medication-selection data is assumed necessary.

Proposed modes are awaiting dispatch, in transit, waiting for recipient, handoff pending, completed, degraded/held, returning and reconciliation required. Transitions require observable guards, below. The service must choose the authoritative custody-transfer event (D-02); the draft uses confirmed physical receipt plus an attributable acceptance record. A delivery command or an unlock action alone is not proof of receipt.

SC-01 — normal authorized handoff

Trigger: dispatching staff assign an identified container to a destination. Preconditions: mission authorized; route/handling conditions are within an agreed envelope; the transporting custodian and intended recipient role are known; a method exists to retain and identify the container. Initial mode: awaiting dispatch.

  1. Dispatching staff confirm container and mission identities and place the container under the transport service's agreed control. The system records dispatch acceptance and presents the destination. Staff resolve discrepancies before departure.
  2. The robot transports the container and reports mission state by the available approved means. The accountable custodian remains recorded during transit.
  3. At the destination, the robot enters waiting-for-recipient mode and requests the designated staff role. A staff member responds. This contact is not a custody transfer.
  4. Staff provide identity; the system or responsible operator checks current authority for this handoff using the approved process. Staff and system match container/mission identity. A mismatch, expired authority or refusal leads to SC-02 or supervisor review with no release.
  5. Once authority and container identity are confirmed, the system enters handoff-pending mode. Staff intentionally accept the transfer; the container is made available using the selected mechanism. The system observes or obtains attributable confirmation of physical receipt and records the agreed custody event. The exact order and mechanism need D-02/D-03 so that a failure cannot silently produce two custodians or none.
  6. Only after the transfer completion conditions are satisfied does the mission become completed. Staff can see that they have accepted custody; dispatch/supervision can see the completed or pending-reconciliation status.

Final condition: receiving staff possess the identified container, the prior transporting custodian is relieved under the agreed policy, and the record reflects the same event. If acknowledgment is missing after apparent removal, enter reconciliation required; do not declare failure and deliver a second container automatically. Connectivity interruption branches to SC-03.

SC-02 — recipient unavailable, declines, or is unauthorized

Trigger: no eligible recipient responds at the destination, staff decline receipt, or authority cannot be established. Initial mode: waiting for recipient; container remains under transport control with the existing accountable custodian.

  1. Present an intelligible waiting/not-completed state. Do not leave the container unattended, transfer it to a convenient nearby person, or record delivery based on arrival.
  2. Use the approved contact method to notify the receiving team and duty supervisor. Record whether the notification was sent, delivered or acknowledged; sending it does not establish that someone knows about the delay.
  3. Wait only within the service-approved waiting period, route occupancy constraints, energy reserve and container handling conditions. No values are supplied. If continued waiting would violate a limit, use the predefined contingency and escalate; do not assume a supervisor will respond in time.
  4. The supervisor chooses an allowed disposition: continue waiting, name an authorized substitute, arrange authorized assisted collection, or return to the dispatching service. Reassignment is explicit, traceable and checked against current authority; it is not a robot guess.
  5. A substitute recipient rejoins SC-01 at identity/authority verification. An authorized return ends only when dispatch staff accept physical possession and return custody. Cancellation while still carrying the container changes mission intent, not custody.

Final conditions: either a valid handoff completes, an authorized return completes, or the mission remains visibly held with a named accountable custodian and escalation owner. Absence of both recipient and supervisor is an unresolved operational contingency in D-04, not permission to release.

SC-03 — connectivity loss

Trigger: loss of connectivity needed for supervision, authorization or custody records. Detection: the system identifies the affected service and makes degraded state locally observable by an available method; network alert delivery cannot be assumed during the outage. Detection latency and remaining functions need D-03/D-05.

Loss point Proposed operational response and custody consequence
Before dispatch or en route Do not initiate a new mission that depends on unavailable authorization or supervision. For an active mission, retain container control and the existing accountable custodian. Use an approved local route to an agreed holding point or controlled halt, according to the motion/obstruction assessment. Do not assume that stopping immediately in a doorway is acceptable or that navigation works offline.
At recipient check, before release Hold the handoff if current authority cannot be verified. An offline authorization route is allowed only if the service explicitly approves its scope, freshness/revocation rules and record method. Cached identity alone does not establish current authority.
During physical handoff, before completion is certain Determine what can actually be observed. If still retained, keep it retained. If staff already possess it, do not pretend robot custody persists or automatically take it back. Enter reconciliation required, show transfer uncertainty, retain mission/container/identity/time evidence and invoke the approved local supervisor contact or witnessed fallback.
After confirmed physical receipt and acceptance but before central acknowledgment Preserve the completion event in the approved local or witnessed record and flag synchronization pending. Do not repeat the handoff, replay a release command or assign a second delivery merely because the server did not acknowledge. If no trustworthy local record exists, treat it as an uncertain transfer and reconcile.

Functions that depend on connectivity remain unavailable. Local containment, motion, recipient prompts and record persistence are design assumptions to verify, not capabilities established by this scenario. D-03 must identify a viable manual fallback if the platform cannot preserve the needed state. While held, handling-condition and energy limits continue to apply; communications loss does not pause them. The appropriate clinical service decides the disposition of a container whose handling acceptability is in doubt.

SC-04 — recovery and resumption

Trigger: communication or a failed capability returns, or authorized recovery staff attend. Initial mode: degraded/held or reconciliation required.

  1. The system reports restored service while retaining the prior mission, fault and custody state. Reconnection alone does not trigger movement, release or a new mission.
  2. The supervisor and system reconcile container identity and actual possession against local and central events. Resolve incomplete or conflicting transfers with the people involved. Preserve the discrepancy and resolution rather than overwriting the history to make records agree.
  3. Revalidate current recipient authority, destination, mission status, handling conditions, route and available power. Discard or explicitly reject expired/duplicate queued commands; identify events so reconnect/retry does not cause a second physical transfer.
  4. With custody known and all required guards satisfied, the authorized supervisor/operator explicitly chooses resume, reassign, return, assisted collection or cancellation. Continuing to hold is a valid unresolved state if the guards cannot be established.
  5. Resume at a defined point: in-transit mission resumes transport; an unreleased container resumes SC-01 at authority verification; an already completed handoff reconciles its record without another release; a return resumes the authorized-return path in SC-02.

Final condition: one known accountable custody state, an explicit mission disposition, resolved or visibly outstanding discrepancies, and an operator-visible status. Restored network availability without these conditions is not completed recovery.

Decisions, assumptions and observations

ID Operational decision to obtain; proposed owner Design assumption that must not be mistaken for that decision
D-01 Which staff roles may receive each mission and who may reassign? Service/authorization owner Badge, password, biometric or online service is a mechanism choice; none is supplied
D-02 What exact physical/acknowledgment event transfers custody, and how is a disputed event resolved? Dispatch/receiving services A lock sensor, camera or database transaction may provide evidence but does not alone define accountability
D-03 Which transport/handoff functions may continue offline, with what authority freshness and audit fallback? Service owner + platform lead Local navigation, secure retention, offline credentials and persistent logs are unverified capabilities
D-04 What are the waiting/escalation/return rules, reachable duty roles, handling limits and no-response contingency? Operations + responsible clinical service A notification or nominal staffing roster does not establish timely human availability
D-05 What are outage-detection and controlled-halt/holding rules, energy reserve, local indicators and recovery authority? Operations + platform safety lead Connectivity and motion failure are different; no safe halt position or sensor reliability is supplied

Proposed validation is a staffed walkthrough followed by controlled transport trials with representative containers, roles and outages. No trial has run. Agree time and workload targets before claiming acceptable service performance.

Validation case Observable condition for a useful decision
VC-01 / SC-01 normal and wrong-recipient attempts Authorized staff can identify and accept the correct container; wrong/expired/declining recipients receive no release; physical possession and custody record agree. Observe steps, errors and staff effort.
VC-02 / SC-02 recipient and supervisor unavailable Container stays controlled, a named custodian persists, status does not show delivered, and the approved timeout/contingency produces an observable authorized hold or return. Measure waiting and response times against subsequently agreed limits.
VC-03 / SC-03 outage at each handoff phase Record which functions survive; no release without the approved authorization basis; no unrecorded assumed transfer. Interruption during removal produces a visible uncertain state and successful human reconciliation.
VC-04 / SC-04 reconnection with duplicate commands, expired authority or conflicting records No automatic repeat release or motion; stale commands are rejected; current authority and custody are reconciled before explicit resumption. The completed mission has one physical transfer with attributable history.
VC-05 / SC-02–SC-04 busy-staff walkthrough Staff can recognize who holds custody and who must act using the information actually available, including network outage. Observe missed prompts, informal workarounds and whether the named supervisor role can fulfill its duty under workload.

These scenarios cover normal handoff and the requested exception/recovery paths. They do not establish exhaustive hazard coverage, clinical efficacy, legal compliance or platform verification.

Cover an unavailable recipient, connectivity loss, and recovery. Preserve authority and custody, distinguish operational decisions from design assumptions, and propose observable validation conditions. Save a coherent draft.

District drinking-water service — concept decision draft

Preserve reliable drinking-water service as the objective. Investigate outage buffering and maintenance isolation before choosing a larger plant. The stated failure is loss of service while the only treatment plant is maintained. Extra production capacity alone does not remove that dependence. The sponsor's preference for low unit production cost is legitimate, but it is not evidence that the preferred plant will keep water available during its own shutdown.

This comparison uses only ../request.md. No demand volumes, outage durations, water-quality results, costs, spare capacity or staffing productivity are supplied. The recommendation is provisional; it is a direction for investigation, not a sized or accepted design.

Outcome, boundary and constraints

The service boundary runs from raw-water access through treatment, usable storage, distribution and delivery to customers, including power, control, consumables, operators, maintenance and storm access. A treatment plant's output is an intermediate result; reliable customer supply also depends on water quality, delivery pressure and distribution availability.

  • Hard staffing constraint as stated: operators can staff only two locations. A concept requiring more staffed locations is infeasible without an explicit change to that constraint. This does not automatically prohibit more physical units, but unattended units cannot be assumed feasible: maintenance visits, competence, alarms and storm recovery still require a staffing/access case.
  • Operating facts to design around: seasonal demand and storm road closures. Treat road access during closures as unavailable, not merely inconvenient. Whether closures coincide with high demand or maintenance needs is unknown.
  • Unspecified outcome limits: acceptable interruption duration/frequency, minimum service and water-quality basis, critical-user needs, storm design conditions and recovery time. The service owner must set these from the district's actual obligations and needs; none is invented here.
  • Preference: the sponsor favors the largest plant for its claimed lower unit production cost. That cost comparison is supplied as the sponsor's rationale, with no costing evidence. It must be reconciled with lifecycle service cost and continuity, not treated as a hard constraint or a verified economic result.

Useful concepts

Concept How it could maintain service What must be true; principal exposure Evidence needed before selection
C-01 Larger central plant More capacity can meet seasonal peaks and replenish reserves faster. Independently isolatable treatment trains could permit partial operation during maintenance. Simply replacing one plant with a larger single shutdown dependency leaves the stated outage mechanism. Train isolation is an added concept, not a supplied feature. Common intake, power, chemicals, controls or distribution may still stop all output. One site may ease staffing, but its workload and support needs are unknown. Why current maintenance interrupts all treatment; capacity available during each maintenance task; common dependencies; seasonal throughput and full service-cost estimate
C-02 Distributed treatment at up to two staffed locations One location may continue producing when the other is maintained; proximity may serve areas cut off by a distribution failure. The surviving unit plus storage must meet the agreed service demand, and water must reach affected customers. Independence is not established by geography: source, power, consumables, operators, flood exposure and pipelines can be shared. Road closures may strand repairs and supplies at either location. More than two staffed sites violates the current constraint. Hydraulic/service zones and interconnection; remaining capacity with one site out; common-cause exposure; actual two-site staffing/shift and maintenance plan; resupply during closures
C-03 Additional clean-water storage with the existing plant Buffer already treated water so delivery continues while treatment is unavailable. May fit current staffed-site capacity if operation/maintenance is supportable. Storage covers a finite deficit; it does not create water or repair inadequate seasonal production. Usable volume, initial fill, water quality/turnover, pumping and delivery must remain adequate. Long or repeated outages can exhaust it; refill before the next outage matters. A tank at a third location is not assumed unattended without review. Outage and road-closure durations; seasonal demand trace; usable reserve and pressure/power; refill headroom; water-quality management and maintenance burden; siting/access
C-04 Hybrid: storage plus maintenance isolation/operational changes Schedule planned work when feasible, isolate maintainable plant sections and use a reserve for residual downtime. Could remove the particular maintenance interruption without a full replacement. Scheduling alone cannot protect against unplanned failure or storm overlap. Isolation depends on existing topology and serviceability. Storage remains finite and common distribution dependencies remain. Maintenance work breakdown, isolation survey, restoration times with/without road access, operable remaining production and reserve needs

Retaining the current arrangement is a useful cost/reference case, but it retains the reported interruption problem. Trucked emergency water cannot be presumed an effective substitute while access roads are closed. Remote control does not itself solve physical maintenance or resupply.

First investigation and the question that can reverse the direction

The most consequential question is: during the longest credible treatment interruption, including storm-delayed restoration at seasonal demand, can maintainable clean-water storage cover the net service deficit until treatment recovers and reserves can be replenished?

If yes, C-03 or C-04 may directly address the failure with a supportable operating arrangement. If no—because the outage is too long, storage cannot be kept usable/delivered, refilling is insufficient, or production itself is inadequate—remaining treatment capacity during maintenance becomes central. C-02 or independently maintainable central trains then deserve priority. This is a conditional recommendation, not a claim that storage is already cheaper or sufficient.

Start with the existing system because it can reveal that distinction at low commitment:

  1. Operations and maintenance: reconstruct each service interruption from maintenance/failure start to restored customer service, including mobilization, road access, repair, restart and refill. Identify which tasks actually force a whole-plant stop and which could be isolated. Include unplanned failures; do not assume their durations equal scheduled work.
  2. Demand and delivery: collect seasonal demand time series, critical-user service needs, current usable storage and start-of-outage fill, treatment output/headroom, distribution constraints and outages. Use consistent time windows; annual average demand can hide the seasonal limiting case.
  3. Joint scenarios: compare normal maintenance, peak-demand maintenance, storm without access, and a plausible overlap. Establish scenario credibility with local records and operators rather than assigning invented probabilities. Inspect power, source, chemicals, pumping and communications as shared dependencies.
  4. Feasibility screen: check both staffing locations and total operating/maintenance workload, water-quality management, delivery continuity and recovery for each concept before a cost ranking. Obtain comparable acquisition, energy, chemicals, staffing, replacement, reserve upkeep, logistics and interruption-cost estimates only for concepts that can meet the outcome.

A transparent water-balance check can use dV/dt = Q_available − D − L, where V is usable clean-water reserve, D is time-varying service demand and L is relevant distribution/storage loss. Across each scenario, reserve must remain above the agreed operational minimum; restoration must provide enough spare output to recover it. Integrating the net deficit gives a preliminary required buffer. This is an unpopulated analysis plan: no volumes or sizing result can be calculated from the supplied facts. Hydraulic delivery and water quality require their own checks; a positive volume balance alone is insufficient.

Decision and measures

Authorize a bounded outage/demand/maintainability study and keep C-02–C-04 open. Do not authorize a plant size solely from unit production cost. The first decision is whether the problem is primarily a bridgeable interruption, insufficient remaining treatment capacity, inadequate overall seasonal production, or a combination.

Compare concepts using customer interruption frequency and duration, people/critical users affected, unmet service volume, water-quality conformance under the adopted local basis, coverage through the agreed no-access interval, time to restore reserve, two-location staffing feasibility, and lifecycle cost per unit of compliant water actually delivered. Set targets and trade weights with the sponsor and operators after establishing the evidence. A hard continuity or staffing failure cannot be averaged away by a favorable cost score.

No performance, cost, reliability or staffing estimates have been invented, and no simulation or field test was executed.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-09/request.md

An isolated district needs reliable drinking-water service. Current service is interrupted when the one treatment plant needs maintenance. Candidate proposals are a larger central plant, smaller distributed treatment units, or additional clean-water storage. Demand varies seasonally. Operators can staff only two locations; access roads close during storms. The sponsor prefers the largest plant because its unit production cost is lowest. Compare useful concepts and explain what you would investigate first. Preserve the sponsor's outcome, distinguish hard constraints from preferences, and identify the question most likely to change your recommendation. Do not make up performance, cost or staffing data.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-10/outputs/output.md

The reported low-light miss remains unresolved. Classifying every miss as a random camera hardware fault is unsupported, and two identical cameras with shared optical and power dependencies do not establish a sufficient mitigation. The daylight demonstration supports only the conditions actually exercised.

ID / reasoning under review Assessment Evidence that would distinguish the alternatives
AU-01: healthy self-diagnostics, missed dark clothing “Healthy” reports the diagnostic's own checks; it does not establish perception adequacy or exclude undetected malfunction. A correctly operating sensor/algorithm may be insufficient for low contrast or lighting. Systematic design, calibration or integration errors and random hardware faults remain separate candidates. Raw images and sensor metadata, exposure/gain, diagnostic coverage and raw status, calibration/configuration, perception outputs and timestamps, known-good comparison under the same scene, and reproducibility across units.
AU-02: all misses are random hardware faults The causal classification cannot be inferred from the missed detection. Low illumination/dark clothing can be a triggering environment for an intended-function limitation; the hazardous event is the resulting vehicle/pedestrian interaction. A malfunction can cause similar behavior. Contrast and illumination sweep with stable hardware/configuration; controlled fault injection separately; review intended behavior and specification limits. Do not use a guessed random failure rate to represent an algorithmic limitation.
AU-03: second identical camera solves the issue Identical sensing and processing may share the same low-light limitation. The windscreen can impose shared attenuation, dirt, fog, water, glare or obstruction. The common converter can disable or disturb both channels. Other shared software, compute, network, clocks, calibration and mounting dependencies need examination. Joint-failure observations, resource/fault-path diagram, independence argument, common-supply tests, windshield degradation tests, and analysis of whether fusion preserves or suppresses useful disagreement. Do not multiply single-camera miss rates as if independence were established.
AU-04: daylight pass closes the problem The known trigger was not exercised. A pass without configuration, stimulus and independent outcome data is also only a reported result. Reproduce the low-light condition and boundaries; retain the daylight case as a control. Include adverse outcomes, inconclusive runs and known limitations.

The standards distinction supports separate causal work: ISO 21448:2022's public scope includes functional/performance insufficiencies and foreseeable misuse, while excluding faults addressed by ISO 26262. ISO 26262-1:2018's public scope addresses malfunctioning behavior of safety-related E/E systems. These are complementary investigations, not labels assigned from diagnostic status. ISO 21448:2022, public abstract, ISO 26262-1:2018, public abstract.

The next evidence package should contain:

  1. Item and responsibility baseline. State the assistance function, intended operating conditions and boundaries, vehicle speed/environment assumptions, sensing-to-action chain, activation/deactivation rules, and who controls warning, braking and steering. Specify the driver's actual monitoring/task responsibilities and what the system promises; no automation level or handover capability was supplied. Identify who can change the operating envelope and who can accept residual risk under the program basis.
  2. Reproducible incident record. Freeze vehicle, cameras, windscreen, software/model versions, calibration and power configuration. Retain synchronized raw sensing, diagnostic status, detection/tracking and confidence, decisions, warnings, brake/steer commands and actual motion. Measure scene illumination/contrast, pedestrian trajectory, distance, speed, occlusion and ground truth independently of the camera under test. Establish whether “miss” means no detection, late detection, dropped track or no protective action.
  3. Scenario and hypothesis matrix. Pair daylight/low-light runs, dark/light targets and contrasting backgrounds; then probe lighting-transition, headlamp/glare, wet/fogged/dirty windscreen, crossing speed/occlusion and distance boundaries. Use safe surrogate targets in a controlled facility. Choose combinations from the incident mechanism and intended envelope, rather than a nominal average success percentage. Include false-positive interventions as well as misses. Record which factors are controlled and where interactions are deliberately combined.
  4. Separate malfunction and dependency evidence. Characterize the diagnostic's detectable fault set and detection/reaction timing using representative injected faults. Examine degraded or intermittent common converter output, camera loss/stale frames, shared compute overload and calibration errors where applicable. Include simultaneous and latent dependencies; injection coverage alone cannot prove the absence of other faults.
  5. Mitigation comparison. Compare current and dual-camera configurations against the same challenging scenarios and independent oracle. Assess proposals such as a changed optical/perception design, appropriately different sensing, an enforceable operating restriction or revised system behavior. None is accepted in advance: diversity needs evidence, and an operating restriction needs a way to recognize and handle the boundary. Evaluate added fusion delay, false alarms, maintenance and new failure paths.
  6. Predeclared outcome and responsibility checks. Derive the required detection range, latency and intervention/warning timing from the actual vehicle response and scenario; values remain unresolved. Measure sensor-to-physical-response timing, collision/clearance outcome, misses and false positives by condition, with sample size and uncertainty rationale. Assess whether a driver can understand the indication and respond within the available time and visibility. A warning does not transfer responsibility automatically or create time the driver lacks.

The engineering/safety owners should reconcile this evidence into the item and hazard analyses, proposed functional changes and a justified validation envelope. Confirm applicable standards editions, vehicle regulations, hazard assessment and decision authority before assigning an ASIL, crediting decomposition, selecting acceptance thresholds or recording accepted risk. Full licensed ISO clauses were not read; the public publisher abstracts were accessed on 2026-11-13 and support scope only.

No new test was executed. The low-light miss, healthy diagnostic report and daylight pass are supplied team reports, not independently inspected evidence. All next-package activities are proposed. Six cases shared one participant context; this was not an isolated per-case run.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-10/request.md

A driver-assistance team reports that a camera misses dark clothing in a low-light crossing scenario although its self-diagnostics report healthy. They propose classifying all missed detections as random camera hardware faults and solving them with a second identical camera behind the same windscreen, powered by the same converter. A demonstration passed in daylight. Review the reasoning and propose the next evidence package. Distinguish intended behavior limitations, malfunctions, environment, dependencies and driver/system responsibilities. Do not assign assurance classes or claim risk acceptance without the program basis.
