This proposed operating concept preserves the center's priority-approval role and each supply organization's authority over its own resources. It is a draft for agreement and exercise, not an existing agreement or authorization to dispatch.

The supplied facts are: a joint coordination center, three independently managed teams, delivery of approved medical supplies after a flood, potentially six hours without communications, limited vehicle capacity and different stock records. No delegation, priority expiry rule, dispute procedure or shared inventory authority was supplied. The concept therefore distinguishes what is known from arrangements the participants still need to accept.

Actor Established boundary Proposed operational arrangement requiring agreement
Coordination center Approves priorities. Issues versioned approved demand/priority records, reconciles unmet demand and proposes allocations. Changes to priorities remain attributable to the center. Approval of a priority does not itself compel another organization's resource commitment.
Teams A, B and C Independently managed; each has limited capacity and its own stock records. Each confirms available stock, vehicles, staff, route feasibility and supply handling capability; accepts, partially accepts or declines a proposed task with reasons. Each retains control of its own dispatch and resource records.
Receiving site / authorized recipient Delivery requires a destination and receipt; their identity and authority are not supplied. Confirm a recipient and delivery acknowledgement method before dispatch; record delivered quantity and exceptions. Clinical need/approval roles must be identified rather than assigned to drivers.
Each organization's designated decision-maker No shared superior or dispute arbiter is established. Nominate contacts and alternates for resource, supply-quality and priority disputes; approve outage delegation and restoration rules within their actual authority.

The operational boundary includes demand/priorities, offer/commitment, load/dispatch, delivery acknowledgement and reconciliation. It depends on external routes, destination accessibility, supply approval and each organization's logistics systems. It does not authorize new supplies, clinical decisions, commandeering resources, surveillance or weapons tasks.

During connected operation, the center issues an identified priority version. Teams respond with feasible commitments. A proposed shared record carries task ID, destination/recipient, approved supply identifier, quantity and unit, priority version and author, issue time/time basis, validity conditions, assigned/accepting team, stock reservation and delivery status. Local item codes map to this exchange vocabulary while preserving original codes and provenance. Different units, packaging or uncertain quantities are discrepancies to resolve, not numbers to merge silently. The accepting team checks capacity and handling constraints before committing; partial fulfillment returns an explicit unmet balance to the center.

Before an outage, participants need an agreed offline operating envelope: which already accepted tasks may continue, whether local substitutions or reprioritization are permitted, what supply/route changes require renewed approval, and what makes a priority stale. The possible six-hour outage is a resilience scenario, not an automatic six-hour validity period. If validity cannot be established or a changed condition invalidates a task, this draft proposes holding the affected new commitment and recording unmet need until authority is restored. Any emergency exception must come from an identified existing policy or an expressly approved delegation; none is invented here. Safe custody and actions already in progress remain subject to the responsible organization's actual procedures.

SCN-01 is one proposed degraded-operation exercise. Its extra events are synthetic injects, not facts about an actual flood response.

Step / state Action, observation and exchange Authority and exit condition
1. Connected, before loss Center releases priority version P1; A, B and C confirm their accepted tasks, stock reservations and remaining capacity. Exercise controllers retain the agreed starting snapshot and participant acknowledgements. Center approves P1; each team commits its own resources. If no offline authority/validity rules have been agreed, the exercise records that gap rather than assuming them.
2. Communications unavailable At exercise time T0, links become unavailable for a scheduled six-hour interval. Actors detect loss using an agreed timeout and record the last confirmed exchange; they attempt only approved alternative channels. A missing acknowledgement is not consent. Detection timeout and alternative-channel ownership are open agreement items.
3. Local degraded operation Teams continue only tasks within their actual approved commitments and any agreed offline envelope, with local dispatch/delivery journals. Center marks remote status uncertain and records new priorities without pretending they were received. No team acts as the center or commits another team's vehicles. A local record identifies author, event time and task ID, and distinguishes planned, dispatched and delivered.
4. Stock/route inject Team A finds fewer usable units than its record; B encounters a blocked route; C receives a locally reported urgent request. They record feasibility changes, delivery balances and any limits on continued work. A and B use their own valid safety/resource authority; changes requiring priority approval wait. C cannot treat an unconfirmed report as a new approved priority. Proposed emergency escalation is exercised only if explicitly authorized beforehand.
5. Staleness boundary A controller injects an expired/conditional P1 task or a known destination change while the center's P2 update is unreachable. Teams expose the version and age of the information they are using. Apply the agreed expiry/condition rule. Without one, the permitted action is unresolved; this draft proposes a hold on the affected new commitment and escalation, not invented authority to select priorities. Unaffected valid commitments need their own disposition.
6. Link restored, reconciliation At T0 + 6 hours in this exercise, exchange priority versions, commitments, dispatch/delivery receipts, remaining physical stock and unserved demand. Detect delayed/duplicate messages; preserve both conflicting entries with provenance. A restored link does not authorize automatic replay or immediate normal dispatch. The center reconciles priority intent; each organization confirms its actual resources and actions.
7. Disagreement and resumption Suppose P2 assigns a task another team already completed and stock balances disagree. Confirm receipt/delivery evidence, release or correct affected reservations through the owning organization, and obtain a revised priority/commitment acknowledgement. Center resolves its priority decision; stock owners resolve stock facts; disputed supply quality needs its designated authority. If factual/authority disagreement persists, escalate to the nominated parties and hold the affected allocation. No unilateral joint arbiter is assumed. Resume each reconciled task only after the relevant approvals and team acceptance.

The exercise evidence package needs the actual authority/delegation records; roster and alternates; priority/validity and dispute rules; common item/unit mappings; vehicle and handling constraints; starting stock/commitments; scenario/inject schedule; proposed stop conditions; and participant-approved expected actions. Controllers should retain timed messages, acknowledgements, local journals, delivery receipts, discrepancy decisions and final balances. Compare approved versus committed/dispatched/delivered quantities, duplicate tasks, authorization/version errors, unmet demand, detection/reconciliation time and staff workload. Set acceptable limits with the participants before claiming success; no target values were supplied.

A tabletop can establish whether the organizations interpret the agreement consistently. A later communications-loss drill and representative logistics exercise can assess recording, capacity and handover behavior. Neither a draft nor a successful tabletop demonstrates actual flood delivery performance. Final conditions are either reconciled commitments with explicitly approved resumption, or an identified unresolved allocation with custody, owner and escalation recorded.

Evidence status: all arrangements and exercise activities above are proposed; no agreement, dispatch, exercise or test has occurred. No external policy or military acquisition basis was imported. Six cases shared one participant context, so this was not a separately isolated exercise run.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-11/request.md

A humanitarian logistics operation uses a joint coordination center and three independently managed supply teams. The mission is to deliver approved medical supplies after a flood. Communications may be unavailable for six hours. The center approves priorities; local teams have limited vehicle capacity and different stock records. Draft an operating concept and one degraded-operation scenario that preserves authority, acknowledges each organization's autonomy, and defines the evidence needed to exercise the arrangement. Do not add weapons or surveillance tasks. Identify how stale priorities and restoration disagreements are resolved without inventing an agreement.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-12/outputs/output.md

Flood-permit service — recommendation to the director

The online application has reduced applicant effort from 40 minutes to 10 minutes. That is a useful improvement, but the service still takes 30 days to reach approval and urgent work is delayed. The next decision should target the time between submission and a usable decision. A chatbot may help applicants understand the process; the supplied facts do not show that it will increase engineering-review capacity, retrieve land records sooner or make outside inspections available.

The service crosses several queues and organizations:

Application → completeness/triage → engineering review, land records and inspection dependencies → authorized decision → applicant notification

That is a provisional map, not a claim that all reviews run in parallel or in that order. Map the actual dependencies. The shared bottlenecks may involve insufficient capacity, work waiting for another input, repeated corrections, scheduling or priority rules. We know the bottlenecks are shared; we do not yet know which mechanism accounts for most delay. Making intake easier could increase arrivals into the same queues, and automating questions could free reviewers' time, but neither effect is established by the supplied information.

Use three connected boundaries. The applicant boundary begins when someone seeks permission and ends with a clear decision they can act on, including requests for correction, refusal and accessibility needs. The operating boundary includes intake, triage, engineering, records, inspections, handoffs, rework and decision authority. The resource boundary includes the other city services and organizations competing for those same reviewers, records staff and inspectors. A faster permit queue that simply delays their other obligations is not an established system improvement. Outside inspection providers may be beyond the director's direct control; their commitments and escalation contacts still belong in the service design.

Measure the service before choosing the automation:

Measure What to observe and why
End-to-end elapsed time First submission to communicated decision, separating ordinary and urgent cases; report the distribution and oldest open cases, not only an average. Establish what the reported 30 days actually measures.
Waiting versus active work Time entering each queue, work start/finish, missing-input waits and handoff delays. These distinguish a capacity shortage from coordination or rework.
Flow and backlog Arrivals, completed decisions and open work by stage and case type, including age. Track shared resource demand from other services, not just permit staffing.
Completeness and rework Missing/incorrect submissions, correction cycles and reasons, where defects originate, and who must redo the work. These reveal whether better guidance would remove material delay.
Urgent service Time to triage, time to decision, cases missing an agreed urgent target, and the consequence of delay. The authorized owner must define urgency and targets; none are supplied.
Quality and burden Review errors, reopened decisions, applicant/staff effort and effects on routine cases and other services. Faster decisions are useful only if the required review remains effective.

Trace a recent cohort across all involved teams using case events, then inspect representative urgent, delayed, returned and still-open cases with the people doing the work. Include unfinished applications so completed cases do not hide the longest waits. Use common timestamp definitions and identify missing records; a blank timestamp does not mean zero waiting. The event trace and staff walkthrough should explain the mechanism before anyone promises a reduction in the 30-day figure.

My conditional recommendation is to authorize a bounded service-flow review and a jointly owned urgent-work pilot before a general chatbot build. Assign one owner to reconcile the queues and decision rights with engineering, land records and inspection providers. If urgent cases are waiting because they enter ordinary queues without a visible owner or scheduling rule, pilot an explicit triage/escalation path and coordinated review slots. Set the authority, entry criteria and fairness rules first; expedited coordination does not waive required review. Observe urgent elapsed time alongside routine-case aging, other-service delays, rework and decision quality.

If the trace instead shows that incomplete applications or repetitive status questions consume substantial bottleneck staff time, compare improved forms, clear guidance and visible case status with a narrow chatbot pilot. Judge any chatbot by reduced rework or recovered review time and resulting service delay, plus answer accuracy and escalation failures—not conversation count. It should not imply approval, invent a case status or make the authorized permit decision. If delay is principally a shortage of qualified review or inspection capacity, the director needs a staffing, scheduling or interagency service decision; adding another intake interface would leave that constraint in place.

The questions most likely to change this recommendation are: Where do urgent cases spend their waiting time, and who can change that queue's allocation? What proportion of reviewer effort is caused by avoidable applicant questions or corrections? Which sequencing and review steps are fixed obligations, and which are local working practices? These can be answered while developing the flow pilot. No full requirements document, new legal interpretation or quantified chatbot benefit is justified by the current facts.

Basis: supplied HO-12 request. This is a conditional recommendation; no service data analysis or pilot was executed.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-12/request.md

A city digitized its flood-permit service. Online applications now take applicants 10 minutes instead of 40, but approval still takes 30 days and urgent work is delayed. Engineering review, land records and outside inspections are shared bottlenecks. The director asks for an AI chatbot. Explain the system problem to the director, propose useful boundaries and measures, and recommend the next decision. You may ask targeted questions, but produce a useful conditional recommendation from the given facts. A full requirements document is not requested.

Controller architecture, revision A

COMP-1 input interface forwards the sensor input to COMP-2 detector. COMP-2 sends the alarm command to COMP-3 local annunciator over IFC-2. IFC-1 is the sensor-to-detector interface. IFC-3 carries operator stop/resume intent to COMP-2.

Current worst-case path allocation, assumed serial and nonoverlapping:

Stage Maximum
COMP-1 interface processing 150 ms
COMP-2 detection 80 ms
COMP-3 warning assertion 30 ms

The recorded state diagram says: OPERATING -> INHIBITED on local stop or missing data; INHIBITED -> OPERATING when stop is released and valid data returns. No separate resume guard is shown.

Controller architecture, revision B — proposed revision

Status: coherent document proposal responding to CR-1, with unresolved implementation selection and verification. IDs and component/interface responsibilities are preserved. No physical timing measurements for revision B are available.

COMP-1 input interface forwards the sensor input to COMP-2 detector. COMP-2 sends the alarm command to COMP-3 local annunciator over IFC-2. IFC-1 is the sensor-to-detector interface. IFC-3 carries operator stop/resume intent to COMP-2.

REQ-7 alert path and budget

The initiating event remains the valid pressure input first meeting the high-pressure condition during operation. The end event remains assertion of the local high-pressure warning. CR-1 changes neither event, input validity nor operating conditions. Do not restart the timing clock at COMP-2's detection output or stop it at the command on IFC-2; either would omit part of the defined claim. The exact observation points must be tied to the existing project-controlled input contract and warning interface, which are not supplied in detail.

The inherited allocation remains visible as an unresolved budget, not a claim of compliance:

Stage Inherited maximum Responsibility
COMP-1 interface processing 150 ms Input acceptance and forwarding through IFC-1
COMP-2 detection 80 ms Determine high-pressure condition; issue warning command
COMP-3 warning assertion 30 ms Assert the local warning received through IFC-2
Serial, nonoverlapping total 260 ms REQ-7 end-to-end path
REQ-7 revision-B limit 200 ms Approved by CR-1
Allocated margin before any omitted delay −60 ms Unresolved

These maxima are allocations under the stated serial/nonoverlapping assumption. They do not demonstrate an actual 260 ms observation or simultaneous achievement of all maxima. They cannot support the new guarantee as written. Identify any sensing/queue/transport/scheduling/assertion delays not already included; call their justified total H. Do not double-count delays already within stage bounds or assume H is zero.

The team has selected no implementation change. Engineering options, all unselected:

  • Reduce serial work/latency. With COMP-2 and COMP-3 unchanged, COMP-1 would need a justified bound ≤ 90 ms − H. Alternatively redistribute reductions among stages so I + D + A + H ≤ 200 ms, with explicit uncertainty/margin treatment. Inspect queueing and scheduling as well as processing time. No feasible reduction is yet demonstrated.
  • Change the critical path or introduce valid overlap. Only if input causality permits it could parallel interface/detection yield max(150,80) + 30 = 180 ms, leaving at most 20 ms for all other terms. The present forwarding relationship implies a dependency; declaring concurrency without a new valid-input mechanism is not a repair. A revised local alert path must preserve the original trigger and actual local warning endpoint.
  • Replace/repartition a limiting function or component. Obtain measurements and supplier/implementation bounds first; consider interference with motion inhibition and other tasks. No new hardware, priority scheme or supplier capability is assumed.
  • If the 200 ms requirement proves infeasible: take an explicit trade back to the change authority. This package keeps the approved 200 ms criterion; it does not restore 500 ms or treat a waiver as verification.

IFC-1 needs the existing pressure units, threshold/validity semantics, rate, delay and error behavior recorded by reference to controlled project parameters. IFC-2 needs command semantics, transfer delay and correspondence to locally observable warning assertion. IFC-3 needs distinct local stop state and explicit local resume intent, with ordering/validity semantics. Those details are not supplied and remain open; their absence is not permission to alter them.

REQ-8 and N-02 recovery correction

The revision-A state record allowed INHIBITED → OPERATING when stop was released and valid data returned, with no resume guard. That contradicts both the unchanged REQ-8 and authoritative N-02. It is replaced in this proposed architecture as follows. Names OPERATING and INHIBITED are retained; in this transition description they describe motion permission. They do not redefine REQ-7's operating conditions or imply warning suppression during a motion inhibit.

Current state and event Guard/action Next state and observable condition
OPERATING; local stop asserted COMP-2 commands motion inhibition and latches the inhibit cause; active stop dominates any simultaneous resume INHIBITED; motion remains inhibited and local stop latch is visible
OPERATING; missing data Preserve the inherited transition to inhibition and record the data-loss cause; missing-data detection parameters remain the existing project contract INHIBITED; motion inhibited; cause/status visible
INHIBITED; local stop released Update current input state; retain the latch and motion inhibit INHIBITED; release is not a resume event
INHIBITED; sensor data or network returns Update health/connectivity state; retain the latch and motion inhibit INHIBITED; restoring service is not authorization, and the stop latch remains visible
INHIBITED; explicit local resume intent through IFC-3 Accept only with stop released and valid data present; if another applicable inhibit remains, retain inhibition. The explicit local action is necessary, not implied by health restoration OPERATING only when eligible; otherwise remain INHIBITED with reason visible
Any state; stop assertion and resume arrive together Stop takes precedence INHIBITED

Distinguish active causes from the retained recovery latch: a cause may be gone while deliberate resumption is still required. An eligible resume permits the existing operating logic to act; it is not itself an invented unconditional motion command. Treat replayed network commands or a resume request made while ineligible as incapable of clearing a later latch; this is a proposed implementation rule to enforce explicit local recovery, to be checked in VER-8. Detailed edge/level handling and reset behavior require the interface owner.

The source operator note is preserved verbatim in source.md. Visibility must survive communications restoration and remain meaningful across a shift handoff. The source has not identified an indicator component or display interface for this latch. Allocate responsibility for reporting the latch to COMP-2, and leave the display binding open for design. COMP-3 is the high-pressure annunciator; do not silently reinterpret it as a motion actuator or a stop-latch display.

COMP-2's motion-inhibit output and the physical motion recipient are also not specified in the supplied architecture. Their binding and observable effect must be established before claiming REQ-8 implementation compliance. A controller flag alone is not evidence that motion is inhibited.

The 460 ms record is 200 ms above the 260 ms allocation sum, but this difference cannot be attributed to a specific overhead without comparable setup/timestamp evidence. Resolve it before trusting a new timing budget. No claim that all old functions failed follows from that discrepancy.

VER-7 — changed timing requirement

Addresses: REQ-7/N-01 and CR-1. Methods: end-to-end timing analysis plus instrumented integration test on the selected revision-B implementation. Proposed owner/reviewer: timing test lead and requirement/architecture reviewer; actual assignments pending.

Before execution, freeze the revised requirement and design, COMP-1–COMP-3 hardware/software/configuration identities, IFC-1/IFC-2 implementation, project-controlled pressure threshold/validity contract, operating conditions, clock source, test harness and instruments. Retrieve the unchanged threshold and validity values; do not invent replacements or alter the trigger to obtain a favorable result. Document loads, scheduling, communication behavior and relevant environmental conditions. Choose an instrument whose uncertainty is suitable for the 200 ms decision and record calibration/timestamp alignment.

The procedure will:

  1. Establish equipment operation under the unchanged project definition; apply a valid pressure input below the controlled high-pressure threshold and confirm initial warning state.
  2. Apply an input that first meets the high-pressure condition. Record t0 at that defined valid-input event; map the observation point to the existing input contract. Do not move t0 downstream to COMP-2 detection. Capture intermediate stage times without replacing the end-to-end measurement.
  3. Record t1 when the local high-pressure warning is actually asserted at COMP-3. A software command, bus message or acknowledgment alone is not the end event. Match the sensing method to the annunciator's physical form, which is not supplied.
  4. Measure Δt = t1 − t0 and uncertainty. Repeat over the specified load/environment envelope, queue/scheduling and sample-phase boundaries, and relevant communication conditions. Include cases around the project-controlled pressure/validity boundaries; invalid input must not be relabeled valid to simplify measurement. Confirm repeated qualifying events and any reset sequence follow the existing warning semantics.
  5. Use worst-case analysis to justify coverage beyond observed trials and reconcile any discrepancy with stage budgets. Determine the number and selection of trials from the actual timing model; no sample count, percentile or reliability claim is invented.
  6. Regress REQ-8 where timing changes affect COMP-2 scheduling/resources or IFC-3. Exercise warning behavior during motion inhibition whenever that lies within the unchanged operating conditions; do not silently redefine those conditions.

Acceptance: the defined end-to-end warning assertion is within 200 ms for the required operating conditions. Use a documented uncertainty rule; a conservative measured pass requires Δt + U ≤ 200 ms for the applicable nonnegative uncertainty bound U, plus an adequate worst-case coverage argument. A result above 200 ms is a failure for its executed configuration. A result whose uncertainty straddles the limit, whose stimulus validity is unknown or whose endpoint was not observed is inconclusive, not a pass. The existing 260 ms allocation must be repaired or replaced with a justified tighter bound before a general timing guarantee is supportable.

Record raw timestamps/observations, exact baseline hashes, setup and instrument identity, environment/load, procedure revision, deviations, uncertainty, maximum measured latency and analysis assumptions. Preserve failures. Planned output is evidence/revision-b-results.json plus referenced raw data; neither exists now. An authorized reviewer must assess applicability and any residual gaps before a separate acceptance decision.

VER-8 — stop, recovery, motion and retained visibility

Addresses: unchanged REQ-8, N-02 and the protected operator note. Methods: implementation inspection and controlled integration test with observable motion inhibition, local stop/resume events, communications and sensor validity. Proposed owner/reviewer: controls test lead and operator representative.

Resolve the motion-output/recipient and latch-display bindings before execution. Record their configuration and instrument both logical permission and actual motion response. No stop-time bound is supplied in REQ-8; do not invent a deadline or treat a state bit as physical-motion evidence.

Case Stimulus Required observation/criterion
VER-8.a While motion is requested, assert local stop Motion is inhibited while stop is asserted; retained latch is visible. Local stop dominates a competing resume/motion request.
VER-8.b Release stop with valid data available; provide no resume Motion remains inhibited after release. No automatic transition to OPERATING.
VER-8.c Assert stop, lose data/network, then release stop; restore data/network without resume Inhibit persists through restoration, stop latch remains visible and no motion is authorized. A shift-handoff walkthrough can establish whether the display communicates that retained state.
VER-8.d Restore data before releasing stop, and then release without resume Same retained inhibition and visibility; event order must not create automatic recovery.
VER-8.e Exercise inherited missing-data inhibit without a manual-stop event; restore data without resume N-02 recovery rule holds: data restoration alone does not authorize motion.
VER-8.f Request explicit local resume while stop remains asserted or data remains invalid Remain inhibited. Later release/restoration must not treat that rejected request as a fresh authorization. Test a held/replayed request under the agreed IFC-3 semantics.
VER-8.g With stop released, valid data and all other applicable guards satisfied, perform explicit local resume The latch clears only via the eligible action; motion permission changes consistently with the operating logic. Observe subsequent commanded motion to avoid a test that passes merely because no motion was requested.
VER-8.h Reconnect with queued remote commands; apply simultaneous stop/resume Reconnection and queued remote commands do not substitute for local resume; stop remains dominant. Record ordering and operator-visible outcome.

The old visibility intent remains a portion of this plan, but visibility alone cannot verify REQ-8. Separate raw motion, latch, interface and display observations; give every case an executed outcome only after it runs. Operator interpretation is a validation observation distinct from controller requirement verification.

Current coverage: REQ-7 and REQ-8 have planned activities; zero revision-B executions/results are supplied or produced, and neither requirement is verified or accepted for B by this package.

The integration lead should retain the spreadsheet unit labels as a documentation improvement and keep the lesson open pending implementation and operational evidence.

Source-reported facts. NASA's Phase I report says the interface specification already required impulse in newton-seconds, while the ground software supplied pound-force-seconds. The receiving navigation software interpreted those values as metric. The report also identifies weaknesses in communication, transition from development to operations, and ground-software verification. I accessed the report's extracted text, including printed pages 6–7 and 16; I have not reviewed every page. Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I, 10 November 1999.

Causal interpretation. A written unit requirement existed, but the implemented producer and consumer did not satisfy a shared physical meaning. Communication and lifecycle weaknesses helped that discrepancy survive. Adding another label cannot establish that the numbers obey the label, that transformations preserve meaning, or that an operational anomaly reaches someone able to resolve it. This is my interpretation of the transfer lesson, rather than an additional historical finding.

Proposed controls and distinguishing observations. Assign the integration lead responsibility for the complete exchange, with named producer, consumer, and operations owners. Agree the following evidence before closing the action:

Claim Proposed control Observation needed
Interface is documented Controlled definition of quantity, units, frame/sign, timing, validity, format/version, error behavior, and both owners Reviewed specification and matching spreadsheet definitions. This establishes agreement only.
Producer and consumer implement that agreement Check conversion at the actual producer–consumer boundary; use explicit units and reject missing or unsupported unit information Known nonzero physical inputs traverse the production-representative export, transfer, import, and calculation chain. Intermediate values and final physical results match an independently calculated reference within agreed tolerances. Record exact software and data versions.
A misleading value will be detected Exercise missing units, wrong units, wrong scaling with a correct-looking label, stale data, and conversion applied twice Tests distinguish valid conversion from each injected error and show the specified rejection or alarm. A type check alone cannot detect a number incorrectly labeled with an allowed unit.
Operations can recognize and resolve a discrepancy Independent result cross-check, mission-derived discrepancy thresholds, formal anomaly ownership, escalation, and development-to-operations handover A rehearsal with the intended operators introduces a disagreement. Records show detection, acknowledgment, accountable investigation, disposition, and communication before the relevant decision deadline.

Use reference calculations that do not reuse the production conversion routine. Agree tolerances, deadlines, and the consequence of unresolved disagreement from this mission's needs; none are supplied here. Preserve failed and inconclusive results. Recheck applicability after interface or software changes.

Closure requires the integration lead to review those results against the intended configuration and operations, with residual gaps explicitly assigned. No modern implementation, test result, or approval was supplied; these controls are proposals, and no test has been executed here.

The log proves too little: a transport acknowledgment does not establish that an operator saw, accepted, or performed the instruction. An unattended dashboard can receive data successfully while the operational handoff fails.

The historical basis here is the request-supplied statement from RFC 793 (1981), section 2.6. I have not independently retrieved the RFC. The following contract is a proposed application of that distinction.

State or property Evidence that could support it Remaining gap
Transport receipt Transport reports acknowledgment of the relevant bytes Application processing and human attention remain unknown.
Application receipt Recipient application validates and records the identified instruction Receipt does not establish display.
Display Application records that the current instruction was rendered on the intended operator's display Rendering does not establish that someone looked at it or understood it.
Operator acknowledgment Identified person deliberately responds to that instruction, distinguishing “seen,” “accepted,” and “declined” A response alone does not establish authority or action.
Authority Identity and current role/delegation permit this person to accept and act on this target; operational responsibility is assigned Authorization does not establish execution.
Performed action Target-state observation shows the specified shutdown outcome, with time and configuration A button press or command acceptance alone is insufficient.

The minimum contract should give each instruction a unique ID, target, content/revision, authorized issuer, deadline/expiry, and explicit acceptance meaning. Correlate receipt, display, acknowledgment, acceptance/rejection, command, and observed outcome to that ID. Keep failure and unknown states visible. Check current operator authority when accepting and executing; record who held it. Retries must not create duplicate action, and expired or superseded instructions must be rejected.

Assign a staffed recipient and an accountable backup. Shift handover must explicitly transfer every outstanding instruction and its state. Set acknowledgment and action deadlines from the system's consequences; the packet gives no defensible numeric values. Unacknowledged work must escalate to an available authorized person through a route that does not depend solely on the unattended display. The system's approved contingency governs timeout behavior; automatic shutdown is not justified by this packet alone.

A proposed verification scenario is to send a uniquely identified shutdown instruction during shift change while the dashboard is unattended. Allow transport and application receipt. Verify that the system retains an unacknowledged state and escalates by the agreed deadline, without logging operator acceptance or completion. Attempt acceptance by an unauthorized person and verify refusal. Transfer responsibility to the incoming authorized operator, record deliberate acceptance, then check the target's shutdown state separately. Repeat a message and present an expired message to check duplicate and expiry handling. Include a command that fails to achieve shutdown: its outcome must remain failed or unknown, never completed on the strength of an ACK.

Retain message-correlated application, identity, handover, escalation, and target-state records with comparable timestamps. These are planned checks, not observed results; no approval or performed shutdown is established by the supplied evidence.

The two “response times” currently measure different intervals. Starting the automatic clock at hazard onset includes time that the human clock omits by starting after recognition and diagnosis. Those labels cannot support a comparison of complete emergency response. The stopping event must also match: issuing a command and bringing the hazard under control are different outcomes.

The request-supplied historical fact from NTSB/AAR-10/03, sections 1.16.3 and 2.3.2, illustrates why decision time matters to simulator conclusions. I have not independently retrieved that report. It does not supply a numerical correction for this new system.

Use a common measurement contract:

Contract item Proposed definition
Main measure Elapsed time from independently timestamped hazard onset, t0, to the same observable controlled state, tS. Define the state and required duration of stability before testing. Measure tS − t0 for both responses.
Supporting events Record detection/recognition, diagnosis/decision, command, and physical action timestamps where observable. Include automatic sensing and decision latency as well as human latency. Identify inferred or unobservable events.
Conditions Match initial plant state, hazard severity, available information, communications, actuation limits, and relevant failures. Represent realistic operator workload, training, staffing, and surprise. Do not give automation direct simulator truth unless the real installation has equivalent information.
Recording quality Use synchronized clocks or a measured alignment, stated sampling resolution, event rules, uncertainty, and exact simulator/system versions. Preserve raw traces and deviations.
Outcome reporting Report timing distributions and scenario conditions together with unsuccessful responses, wrong actions, false activations, and timeouts. Do not discard nonresponses to make the successful cases appear fast.
Decision rule Agree required outcome, deadline, and tolerable failure behavior from the operational safety need before comparing results. No such limits are supplied.

Where task phases overlap, the timestamp trace remains authoritative; summing separately measured averages can misstate total time. Repeated simulator runs should control practice and foreknowledge, for example through varied scenarios and balanced order. Document the simulator's fidelity limits before applying results to operations.

If raw timestamps contain a common onset and outcome, recompute comparable intervals. Otherwise collect new matched runs; relabeling the existing columns cannot restore missing time.

Present data cannot establish which complete response is faster, whether either meets an operational deadline, whether automation should replace an operator, or which option is safer. Speed without correct action and a controlled outcome is inadequate evidence. At most, sufficiently documented existing results describe their own measured subintervals and conditions. This contract is proposed; no new comparison has been executed.

Source: evals/evidence/performance-20261113/task-domain/HO-17/outputs/output.md

Testing every user control independently does not establish complete interface behavior. It can miss dependence on earlier edits, queued commands, timing, operating mode and recovery state. The appropriate next claim is a bounded, stated sequence/state coverage claim supported by independent output observations.

The historical input is only the supplied fact from Leveson and Turner's 1993 Therac-25 investigation: particular editing sequences and timing exposed dangerous state interactions. No further incident detail is inferred, and the historical paper was not retrieved. That observation motivates interaction tests; it does not demonstrate that this teaching prototype has the same mechanism or justify transferring a medical-device class. The prototype has no patient use.

The following is a proposed finite test design, not executed results. Obtain the actual interface/state description, allowable settings, timing/acknowledgement rules and output definition first. Generic placeholders below are P (an output-affecting parameter), M (a mode), and states Editing, Ready, Running, Stopped and Fault/Recovery. These are proposed test abstractions, not asserted device features. Map them to real states/controls; mark an absent feature not applicable with a reason. Freeze build/configuration and use a safe surrogate load or output inhibition appropriate to the prototype.

Agree these candidate invariants before judging tests: the applied configuration matches the explicitly accepted configuration; edits/cancelled or stale commands cannot silently change an active output; start/stop and recovery have documented semantics; incompatible mixed mode/parameter combinations cannot be applied; and output stays within the agreed laboratory envelope. These are review proposals until the team accepts or replaces them with the real requirements. Define measurement tolerances and time limits from the instrument, not from the Therac history.

ID Proposed sequence/state test Discriminating observation / candidate defect
SQ-01 From a fresh initial state, set P1, accept, start, stop. Repeat the same final settings after a different valid prior run. Compare independently measured output and applied configuration; exposes hidden history dependence for identical final selections.
SQ-02 Edit P1→P2→P1, accept, start; compare with direct P1. Perform once with deliberate pauses and once at the fastest supported input rate. Final applied setting and physical output should agree with the accepted P1; tests stale intermediate state and lost updates.
SQ-03 Start from M1/P1; change mode then parameter, and in a paired run change parameter then mode, reaching the same permitted M2/P2. Accept/start. Compare the two runs and mode/parameter consistency; tests order-sensitive partial updates.
SQ-04 Change P1→P2 then cancel; navigate away/back, start using the accepted configuration. Pair with change then accept. Distinguish committed and draft values at the output boundary; tests stale cache or cancelled edits becoming active.
SQ-05 Submit an edit and then Start just before, at and just after the edit-acceptance boundary. Determine which complete configuration is applied and whether Start is refused/queued as specified. No mixed configuration is accepted merely because the display looks correct.
SQ-06 While Running, attempt an edit or mode change; exercise the documented reject, defer or controlled-change path, then stop/restart. Observe active output during and after the attempt; tests confusion between next-run settings and active settings.
SQ-07 Rapid Start→Stop→Start; separately repeat/double-submit Start and Stop at their supported boundary timing. Count physical activations and stop/restart transitions; tests duplicate commands, stale queued actions and non-idempotent handling.
SQ-08 Stop while an edit or start acknowledgement is pending, then wait without a further Start. Observe the complete output path for unintended late activation or resumption; a UI “Stopped” state is not the sole oracle.
SQ-09 If a defined recoverable fault can be safely simulated, introduce it during Editing/Ready and during Running; acknowledge/clear it. Observe inhibited output, retained settings and whether a fresh start authorization is required by the agreed recovery behavior. Fault clearance alone must not be assumed to mean restart.
SQ-10 Safely reset/restart at the commit boundary and during Running; inspect saved configuration and queued command state before any new command. Detect partially persisted settings and stale automatic actuation after reboot. Use a documented reset mechanism and safe load.
SQ-11 If commands cross a separable interface, delay an acknowledgement and replay an older command after a newer stop or configuration change, using an approved test harness. Correlate command/version identity with physical output; tests stale-message rejection and ordering. If no such interface exists, record non-applicability.
SQ-12 Enter a defined invalid/boundary setting after a valid run, attempt acceptance/start, correct it to a valid setting, then start. Include specified minimum/maximum valid values. Verify invalid input handling and recovery without a hybrid of old/new settings; compare output against the valid final setting and declared limits.

This is twelve test families with a finite execution schedule. Use two concrete valid configurations and the defined invalid/boundary values; execute each listed pair/branch. For SQ-05, SQ-07 and SQ-10, schedule exactly three offsets around the relevant measured transition (−Δ, 0, +Δ), where Δ and timing jitter are documented from the test harness. The “at” case is a measured interval with uncertainty, not a claim of perfect simultaneity. Publish the expanded case list and fixed repeat count before execution. These selections target distinguishable failure mechanisms; they do not claim every sequence or schedule is covered.

Observe output with a calibrated external sensor appropriate to what the instrument actually produces—for example, voltage/current into a safe load or a position/force/flow measurement if that is the output. Record measurement range, sampling bandwidth, latency, uncertainty and calibration. Independently capture relevant actuator/interface signals and a timestamped user-action trace. Application logs and display capture help reconstruct state but cannot be their own sole success oracle. A separate observer or acquisition path should use the accepted settings/test specification, rather than simply echoing values computed by the same code under test; assess shared clocks, sensors and processing that could conceal a common error.

For each execution retain test ID, state/configuration, exact ordered actions and measured timing, expected result, physical output trace, UI/log trace, discrepancies, and pass/fail/inconclusive disposition. Compare paired runs against predefined tolerances and maximum transient/latency limits. Where the expected behavior is undecided, mark the case blocked on that requirement rather than counting it as a pass. Stop the laboratory run at agreed safe bounds and preserve anomalous traces before changing the software.

Residual limits include longer histories, untested timing windows, scheduler variability, hidden states, unmodeled faults, physical conditions and biases in the measurement chain. After the finite suite, use observed counterexamples and a reviewed transition model to select further stress, concurrency or state exploration. A clean result would support only these scenarios, configurations and observation limits; it would not prove a complete interface, general safety or clinical suitability.

No prototype, test logs, firmware or instruments were available or exercised. These tests remain proposed. Six cases shared this participant context; historical transfer and test-design reasoning were not performed in a fresh isolated session per case.

Record counts and schema checks are necessary migration checks, but cannot establish that the register describes the installed assets. The review should start with decisions the digital twin will influence and the consequences of a wrong attribute.

The request supplies the historical finding from NTSB/PAR-11/01, section 1.7.2: an incorrect material description propagated into the GIS, while physical investigation found different construction. I have not independently retrieved the report. The review below is a proposed transfer of that lesson, not a finding about this register.

Prioritize attributes that can change operating limits, inspection methods, repair choices, or isolation decisions. Depending on the assets and intended uses, these may include material/grade, seam or construction type, wall thickness, diameter, installation and modification dates, operating status, and location/topology. Asset identity and segment boundaries come first: excellent evidence about the wrong segment does not resolve the decision.

For each important attribute, preserve its original value, units, source document and locator, date, asset association, author or authority where known, transformation history, and uncertainty. Distinguish reported, inferred, directly observed, and unresolved values. A copied field is not independent corroboration. Retain conflicting values and their sources; do not silently replace an unknown with a default or select the newest record without assessing its basis.

Check the complete import for missing and duplicate IDs, keyed value reconciliation, joins and segment splits, units, transformation rules, null/default handling, relationships, and location plausibility. Preserve source snapshots and mapping versions. These checks address information transfer; separately reconcile decision-critical attributes against installation, maintenance, replacement, and suitable physical evidence.

Start with the following small, purposive inspection set. These are selection categories, not existing asset IDs or a statistically representative sample:

Select one record or segment in each category Main inspection question
High-consequence asset with an old, weakly sourced construction description What supports the construction and limit used by the decision?
Asset with conflicting material or seam descriptions Do both sources refer to the same physical item, and which evidence explains the conflict?
Asset recorded as modified or replaced Does the register reflect the installed configuration and modification boundary?
Segment crossing an import join, split, or location boundary Were attributes attached to the correct physical extent?
Routine asset with recent, well-supported records Does a straightforward case preserve its evidence and values through the same transformation?

For each selected item, reconcile documentary lineage first, then plan an authorized, technically suitable physical check where it can discriminate the disputed attribute. Specify the inspection's identification method, measurement limits, competent reviewer, and retained evidence. A visual check alone may not establish grade, thickness, or seam construction. No field inspection is authorized or claimed by this exercise.

Log discrepancies with affected decisions, owners, and resolution evidence. Expand review to records sharing the suspect source or transformation; do not infer the defect rate from this purposive set. Withhold unsupported decision outputs or use an explicitly justified interim basis until the responsible authority resolves them.

A clean import demonstrates that the tested transfer rules preserved and structured source information. It does not establish historical accuracy, present physical condition, fitness of every model calculation, or readiness for unrestricted operational decisions. Accept migration integrity and each intended use on separately stated evidence.

Conditionally proceed with a concept that connects heterogeneous existing services while retaining accountable institutional ownership. Reopen identity, personal-data access, security, and accountability as core design questions before allowing the concept to handle real benefit cases.

The historical basis is the request-supplied account of the 1989 CERN WWW proposal. I have not independently retrieved it. Its priorities arose in that proposal's setting; they do not establish suitable priorities for a public benefits service.

The transferable ideas are useful: provide consistent discovery across different systems; connect to existing information rather than requiring wholesale replacement; use explicit interface meanings; and let responsible institutions maintain their authoritative information. These ideas could reduce duplicate data entry and help applicants navigate fragmented services. Those benefits remain hypotheses to evaluate with applicants and staff.

The assumptions requiring new decisions are consequential:

Question to reopen Why it changes this concept
Who may see which person's information, for what purpose? A reachable link or a connected institution must not automatically confer access to a benefit case. Specify permitted data flows, minimization, retention, and the applicable basis for sharing with accountable owners.
How are identity, delegation, and authority distinguished? Knowing a person's identity does not prove entitlement to another person's records or authority to decide a benefit. Define applicant, representative, caseworker, and institutional permissions, including expiry and revocation.
Which institution owns each fact and decision? Data exchange must preserve provenance, correction routes, and responsibility. Conflicting or stale records need a disposition process; integration must not silently create adjudication authority.
How will people obtain service during exceptions? Account recovery, inability to use digital identity, outages, disputed records, and handovers need staffed routes that preserve the applicant's ability to pursue the service.
Who can reconstruct and challenge an outcome? Record accountable access and decision events, with appropriate protection of those records, and provide review and correction mechanisms.

A candidate boundary is public access to general guidance, with controlled access to personal case work. Keep authorization effective at each agency interface, maintain source provenance, and assign explicit responsibility for decisions. Decentralized ownership and a consistent user experience can coexist, but only if agencies agree those contracts and can support the work.

The service owner can authorize a concept prototype using synthetic cases while owners resolve the data/role matrix, delegation rules, authoritative sources, correction process, and assisted-service model. Before real personal-data use, require evidence from scenarios covering legitimate access, cross-household access denial, representative revocation, conflicting records, agency outage, and shift handover. Evaluate both privacy protection and successful access to the service; a technically secure path that eligible users cannot complete is inadequate.

Proceed to operational use only for the scope whose responsibilities and evidence have been accepted by the appropriate owners. No jurisdiction, legal basis, institutional agreement, usability result, or security test is supplied here, so this is a conditional concept recommendation, not a compliance or deployment finding.

Revised quiz observations, bank 0.2.0

Three new participants answered the same 24 development questions after the bank's choices, ambiguous stems and scoring contracts were independently repaired. All three arms selected 24/24 keyed answers: no packaged skills, task skills, and task-plus-domain skills. The comparison is descriptive.

Independent explanation review rated each arm 94/96 across 48 criteria. The same two partial criteria remained in every arm: allocating responsibility for stale data semantics (SEJ-029) and specifying a concrete way to resolve test-applicability disagreement (SEJ-048). No critical errors or material key disagreement were found. This is a selection ceiling with small reasoning gaps, not evidence that the skills improve performance or that the benchmark discriminates expert systems engineering.

Each arm retains its packet, original answers, usage when supplied, independently bound review, and reviewed score. All three original answers truthfully used the template's model:null value, which the scorer rejected. The same producers created metadata-only corrected copies using the explicit string unknown and an amendment note. Answers, packet bindings, run IDs and original timestamps were unchanged; the raw submissions and old/new hashes are preserved. Future templates now default to unknown.

The exact 0.2.0 source capsule retains the bank, key, catalog, skills and scoring implementation. Reproduce a reviewed score with that version, using a new output path:

python3 evals/archive/benchmark-0.2.0/scripts/benchmark.py score --packet evals/evidence/quiz-0.2.0-20261114/none --answers evals/evidence/quiz-0.2.0-20261114/none/answers-metadata-corrected.json --review evals/evidence/quiz-0.2.0-20261114/none/review.json --output /workspace/mbse-score-reproduction.json

Bank 0.2.1 subsequently aligns three explanations/criteria with their existing choices; all 60 answer selections and all question text remain unchanged. These observations and reviews remain bound to 0.2.0 rather than being relabeled. The independent benchmark review and 0.2.1 addendum record both revisions and their limits.

Participants had instruction-restricted packet access on a shared host with ambient skill descriptions and general guidance. Exact model identity/settings, tokens and costs were unavailable. Each arm is one context, not repeated samples; reviewers are separate agents, not a human expert panel. No native activation, statistical effect, leaderboard position or broad engineering competence is inferred.
