Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning project defines its system-of-interest as the authority's own warning service, excluding supplier infrastructure. A commercial rainfall feed is required, and the authority remains accountable for warnings when that feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. Allocate availability to the supplier contract and verify internal warning logic with timely inputs, assessing each organization separately.
  • B. Include supplier infrastructure inside the implementation boundary and allocate its availability controls to the authority responsible for warnings.
  • C. Model supplier delay as a fixed external parameter so internal design can proceed before delayed-feed response ownership is agreed.
  • D. Keep the supplier external to the chosen boundary; specify its dependency contract and the authority's response to delayed data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which proposed actions establish a defensible decision basis from the supplied facts, without first assuming a cause or a target? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing turnaround, inspection and change-control outcomes, including the operating conditions in which each must be protected.
  • B. Use maintenance ownership of signoff to assign it primary responsibility for delay, then measure the effect of automating its approval step.
  • C. Adopt the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold for the new process, then investigate exceptions when that threshold is missed.
  • D. Trace the timing of late changes, inspection work and decisions across roles to distinguish their contributions to the observed turnaround.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which actions are justified by the supplied lifecycle facts without adding an unprovided policy or disposal requirement? Select all supported options.

  • A. Adopt physical destruction of every retired module as the required disposal method, based on the stated presence of configuration keys.
  • B. Define who will provide compatible replacements and spares if the supplier ends support during the planned fifteen-year service period.
  • C. Define how replacement modules receive and verify the authorized configuration before they are returned to the operating sensor network.
  • D. Define credential retirement and data-removal outcomes for removed modules, then select disposal methods against the applicable requirements and evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Compare failures over equal exposure and use the tighter uncertainty interval to choose between alternatives with similar observed reliability.
  • B. Select the faster-restoring alternative and resolve purchase cost and specialist access during deployment planning.
  • C. Compare restoration and access conditions alongside failure occurrence before estimating mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • D. Require field observations of both restoration processes before developing an availability estimate suitable for the purchase decision.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. The minimal cut sets are {A,B} and {A,C}; either conjunction is sufficient, and both occurrences of A represent the same event.
  • B. The minimal cut sets are {A1,B} and {A2,C}; repeated positions represent separate instances when evaluating the tree.
  • C. The minimal cut sets are {A} and {B,C}; factoring the shared term separates its failure from the downstream conjunction.
  • D. The minimal cut set is {A,B,C}; both branches appear beneath one top event and contribute to its combined condition.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Model how alarm load changes attention, acknowledgment and escalation, then connect those responses to unresolved events.
  • B. Identify operators and shifts with the longest acknowledgment delays, prioritizing refresher training before changing detector or escalation settings.
  • C. Refit the detector threshold against incident labels, increasing the penalty for missed events to offset the rise in unresolved cases.
  • D. Apply the earlier acknowledgment distribution to the new alarm rate to estimate the additional staffing required.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Report twenty unit-hours with zero events; any reliability estimate needs an explicit exposure model, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • B. Use reciprocal accumulated exposure as a conservative failure-rate estimate and carry that single rate into reliability planning.
  • C. Exclude zero-event observations from reliability comparison and use the test to plan a campaign long enough to observe failures.
  • D. Pool the twenty unit-hours into a survival duration and compare it directly with the uninterrupted mission required of one unit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Add outage handling to the implementation while retaining the established liveness contract, then test the new recovery procedures.
  • B. Review the availability assumption and analyze outage/recovery behavior, preserving the existing proof as conditional evidence.
  • C. Repeat the check with more requests to establish that the result scales with demand.
  • D. Retain the proof and verify resource availability separately, treating successful recovery tests as support for the original continuous-availability assumption.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. Add measurable deadlines to each diagnostic so the two children fully specify the parent response to either sensing loss.
  • B. The children require an allocation to separate sensors, because the parent's either-condition wording implies that sensing and shutdown must have redundant hardware paths.
  • C. Both loss conditions are covered, but a common diagnostic identifier is needed to consolidate the children under the parent.
  • D. The decomposition retains the two diagnostic triggers but omits the required shutdown response; define how either diagnosis causes the specified system action.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Use the newer meeting value for preliminary trades while retaining 40 kg in the contract register, then reconcile the two at the next baseline review.
  • B. Trade options across the 40–45 kg range and recommend the highest-scoring design, treating the meeting note as evidence that the sponsor accepts that range.
  • C. Use 40 kg as the obligation and 45 kg as a proposed change, showing the design consequence and the approval needed to adopt it.
  • D. Freeze the mass-dependent concept comparison until the change is approved, so exploratory results cannot influence a decision made against the still-binding contractual limit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Require a common engineering unit in every software module, then use static type checks to demonstrate that integration and operational transition risks are addressed.
  • B. Centralize quantity conversion in one integration component, then verify its calculations while retaining each producer's existing assumptions about units and message meaning.
  • C. Add unit labels and approval signatures to the controlled interface specification, using that record as producer acceptance evidence.
  • D. Verify actual producer-consumer exchanges against explicit unit semantics and representative operational data, with ownership for detecting and resolving discrepancies.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. Confirm the supplier's average update performance over representative workloads, then retain the controller's five-second limit if it exceeds the observed mean interval.
  • B. Agree which team reports missing updates, then retain independent local clock references because freshness is checked separately within each organization's component.
  • C. Choose the protocol and retry policy, then derive allowable data age from the resulting maximum retry duration.
  • D. Define timestamps, age limits, guaranteed update bounds and invalid-data responses so both parties can establish when a measurement is usable.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. Include the cost and value of reversible learning: compare how each choice exposes the project to uncertain demand and later migration.
  • B. Prefer the reversible trial and defer migration analysis until measured demand establishes whether another architecture is needed.
  • C. Prefer B if its expected long-run performance is higher, then absorb forecast changes within its infrastructure commitment rather than reopening the architecture decision.
  • D. Compare both options at the mean demand forecast and discount future operating costs, leaving trial reversibility outside the score to avoid double-counting uncertainty.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Compare laboratory performance and purchase cost, allocating support and integration constraints to the selected option’s implementation plan.
  • B. Compare delivered field capability, including sensing, integration, support and supply constraints; keep uncertain assumptions and their decision owners explicit.
  • C. Compare estimated lifecycle costs using a common contingency factor, then select the cheaper option if the supplier can document compliance with the sensor specification.
  • D. Compare the sensor functions that the program directly controls, then evaluate external integration and supply constraints separately so vendor limitations do not bias architecture selection.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Relabel the calculated outcomes as predictions while retaining the 20-minute input in the executive summary, because modeling distinguishes them from field observations.
  • B. Restore the value's assumption status and identify which conclusions depend on it, preserving useful calculations as explicitly conditional results.
  • C. Exclude the model's results from the decision package until restoration data is obtained, because an assumed input cannot support any useful engineering comparison.
  • D. Substitute a longer restoration allowance and retain the conclusion, using conservatism to cover the missing measurements.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-039: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation

The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.

What is the strongest transferable lesson? Select one option.

  • A. Compare each alternative’s best successful trajectory and use its performance margin to determine the preferred crew response.
  • B. Compare alternatives using the information and recognition-to-action timing available at the actual decision point, stating what each simulation assumes.
  • C. Compare aircraft capability from the instant of hazard onset, then treat recognition and diagnosis as separate training factors outside the alternative-feasibility assessment.
  • D. Use the delayed simulator attempt as the representative case, then extrapolate its outcome to the range of feasible return decisions in the actual event.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-043: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence

The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.

What should a review require? Select one option.

  • A. Estimate anomaly acceptability from the proportion of successful affected missions, then revisit the decision when another anomaly changes that rate.
  • B. Explain the anomaly mechanism and evidence, including whether prior successes cover the present conditions and what remains unresolved.
  • C. Ask the subsystem owner to confirm that the current event resembles previous cases, then carry forward the previously accepted disposition.
  • D. Retain the disposition until anomaly frequency materially changes, while improving collection of flight performance data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-044: London 2012: a supplier cannot deliver

The National Audit Office's post-Games review describes extensive operational preparation for London 2012 and contingency action when the security contractor could not provide planned staffing.

Which preparation best transfers to a new major event? Select one option.

  • A. Increase staffing surveillance before the event and track recruitment milestones, using early forecasts as the main control on delivery risk.
  • B. Contract with reserve suppliers and verify their commercial commitments, activating the reserve contract when the primary provider reports a shortfall.
  • C. Rehearse plausible shortfalls with the decision authorities and reserve resources, verifying readiness and changes needed to sustain operations.
  • D. Define an escalation organization and rehearse executive decisions, leaving reserve staff preparation to the agency assigned responsibility during activation.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-048: Reporting disagreement

Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.

Which report is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Explain both evidence arguments, isolate whether seal geometry changes test applicability, and name the decision or investigation needed to resolve it.
  • B. Keep the old test provisionally applicable because materials are unchanged, flagging geometry for confirmation in the next scheduled environmental campaign.
  • C. Declare the old test inapplicable because geometry changed, remove its trace link, and recommend repeating the complete environmental qualification.
  • D. Ask a third reviewer to resolve the disagreement by today, reporting the majority judgment with the original evidence attachments.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-049: Choosing a useful view

A review board cannot tell who controls motion during startup, normal operation, manual stop and recovery. It already has a component hierarchy with complete part names.

Which additional view best answers the question? Select one option.

  • A. Add an interface view showing command and status connections, including each message direction and the component that sends it.
  • B. Add a state and authority view linking transitions and guards to the components permitted to enable, stop or resume motion.
  • C. Add a function-allocation view linking each motion-related function to its implementing component, including the organization responsible for each function.
  • D. Add a nominal startup sequence showing operator commands and component responses, using its final operating state to represent motion authority.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-053: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer

RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.

What should the review conclude? Select one option.

  • A. Add retries until the connection receives an acknowledgment within its timeout, then use the bounded exchange to establish completed action.
  • B. Supplement TCP receipt with an application-server delivery log, treating successful delivery to the operator console as evidence of action.
  • C. The log establishes transport receipt at that layer; operator action requires a relevant observation and acknowledgment in the application workflow.
  • D. Have the operator console acknowledge message display and use that event to close the action, retaining transport logs for diagnosis.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-054: DNS: a historical design trade

RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.

What transfers from the source? Select one option.

  • A. Remove caching from the control path and accept the extra server load, treating rapidly changing data as incompatible with local reuse.
  • B. Choose a lifetime shorter than the mean update interval, then use that relationship to justify freshness independently of individual control actions.
  • C. Set the lifetime from measured server-load savings and reduce it when operators report that stale values are affecting control decisions.
  • D. Evaluate update behavior and stale-data consequences for this application; the source explains the trade but does not provide its acceptable limits.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-058: A supplier changes its service contract

A cloud service previously guaranteed delivery of events in order. Its new version preserves all events but allows reordering. The consumer uses arrival order to authorize a sequence of physical actions.

Which review scope is necessary? Select one option.

  • A. Revalidate message schemas and event counts, then keep existing action tests if every transmitted event reaches the consumer without field changes.
  • B. Add a reorder buffer with a fixed waiting period, then retain the consumer logic and tests once normal ordering is restored.
  • C. Review ordering assumptions in consumer state and authority logic, including recovery, delay and duplicates, and reassess the affected verification evidence.
  • D. Requalify the consumer’s physical-action components, treating the cloud change as a supplier concern once the event delivery count is verified.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-059: A rejected alternative becomes relevant

A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.

What should the concept review do? Select one option.

  • A. Reopen the alternatives against indoor coverage and limited battery support, retaining the old rationale while evaluating changed assumptions and lifecycle costs.
  • B. Retain wired sensing for the first indoor release and reassess radio after measured maintenance costs justify reopening the earlier trade.
  • C. Compare wired and radio using the original criteria and weights, updating coverage estimates to reflect the indoor infrastructure now available.
  • D. Select radio provisionally because the original coverage concern is resolved, then assign battery staffing to the deployment support plan.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Source: evals/evidence/quiz-0.2.0-20261114/task-domain/request.md

Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning project defines its system-of-interest as the authority's own warning service, excluding supplier infrastructure. A commercial rainfall feed is required, and the authority remains accountable for warnings when that feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. Allocate availability to the supplier contract and verify internal warning logic with timely inputs, assessing each organization separately.
  • B. Include supplier infrastructure inside the implementation boundary and allocate its availability controls to the authority responsible for warnings.
  • C. Model supplier delay as a fixed external parameter so internal design can proceed before delayed-feed response ownership is agreed.
  • D. Keep the supplier external to the chosen boundary; specify its dependency contract and the authority's response to delayed data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which proposed actions establish a defensible decision basis from the supplied facts, without first assuming a cause or a target? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing turnaround, inspection and change-control outcomes, including the operating conditions in which each must be protected.
  • B. Use maintenance ownership of signoff to assign it primary responsibility for delay, then measure the effect of automating its approval step.
  • C. Adopt the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold for the new process, then investigate exceptions when that threshold is missed.
  • D. Trace the timing of late changes, inspection work and decisions across roles to distinguish their contributions to the observed turnaround.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which actions are justified by the supplied lifecycle facts without adding an unprovided policy or disposal requirement? Select all supported options.

  • A. Adopt physical destruction of every retired module as the required disposal method, based on the stated presence of configuration keys.
  • B. Define who will provide compatible replacements and spares if the supplier ends support during the planned fifteen-year service period.
  • C. Define how replacement modules receive and verify the authorized configuration before they are returned to the operating sensor network.
  • D. Define credential retirement and data-removal outcomes for removed modules, then select disposal methods against the applicable requirements and evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Compare failures over equal exposure and use the tighter uncertainty interval to choose between alternatives with similar observed reliability.
  • B. Select the faster-restoring alternative and resolve purchase cost and specialist access during deployment planning.
  • C. Compare restoration and access conditions alongside failure occurrence before estimating mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • D. Require field observations of both restoration processes before developing an availability estimate suitable for the purchase decision.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. The minimal cut sets are {A,B} and {A,C}; either conjunction is sufficient, and both occurrences of A represent the same event.
  • B. The minimal cut sets are {A1,B} and {A2,C}; repeated positions represent separate instances when evaluating the tree.
  • C. The minimal cut sets are {A} and {B,C}; factoring the shared term separates its failure from the downstream conjunction.
  • D. The minimal cut set is {A,B,C}; both branches appear beneath one top event and contribute to its combined condition.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Model how alarm load changes attention, acknowledgment and escalation, then connect those responses to unresolved events.
  • B. Identify operators and shifts with the longest acknowledgment delays, prioritizing refresher training before changing detector or escalation settings.
  • C. Refit the detector threshold against incident labels, increasing the penalty for missed events to offset the rise in unresolved cases.
  • D. Apply the earlier acknowledgment distribution to the new alarm rate to estimate the additional staffing required.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Report twenty unit-hours with zero events; any reliability estimate needs an explicit exposure model, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • B. Use reciprocal accumulated exposure as a conservative failure-rate estimate and carry that single rate into reliability planning.
  • C. Exclude zero-event observations from reliability comparison and use the test to plan a campaign long enough to observe failures.
  • D. Pool the twenty unit-hours into a survival duration and compare it directly with the uninterrupted mission required of one unit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Add outage handling to the implementation while retaining the established liveness contract, then test the new recovery procedures.
  • B. Review the availability assumption and analyze outage/recovery behavior, preserving the existing proof as conditional evidence.
  • C. Repeat the check with more requests to establish that the result scales with demand.
  • D. Retain the proof and verify resource availability separately, treating successful recovery tests as support for the original continuous-availability assumption.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. Add measurable deadlines to each diagnostic so the two children fully specify the parent response to either sensing loss.
  • B. The children require an allocation to separate sensors, because the parent's either-condition wording implies that sensing and shutdown must have redundant hardware paths.
  • C. Both loss conditions are covered, but a common diagnostic identifier is needed to consolidate the children under the parent.
  • D. The decomposition retains the two diagnostic triggers but omits the required shutdown response; define how either diagnosis causes the specified system action.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Use the newer meeting value for preliminary trades while retaining 40 kg in the contract register, then reconcile the two at the next baseline review.
  • B. Trade options across the 40–45 kg range and recommend the highest-scoring design, treating the meeting note as evidence that the sponsor accepts that range.
  • C. Use 40 kg as the obligation and 45 kg as a proposed change, showing the design consequence and the approval needed to adopt it.
  • D. Freeze the mass-dependent concept comparison until the change is approved, so exploratory results cannot influence a decision made against the still-binding contractual limit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Require a common engineering unit in every software module, then use static type checks to demonstrate that integration and operational transition risks are addressed.
  • B. Centralize quantity conversion in one integration component, then verify its calculations while retaining each producer's existing assumptions about units and message meaning.
  • C. Add unit labels and approval signatures to the controlled interface specification, using that record as producer acceptance evidence.
  • D. Verify actual producer-consumer exchanges against explicit unit semantics and representative operational data, with ownership for detecting and resolving discrepancies.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. Confirm the supplier's average update performance over representative workloads, then retain the controller's five-second limit if it exceeds the observed mean interval.
  • B. Agree which team reports missing updates, then retain independent local clock references because freshness is checked separately within each organization's component.
  • C. Choose the protocol and retry policy, then derive allowable data age from the resulting maximum retry duration.
  • D. Define timestamps, age limits, guaranteed update bounds and invalid-data responses so both parties can establish when a measurement is usable.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. Include the cost and value of reversible learning: compare how each choice exposes the project to uncertain demand and later migration.
  • B. Prefer the reversible trial and defer migration analysis until measured demand establishes whether another architecture is needed.
  • C. Prefer B if its expected long-run performance is higher, then absorb forecast changes within its infrastructure commitment rather than reopening the architecture decision.
  • D. Compare both options at the mean demand forecast and discount future operating costs, leaving trial reversibility outside the score to avoid double-counting uncertainty.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Compare laboratory performance and purchase cost, allocating support and integration constraints to the selected option’s implementation plan.
  • B. Compare delivered field capability, including sensing, integration, support and supply constraints; keep uncertain assumptions and their decision owners explicit.
  • C. Compare estimated lifecycle costs using a common contingency factor, then select the cheaper option if the supplier can document compliance with the sensor specification.
  • D. Compare the sensor functions that the program directly controls, then evaluate external integration and supply constraints separately so vendor limitations do not bias architecture selection.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Relabel the calculated outcomes as predictions while retaining the 20-minute input in the executive summary, because modeling distinguishes them from field observations.
  • B. Restore the value's assumption status and identify which conclusions depend on it, preserving useful calculations as explicitly conditional results.
  • C. Exclude the model's results from the decision package until restoration data is obtained, because an assumed input cannot support any useful engineering comparison.
  • D. Substitute a longer restoration allowance and retain the conclusion, using conservatism to cover the missing measurements.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-039: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation

The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.

What is the strongest transferable lesson? Select one option.

  • A. Compare each alternative’s best successful trajectory and use its performance margin to determine the preferred crew response.
  • B. Compare alternatives using the information and recognition-to-action timing available at the actual decision point, stating what each simulation assumes.
  • C. Compare aircraft capability from the instant of hazard onset, then treat recognition and diagnosis as separate training factors outside the alternative-feasibility assessment.
  • D. Use the delayed simulator attempt as the representative case, then extrapolate its outcome to the range of feasible return decisions in the actual event.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-043: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence

The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.

What should a review require? Select one option.

  • A. Estimate anomaly acceptability from the proportion of successful affected missions, then revisit the decision when another anomaly changes that rate.
  • B. Explain the anomaly mechanism and evidence, including whether prior successes cover the present conditions and what remains unresolved.
  • C. Ask the subsystem owner to confirm that the current event resembles previous cases, then carry forward the previously accepted disposition.
  • D. Retain the disposition until anomaly frequency materially changes, while improving collection of flight performance data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-044: London 2012: a supplier cannot deliver

The National Audit Office's post-Games review describes extensive operational preparation for London 2012 and contingency action when the security contractor could not provide planned staffing.

Which preparation best transfers to a new major event? Select one option.

  • A. Increase staffing surveillance before the event and track recruitment milestones, using early forecasts as the main control on delivery risk.
  • B. Contract with reserve suppliers and verify their commercial commitments, activating the reserve contract when the primary provider reports a shortfall.
  • C. Rehearse plausible shortfalls with the decision authorities and reserve resources, verifying readiness and changes needed to sustain operations.
  • D. Define an escalation organization and rehearse executive decisions, leaving reserve staff preparation to the agency assigned responsibility during activation.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-048: Reporting disagreement

Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.

Which report is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Explain both evidence arguments, isolate whether seal geometry changes test applicability, and name the decision or investigation needed to resolve it.
  • B. Keep the old test provisionally applicable because materials are unchanged, flagging geometry for confirmation in the next scheduled environmental campaign.
  • C. Declare the old test inapplicable because geometry changed, remove its trace link, and recommend repeating the complete environmental qualification.
  • D. Ask a third reviewer to resolve the disagreement by today, reporting the majority judgment with the original evidence attachments.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-049: Choosing a useful view

A review board cannot tell who controls motion during startup, normal operation, manual stop and recovery. It already has a component hierarchy with complete part names.

Which additional view best answers the question? Select one option.

  • A. Add an interface view showing command and status connections, including each message direction and the component that sends it.
  • B. Add a state and authority view linking transitions and guards to the components permitted to enable, stop or resume motion.
  • C. Add a function-allocation view linking each motion-related function to its implementing component, including the organization responsible for each function.
  • D. Add a nominal startup sequence showing operator commands and component responses, using its final operating state to represent motion authority.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-053: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer

RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.

What should the review conclude? Select one option.

  • A. Add retries until the connection receives an acknowledgment within its timeout, then use the bounded exchange to establish completed action.
  • B. Supplement TCP receipt with an application-server delivery log, treating successful delivery to the operator console as evidence of action.
  • C. The log establishes transport receipt at that layer; operator action requires a relevant observation and acknowledgment in the application workflow.
  • D. Have the operator console acknowledge message display and use that event to close the action, retaining transport logs for diagnosis.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-054: DNS: a historical design trade

RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.

What transfers from the source? Select one option.

  • A. Remove caching from the control path and accept the extra server load, treating rapidly changing data as incompatible with local reuse.
  • B. Choose a lifetime shorter than the mean update interval, then use that relationship to justify freshness independently of individual control actions.
  • C. Set the lifetime from measured server-load savings and reduce it when operators report that stale values are affecting control decisions.
  • D. Evaluate update behavior and stale-data consequences for this application; the source explains the trade but does not provide its acceptable limits.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-058: A supplier changes its service contract

A cloud service previously guaranteed delivery of events in order. Its new version preserves all events but allows reordering. The consumer uses arrival order to authorize a sequence of physical actions.

Which review scope is necessary? Select one option.

  • A. Revalidate message schemas and event counts, then keep existing action tests if every transmitted event reaches the consumer without field changes.
  • B. Add a reorder buffer with a fixed waiting period, then retain the consumer logic and tests once normal ordering is restored.
  • C. Review ordering assumptions in consumer state and authority logic, including recovery, delay and duplicates, and reassess the affected verification evidence.
  • D. Requalify the consumer’s physical-action components, treating the cloud change as a supplier concern once the event delivery count is verified.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-059: A rejected alternative becomes relevant

A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.

What should the concept review do? Select one option.

  • A. Reopen the alternatives against indoor coverage and limited battery support, retaining the old rationale while evaluating changed assumptions and lifecycle costs.
  • B. Retain wired sensing for the first indoor release and reassess radio after measured maintenance costs justify reopening the earlier trade.
  • C. Compare wired and radio using the original criteria and weights, updating coverage estimates to reflect the indoor infrastructure now available.
  • D. Select radio provisionally because the original coverage concern is resolved, then assign battery staffing to the deployment support plan.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning project defines its system-of-interest as the authority's own warning service, excluding supplier infrastructure. A commercial rainfall feed is required, and the authority remains accountable for warnings when that feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. Allocate availability to the supplier contract and verify internal warning logic with timely inputs, assessing each organization separately.
  • B. Include supplier infrastructure inside the implementation boundary and allocate its availability controls to the authority responsible for warnings.
  • C. Model supplier delay as a fixed external parameter so internal design can proceed before delayed-feed response ownership is agreed.
  • D. Keep the supplier external to the chosen boundary; specify its dependency contract and the authority's response to delayed data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which proposed actions establish a defensible decision basis from the supplied facts, without first assuming a cause or a target? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing turnaround, inspection and change-control outcomes, including the operating conditions in which each must be protected.
  • B. Use maintenance ownership of signoff to assign it primary responsibility for delay, then measure the effect of automating its approval step.
  • C. Adopt the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold for the new process, then investigate exceptions when that threshold is missed.
  • D. Trace the timing of late changes, inspection work and decisions across roles to distinguish their contributions to the observed turnaround.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which actions are justified by the supplied lifecycle facts without adding an unprovided policy or disposal requirement? Select all supported options.

  • A. Adopt physical destruction of every retired module as the required disposal method, based on the stated presence of configuration keys.
  • B. Define who will provide compatible replacements and spares if the supplier ends support during the planned fifteen-year service period.
  • C. Define how replacement modules receive and verify the authorized configuration before they are returned to the operating sensor network.
  • D. Define credential retirement and data-removal outcomes for removed modules, then select disposal methods against the applicable requirements and evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Compare failures over equal exposure and use the tighter uncertainty interval to choose between alternatives with similar observed reliability.
  • B. Select the faster-restoring alternative and resolve purchase cost and specialist access during deployment planning.
  • C. Compare restoration and access conditions alongside failure occurrence before estimating mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • D. Require field observations of both restoration processes before developing an availability estimate suitable for the purchase decision.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. The minimal cut sets are {A,B} and {A,C}; either conjunction is sufficient, and both occurrences of A represent the same event.
  • B. The minimal cut sets are {A1,B} and {A2,C}; repeated positions represent separate instances when evaluating the tree.
  • C. The minimal cut sets are {A} and {B,C}; factoring the shared term separates its failure from the downstream conjunction.
  • D. The minimal cut set is {A,B,C}; both branches appear beneath one top event and contribute to its combined condition.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Model how alarm load changes attention, acknowledgment and escalation, then connect those responses to unresolved events.
  • B. Identify operators and shifts with the longest acknowledgment delays, prioritizing refresher training before changing detector or escalation settings.
  • C. Refit the detector threshold against incident labels, increasing the penalty for missed events to offset the rise in unresolved cases.
  • D. Apply the earlier acknowledgment distribution to the new alarm rate to estimate the additional staffing required.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Report twenty unit-hours with zero events; any reliability estimate needs an explicit exposure model, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • B. Use reciprocal accumulated exposure as a conservative failure-rate estimate and carry that single rate into reliability planning.
  • C. Exclude zero-event observations from reliability comparison and use the test to plan a campaign long enough to observe failures.
  • D. Pool the twenty unit-hours into a survival duration and compare it directly with the uninterrupted mission required of one unit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Add outage handling to the implementation while retaining the established liveness contract, then test the new recovery procedures.
  • B. Review the availability assumption and analyze outage/recovery behavior, preserving the existing proof as conditional evidence.
  • C. Repeat the check with more requests to establish that the result scales with demand.
  • D. Retain the proof and verify resource availability separately, treating successful recovery tests as support for the original continuous-availability assumption.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. Add measurable deadlines to each diagnostic so the two children fully specify the parent response to either sensing loss.
  • B. The children require an allocation to separate sensors, because the parent's either-condition wording implies that sensing and shutdown must have redundant hardware paths.
  • C. Both loss conditions are covered, but a common diagnostic identifier is needed to consolidate the children under the parent.
  • D. The decomposition retains the two diagnostic triggers but omits the required shutdown response; define how either diagnosis causes the specified system action.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Use the newer meeting value for preliminary trades while retaining 40 kg in the contract register, then reconcile the two at the next baseline review.
  • B. Trade options across the 40–45 kg range and recommend the highest-scoring design, treating the meeting note as evidence that the sponsor accepts that range.
  • C. Use 40 kg as the obligation and 45 kg as a proposed change, showing the design consequence and the approval needed to adopt it.
  • D. Freeze the mass-dependent concept comparison until the change is approved, so exploratory results cannot influence a decision made against the still-binding contractual limit.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Require a common engineering unit in every software module, then use static type checks to demonstrate that integration and operational transition risks are addressed.
  • B. Centralize quantity conversion in one integration component, then verify its calculations while retaining each producer's existing assumptions about units and message meaning.
  • C. Add unit labels and approval signatures to the controlled interface specification, using that record as producer acceptance evidence.
  • D. Verify actual producer-consumer exchanges against explicit unit semantics and representative operational data, with ownership for detecting and resolving discrepancies.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. Confirm the supplier's average update performance over representative workloads, then retain the controller's five-second limit if it exceeds the observed mean interval.
  • B. Agree which team reports missing updates, then retain independent local clock references because freshness is checked separately within each organization's component.
  • C. Choose the protocol and retry policy, then derive allowable data age from the resulting maximum retry duration.
  • D. Define timestamps, age limits, guaranteed update bounds and invalid-data responses so both parties can establish when a measurement is usable.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. Include the cost and value of reversible learning: compare how each choice exposes the project to uncertain demand and later migration.
  • B. Prefer the reversible trial and defer migration analysis until measured demand establishes whether another architecture is needed.
  • C. Prefer B if its expected long-run performance is higher, then absorb forecast changes within its infrastructure commitment rather than reopening the architecture decision.
  • D. Compare both options at the mean demand forecast and discount future operating costs, leaving trial reversibility outside the score to avoid double-counting uncertainty.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Compare laboratory performance and purchase cost, allocating support and integration constraints to the selected option’s implementation plan.
  • B. Compare delivered field capability, including sensing, integration, support and supply constraints; keep uncertain assumptions and their decision owners explicit.
  • C. Compare estimated lifecycle costs using a common contingency factor, then select the cheaper option if the supplier can document compliance with the sensor specification.
  • D. Compare the sensor functions that the program directly controls, then evaluate external integration and supply constraints separately so vendor limitations do not bias architecture selection.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Relabel the calculated outcomes as predictions while retaining the 20-minute input in the executive summary, because modeling distinguishes them from field observations.
  • B. Restore the value's assumption status and identify which conclusions depend on it, preserving useful calculations as explicitly conditional results.
  • C. Exclude the model's results from the decision package until restoration data is obtained, because an assumed input cannot support any useful engineering comparison.
  • D. Substitute a longer restoration allowance and retain the conclusion, using conservatism to cover the missing measurements.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Source: evals/evidence/quiz-diagnostic-20261113/README.md

Initial quiz diagnostic, 2026-11-13

Three fresh participants answered the same 24 development questions using no packaged skills, task skills, or task-plus-domain skills. All three selected 24/24 proposed keyed answers. This result exposed a ceiling and establishes no benefit from the skills.

An independent reviewer found that selecting the longest answer, without understanding the problem, succeeds on 54/55 single-choice questions across the bank, including all 12 reserved-public questions. Two multiple-selection stems also admit defensible alternative readings. This bank is unsuitable for a comparative engineering-quality claim.

The summary, surface-cue probe, and unchanged participant responses remain available: no skills, task skills, and task plus domain. Their adjacent manifests, question packets and scores bind the recorded inputs. The original bank and scoring source are preserved before repairs. These schema1 scores are historical; the repaired scorer uses a stricter input contract and does not retroactively validate them.

Participants were instructed to use only their packets. They shared a host that exposed global skill descriptions, so this is not enforced isolation or a causal estimate of skill effectiveness. Exact model identity/settings, tokens and cost were unavailable. The reasoning text has not received independent scoring for this retired-bank diagnostic.

The disposition is to repair question construction, packet/result binding and review controls; retain this failure; use fresh participants for the revised questions; and assess actual engineering work separately.
