Source: evals/evidence/quiz-diagnostic-20261113/none/request.md

Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning service consumes a commercial rainfall feed. The supplier controls its infrastructure. The warning authority remains accountable for issuing timely warnings when the feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. As a fixed environmental assumption until the supplier contract is renegotiated.
  • B. Inside the authority's boundary because accountability implies control of all supporting components.
  • C. Outside the architecture because its implementation cannot be changed by the authority.
  • D. Outside the system-of-interest boundary, with an explicit operational dependency and an owned degraded-service response.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which pair of actions is justified before committing to that automation? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing outcomes and the conditions under which each must be protected.
  • B. Assign the delay to maintenance because it owns the signoff.
  • C. Use the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold.
  • D. Trace late changes and inspection decisions across responsible roles.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which issues belong in the lifecycle review? Select all supported options.

  • A. Whether every module should be physically destroyed on replacement.
  • B. Who maintains compatibility and spares when the supplier ends support.
  • C. How replacement modules acquire the authorized configuration.
  • D. How retired modules lose credentials and retained sensitive data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Equal failure frequency establishes equal operational availability.
  • B. Restoration time and access arrangements must be included before comparing mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • C. Availability cannot be studied until a complete long-term field trial has finished.
  • D. The faster-restoring alternative is preferable regardless of acquisition and mission effects.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. {A,B,C} only.
  • B. Two separate independent copies of A, one in each branch.
  • C. {A} and {B,C}.
  • D. {A,B} and {A,C}.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. A feedback model connecting alarm load, attention, acknowledgment, escalation and unresolved events.
  • B. A ranking of operators by acknowledgment time.
  • C. A detector-only ROC curve with an increased penalty for missed events.
  • D. A human-response model using the old acknowledgment time as a constant.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Pool the twenty units as a single unit tested for twenty consecutive hours without checking assumptions.
  • B. State the observed exposure and zero events, then use an explicitly justified statistical model and uncertainty if estimating reliability.
  • C. Declare the test inconclusive and discard the observations.
  • D. Use one failure divided by exposure as the exact failure probability.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Report the proof as conditional, assess the environment assumption, and analyze request behavior during outage and recovery.
  • B. Remove the availability assumption and call the resulting timeout a requirement defect.
  • C. Increase the proof bound while leaving the environment assumption unchanged.
  • D. Replace the proof with line coverage because the deployed environment is uncertain.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. A third sensor is needed to satisfy the parent.
  • B. The two links establish complete decomposition because each input is represented.
  • C. The children must use identical wording to the parent.
  • D. The required shutdown response and its connection to either diagnostic need explicit treatment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Stop all concept work until the contract is formally changed.
  • B. Keep 40 kg as the current obligation, record 45 kg as a proposed change, and show the trade consequence and needed disposition.
  • C. Use 45 kg because it is the latest statement.
  • D. Average the two values to avoid bias toward either stakeholder.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Add unit labels to the interface document and consider the problem resolved.
  • B. Require one organization to write every component to remove organizational interfaces.
  • C. Convert every engineering quantity to a single storage type.
  • D. Make interface semantics executable at producer/consumer boundaries and verify representative exchanged data with clear ownership.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. The validity/age contract, clock reference, guaranteed update bounds and responsibilities when those conditions are violated.
  • B. Whether the supplier uses UDP or TCP internally.
  • C. The exact color of the stale-data indicator.
  • D. Whether five seconds is a common industry setting.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. The number of requirements each option references.
  • B. The option value of reversible learning, alongside expected performance and implementation effects.
  • C. A rule that the smallest change should always be selected.
  • D. A preference for B because it demonstrates long-term commitment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Only components designed by the program because external products cannot be controlled.
  • B. The sensor plus integration, support, supply and operational constraints, with uncertainties and owners.
  • C. Total project cost with all unknowns assigned the same contingency percentage.
  • D. The sensing function and its measured accuracy only.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Rename the model output a prediction and leave the summary unchanged.
  • B. Delete every result calculated using the assumed value.
  • C. Increase the value until the conclusion becomes conservative.
  • D. Retain the value but restore its assumption status and trace its effect on conclusions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-039: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation

The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.

What is the strongest transferable lesson? Select one option.

  • A. Alternative assessment must include information, recognition and decision delays available at the actual decision point.
  • B. A successful simulator trajectory establishes that the crew should have selected it.
  • C. Human decision time should be removed when evaluating aircraft performance.
  • D. A failed delayed attempt proves no aircraft could have returned under any conditions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-043: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence

The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.

What should a review require? Select one option.

  • A. A causal and evidence-based assessment of the anomaly, including why prior success does or does not bound the present risk.
  • B. A ban on using operational history in risk assessment.
  • C. A count of successful missions as a direct estimate that the anomaly cannot cause loss.
  • D. A requirement that the subsystem owner make the final decision without cross-program review.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-044: London 2012: a supplier cannot deliver

The National Audit Office's post-Games review describes extensive operational preparation for London 2012 and contingency action when the security contractor could not provide planned staffing.

Which preparation best transfers to a new major event? Select one option.

  • A. Duplicate contracts for every event function regardless of consequence.
  • B. A detailed organization chart with no need to rehearse transitions.
  • C. Exercised scenarios connecting delivery shortfalls to decision authority, available reserves and operational changes.
  • D. Contract penalties large enough to remove the need for alternate staffing.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-048: Reporting disagreement

Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.

Which report is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Report disagreement, the evidence supporting each position, the geometry-dependent question and the decision or test needed to resolve it.
  • B. Choose the senior reviewer's conclusion and omit the disagreement.
  • C. Present both conclusions as equally valid without identifying the unresolved mechanism.
  • D. Average the two reviewer ratings and report the resulting confidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-049: Choosing a useful view

A review board cannot tell who controls motion during startup, normal operation, manual stop and recovery. It already has a component hierarchy with complete part names.

Which additional view best answers the question? Select one option.

  • A. A more detailed component hierarchy with supplier names.
  • B. A table of all software function names sorted alphabetically.
  • C. A high-resolution rendering of the enclosure.
  • D. A state/authority view showing transitions, guards and who may enable or inhibit motion, tied to the existing components.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-053: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer

RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.

What should the review conclude? Select one option.

  • A. Replacing TCP with a newer transport protocol resolves the semantic gap.
  • B. TCP acknowledgments are unreliable and should not be recorded.
  • C. The log supports transport-level receipt but not operator action; the application/workflow needs its own relevant acknowledgment evidence.
  • D. The operator action is established whenever both endpoints use TCP.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-054: DNS: a historical design trade

RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.

What transfers from the source? Select one option.

  • A. A long lifetime is correct because the original design favored caching.
  • B. The trade must be evaluated against this application's update and stale-data consequences; the historical mechanism does not supply its acceptance limits.
  • C. Caching should be avoided whenever data can change.
  • D. A cache hit demonstrates that the value is current.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-058: A supplier changes its service contract

A cloud service previously guaranteed delivery of events in order. Its new version preserves all events but allows reordering. The consumer uses arrival order to authorize a sequence of physical actions.

Which review scope is necessary? Select one option.

  • A. Only the API field names and types.
  • B. The supplier's event count, because no data is lost.
  • C. Every requirement in the organization, regardless of dependency.
  • D. The changed ordering semantics, consumer state/authority logic, recovery behavior and related verification evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-059: A rejected alternative becomes relevant

A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.

What should the concept review do? Select one option.

  • A. Delete the previous decision record to avoid confusing reviewers.
  • B. Reuse the old decision because its documented rationale makes it authoritative in every deployment.
  • C. Select radio because the original objection is absent.
  • D. Reopen the alternative against the new context, retaining the old rationale and examining new support constraints.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Source: evals/evidence/quiz-diagnostic-20261113/task-domain/request.md

Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning service consumes a commercial rainfall feed. The supplier controls its infrastructure. The warning authority remains accountable for issuing timely warnings when the feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. As a fixed environmental assumption until the supplier contract is renegotiated.
  • B. Inside the authority's boundary because accountability implies control of all supporting components.
  • C. Outside the architecture because its implementation cannot be changed by the authority.
  • D. Outside the system-of-interest boundary, with an explicit operational dependency and an owned degraded-service response.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which pair of actions is justified before committing to that automation? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing outcomes and the conditions under which each must be protected.
  • B. Assign the delay to maintenance because it owns the signoff.
  • C. Use the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold.
  • D. Trace late changes and inspection decisions across responsible roles.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which issues belong in the lifecycle review? Select all supported options.

  • A. Whether every module should be physically destroyed on replacement.
  • B. Who maintains compatibility and spares when the supplier ends support.
  • C. How replacement modules acquire the authorized configuration.
  • D. How retired modules lose credentials and retained sensitive data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Equal failure frequency establishes equal operational availability.
  • B. Restoration time and access arrangements must be included before comparing mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • C. Availability cannot be studied until a complete long-term field trial has finished.
  • D. The faster-restoring alternative is preferable regardless of acquisition and mission effects.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. {A,B,C} only.
  • B. Two separate independent copies of A, one in each branch.
  • C. {A} and {B,C}.
  • D. {A,B} and {A,C}.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. A feedback model connecting alarm load, attention, acknowledgment, escalation and unresolved events.
  • B. A ranking of operators by acknowledgment time.
  • C. A detector-only ROC curve with an increased penalty for missed events.
  • D. A human-response model using the old acknowledgment time as a constant.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Pool the twenty units as a single unit tested for twenty consecutive hours without checking assumptions.
  • B. State the observed exposure and zero events, then use an explicitly justified statistical model and uncertainty if estimating reliability.
  • C. Declare the test inconclusive and discard the observations.
  • D. Use one failure divided by exposure as the exact failure probability.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Report the proof as conditional, assess the environment assumption, and analyze request behavior during outage and recovery.
  • B. Remove the availability assumption and call the resulting timeout a requirement defect.
  • C. Increase the proof bound while leaving the environment assumption unchanged.
  • D. Replace the proof with line coverage because the deployed environment is uncertain.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. A third sensor is needed to satisfy the parent.
  • B. The two links establish complete decomposition because each input is represented.
  • C. The children must use identical wording to the parent.
  • D. The required shutdown response and its connection to either diagnostic need explicit treatment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Stop all concept work until the contract is formally changed.
  • B. Keep 40 kg as the current obligation, record 45 kg as a proposed change, and show the trade consequence and needed disposition.
  • C. Use 45 kg because it is the latest statement.
  • D. Average the two values to avoid bias toward either stakeholder.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Add unit labels to the interface document and consider the problem resolved.
  • B. Require one organization to write every component to remove organizational interfaces.
  • C. Convert every engineering quantity to a single storage type.
  • D. Make interface semantics executable at producer/consumer boundaries and verify representative exchanged data with clear ownership.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. The validity/age contract, clock reference, guaranteed update bounds and responsibilities when those conditions are violated.
  • B. Whether the supplier uses UDP or TCP internally.
  • C. The exact color of the stale-data indicator.
  • D. Whether five seconds is a common industry setting.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. The number of requirements each option references.
  • B. The option value of reversible learning, alongside expected performance and implementation effects.
  • C. A rule that the smallest change should always be selected.
  • D. A preference for B because it demonstrates long-term commitment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Only components designed by the program because external products cannot be controlled.
  • B. The sensor plus integration, support, supply and operational constraints, with uncertainties and owners.
  • C. Total project cost with all unknowns assigned the same contingency percentage.
  • D. The sensing function and its measured accuracy only.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Rename the model output a prediction and leave the summary unchanged.
  • B. Delete every result calculated using the assumed value.
  • C. Increase the value until the conclusion becomes conservative.
  • D. Retain the value but restore its assumption status and trace its effect on conclusions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-039: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation

The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.

What is the strongest transferable lesson? Select one option.

  • A. Alternative assessment must include information, recognition and decision delays available at the actual decision point.
  • B. A successful simulator trajectory establishes that the crew should have selected it.
  • C. Human decision time should be removed when evaluating aircraft performance.
  • D. A failed delayed attempt proves no aircraft could have returned under any conditions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-043: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence

The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.

What should a review require? Select one option.

  • A. A causal and evidence-based assessment of the anomaly, including why prior success does or does not bound the present risk.
  • B. A ban on using operational history in risk assessment.
  • C. A count of successful missions as a direct estimate that the anomaly cannot cause loss.
  • D. A requirement that the subsystem owner make the final decision without cross-program review.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-044: London 2012: a supplier cannot deliver

The National Audit Office's post-Games review describes extensive operational preparation for London 2012 and contingency action when the security contractor could not provide planned staffing.

Which preparation best transfers to a new major event? Select one option.

  • A. Duplicate contracts for every event function regardless of consequence.
  • B. A detailed organization chart with no need to rehearse transitions.
  • C. Exercised scenarios connecting delivery shortfalls to decision authority, available reserves and operational changes.
  • D. Contract penalties large enough to remove the need for alternate staffing.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-048: Reporting disagreement

Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.

Which report is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Report disagreement, the evidence supporting each position, the geometry-dependent question and the decision or test needed to resolve it.
  • B. Choose the senior reviewer's conclusion and omit the disagreement.
  • C. Present both conclusions as equally valid without identifying the unresolved mechanism.
  • D. Average the two reviewer ratings and report the resulting confidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-049: Choosing a useful view

A review board cannot tell who controls motion during startup, normal operation, manual stop and recovery. It already has a component hierarchy with complete part names.

Which additional view best answers the question? Select one option.

  • A. A more detailed component hierarchy with supplier names.
  • B. A table of all software function names sorted alphabetically.
  • C. A high-resolution rendering of the enclosure.
  • D. A state/authority view showing transitions, guards and who may enable or inhibit motion, tied to the existing components.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-053: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer

RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.

What should the review conclude? Select one option.

  • A. Replacing TCP with a newer transport protocol resolves the semantic gap.
  • B. TCP acknowledgments are unreliable and should not be recorded.
  • C. The log supports transport-level receipt but not operator action; the application/workflow needs its own relevant acknowledgment evidence.
  • D. The operator action is established whenever both endpoints use TCP.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-054: DNS: a historical design trade

RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.

What transfers from the source? Select one option.

  • A. A long lifetime is correct because the original design favored caching.
  • B. The trade must be evaluated against this application's update and stale-data consequences; the historical mechanism does not supply its acceptance limits.
  • C. Caching should be avoided whenever data can change.
  • D. A cache hit demonstrates that the value is current.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-058: A supplier changes its service contract

A cloud service previously guaranteed delivery of events in order. Its new version preserves all events but allows reordering. The consumer uses arrival order to authorize a sequence of physical actions.

Which review scope is necessary? Select one option.

  • A. Only the API field names and types.
  • B. The supplier's event count, because no data is lost.
  • C. Every requirement in the organization, regardless of dependency.
  • D. The changed ordering semantics, consumer state/authority logic, recovery behavior and related verification evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-059: A rejected alternative becomes relevant

A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.

What should the concept review do? Select one option.

  • A. Delete the previous decision record to avoid confusing reviewers.
  • B. Reuse the old decision because its documented rationale makes it authoritative in every deployment.
  • C. Select radio because the original objection is absent.
  • D. Reopen the alternative against the new context, retaining the old rationale and examining new support constraints.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Systems engineering judgment exercise

Answer from the supplied facts. These are engineering reasoning questions, not requests to certify a system. Use only this packet and tools permitted by the evaluation controller. Do not look for answer keys or other runs. Report unavailable facts honestly. Save answers.json using the response template. Select options and provide your own explanation for each item. Record the model/host/settings actually used; do not guess.

SEJ-003: Boundary versus ownership

A municipal flood-warning service consumes a commercial rainfall feed. The supplier controls its infrastructure. The warning authority remains accountable for issuing timely warnings when the feed is delayed.

How should the supplier be represented? Select one option.

  • A. As a fixed environmental assumption until the supplier contract is renegotiated.
  • B. Inside the authority's boundary because accountability implies control of all supporting components.
  • C. Outside the architecture because its implementation cannot be changed by the authority.
  • D. Outside the system-of-interest boundary, with an explicit operational dependency and an owned degraded-service response.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-004: Conflicting outcomes

Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.

Which pair of actions is justified before committing to that automation? Select all supported options.

  • A. Define the competing outcomes and the conditions under which each must be protected.
  • B. Assign the delay to maintenance because it owns the signoff.
  • C. Use the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold.
  • D. Trace late changes and inspection decisions across responsible roles.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-008: End of service

A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.

Which issues belong in the lifecycle review? Select all supported options.

  • A. Whether every module should be physically destroyed on replacement.
  • B. Who maintains compatibility and spares when the supplier ends support.
  • C. How replacement modules acquire the authorized configuration.
  • D. How retired modules lose credentials and retained sensitive data.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-009: Reliability across a mission

Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.

What conclusion follows? Select one option.

  • A. Equal failure frequency establishes equal operational availability.
  • B. Restoration time and access arrangements must be included before comparing mission availability and lifecycle effort.
  • C. Availability cannot be studied until a complete long-term field trial has finished.
  • D. The faster-restoring alternative is preferable regardless of acquisition and mission effects.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-013: A shared event in a tree

A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.

Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model? Select one option.

  • A. {A,B,C} only.
  • B. Two separate independent copies of A, one in each branch.
  • C. {A} and {B,C}.
  • D. {A,B} and {A,C}.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-014: A warning that causes more work

An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.

Which next model is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. A feedback model connecting alarm load, attention, acknowledgment, escalation and unresolved events.
  • B. A ranking of operators by acknowledgment time.
  • C. A detector-only ROC curve with an increased penalty for missed events.
  • D. A human-response model using the old acknowledgment time as a constant.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-018: Zero observed failures

An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.

Which response is most appropriate? Select one option.

  • A. Pool the twenty units as a single unit tested for twenty consecutive hours without checking assumptions.
  • B. State the observed exposure and zero events, then use an explicitly justified statistical model and uncertainty if estimating reliability.
  • C. Declare the test inconclusive and discard the observations.
  • D. Use one failure divided by exposure as the exact failure probability.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-019: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption

A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.

Which next step best strengthens the evidence? Select one option.

  • A. Report the proof as conditional, assess the environment assumption, and analyze request behavior during outage and recovery.
  • B. Remove the availability assumption and call the resulting timeout a requirement defect.
  • C. Increase the proof bound while leaving the environment assumption unchanged.
  • D. Replace the proof with line coverage because the deployed environment is uncertain.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-023: Decomposition loses a condition

The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.

What remains missing? Select one option.

  • A. A third sensor is needed to satisfy the parent.
  • B. The two links establish complete decomposition because each input is represented.
  • C. The children must use identical wording to the parent.
  • D. The required shutdown response and its connection to either diagnostic need explicit treatment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-024: Resolving conflicting authorities

A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.

Which treatment preserves the decision basis? Select one option.

  • A. Stop all concept work until the contract is formally changed.
  • B. Keep 40 kg as the current obligation, record 45 kg as a proposed change, and show the trade consequence and needed disposition.
  • C. Use 45 kg because it is the latest statement.
  • D. Average the two values to avoid bias toward either stakeholder.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-028: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.

Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project? Select one option.

  • A. Add unit labels to the interface document and consider the problem resolved.
  • B. Require one organization to write every component to remove organizational interfaces.
  • C. Convert every engineering quantity to a single storage type.
  • D. Make interface semantics executable at producer/consumer boundaries and verify representative exchanged data with clear ownership.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-029: Ownership at an interface

A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.

Which clarification has the highest immediate value? Select one option.

  • A. The validity/age contract, clock reference, guaranteed update bounds and responsibilities when those conditions are violated.
  • B. Whether the supplier uses UDP or TCP internally.
  • C. The exact color of the stale-data indicator.
  • D. Whether five seconds is a common industry setting.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-033: A reversible trial

Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.

Which factor belongs in the decision? Select one option.

  • A. The number of requirements each option references.
  • B. The option value of reversible learning, alongside expected performance and implementation effects.
  • C. A rule that the smallest change should always be selected.
  • D. A preference for B because it demonstrates long-term commitment.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-034: Build, buy and the supporting system

A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.

What should a build/buy comparison include? Select one option.

  • A. Only components designed by the program because external products cannot be controlled.
  • B. The sensor plus integration, support, supply and operational constraints, with uncertainties and owners.
  • C. Total project cost with all unknowns assigned the same contingency percentage.
  • D. The sensing function and its measured accuracy only.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-038: An estimate becomes a fact

A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.

What correction is needed? Select one option.

  • A. Rename the model output a prediction and leave the summary unchanged.
  • B. Delete every result calculated using the assumed value.
  • C. Increase the value until the conclusion becomes conservative.
  • D. Retain the value but restore its assumption status and trace its effect on conclusions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-039: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation

The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.

What is the strongest transferable lesson? Select one option.

  • A. Alternative assessment must include information, recognition and decision delays available at the actual decision point.
  • B. A successful simulator trajectory establishes that the crew should have selected it.
  • C. Human decision time should be removed when evaluating aircraft performance.
  • D. A failed delayed attempt proves no aircraft could have returned under any conditions.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-043: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence

The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.

What should a review require? Select one option.

  • A. A causal and evidence-based assessment of the anomaly, including why prior success does or does not bound the present risk.
  • B. A ban on using operational history in risk assessment.
  • C. A count of successful missions as a direct estimate that the anomaly cannot cause loss.
  • D. A requirement that the subsystem owner make the final decision without cross-program review.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-044: London 2012: a supplier cannot deliver

The National Audit Office's post-Games review describes extensive operational preparation for London 2012 and contingency action when the security contractor could not provide planned staffing.

Which preparation best transfers to a new major event? Select one option.

  • A. Duplicate contracts for every event function regardless of consequence.
  • B. A detailed organization chart with no need to rehearse transitions.
  • C. Exercised scenarios connecting delivery shortfalls to decision authority, available reserves and operational changes.
  • D. Contract penalties large enough to remove the need for alternate staffing.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-048: Reporting disagreement

Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.

Which report is most useful? Select one option.

  • A. Report disagreement, the evidence supporting each position, the geometry-dependent question and the decision or test needed to resolve it.
  • B. Choose the senior reviewer's conclusion and omit the disagreement.
  • C. Present both conclusions as equally valid without identifying the unresolved mechanism.
  • D. Average the two reviewer ratings and report the resulting confidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-049: Choosing a useful view

A review board cannot tell who controls motion during startup, normal operation, manual stop and recovery. It already has a component hierarchy with complete part names.

Which additional view best answers the question? Select one option.

  • A. A more detailed component hierarchy with supplier names.
  • B. A table of all software function names sorted alphabetically.
  • C. A high-resolution rendering of the enclosure.
  • D. A state/authority view showing transitions, guards and who may enable or inhibit motion, tied to the existing components.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-053: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer

RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.

What should the review conclude? Select one option.

  • A. Replacing TCP with a newer transport protocol resolves the semantic gap.
  • B. TCP acknowledgments are unreliable and should not be recorded.
  • C. The log supports transport-level receipt but not operator action; the application/workflow needs its own relevant acknowledgment evidence.
  • D. The operator action is established whenever both endpoints use TCP.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-054: DNS: a historical design trade

RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.

What transfers from the source? Select one option.

  • A. A long lifetime is correct because the original design favored caching.
  • B. The trade must be evaluated against this application's update and stale-data consequences; the historical mechanism does not supply its acceptance limits.
  • C. Caching should be avoided whenever data can change.
  • D. A cache hit demonstrates that the value is current.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-058: A supplier changes its service contract

A cloud service previously guaranteed delivery of events in order. Its new version preserves all events but allows reordering. The consumer uses arrival order to authorize a sequence of physical actions.

Which review scope is necessary? Select one option.

  • A. Only the API field names and types.
  • B. The supplier's event count, because no data is lost.
  • C. Every requirement in the organization, regardless of dependency.
  • D. The changed ordering semantics, consumer state/authority logic, recovery behavior and related verification evidence.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

SEJ-059: A rejected alternative becomes relevant

A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.

What should the concept review do? Select one option.

  • A. Delete the previous decision record to avoid confusing reviewers.
  • B. Reuse the old decision because its documented rationale makes it authoritative in every deployment.
  • C. Select radio because the original objection is absent.
  • D. Reopen the alternative against the new context, retaining the old rationale and examining new support constraints.

Explain the facts and reasoning that support your selection; identify a consequential limitation if one applies.

Verification guidance: observed failure and transfer check

Independent review located conflicting timing-outcome rules in the original HO-13 verification plan. An observation of 201 ms with a symmetric 5 ms uncertainty bound met both the stated failure rule and the stated inconclusive rule. That output and its partial criterion rating are preserved.

The change record binds the failure to a narrow guidance revision: distinguish uncertainty representations and require consistent outcome rules, including equality and overlap. It presents interval classification as an illustration and leaves the adopted project rule and acceptance authority explicit.

Two new participants completed the same fresh transfer task with prior or revised guidance. Independent assessment rated both responses 2 on all four criteria. Their six interval dispositions and boundary handling were correct. The revised instructions are proportionate to the finding, but this single comparison demonstrates no incremental benefit.

Prior-guidance response and revised-guidance response remain unchanged, with their packet, tool-use and hash records. The original prior-arm record's phrase "inherited parent conversation context" was clarified by its producer: it meant shared ambient instructions, catalog and memory summary, not access to the earlier failure or tuning discussion. Both dispatches used fork_turns=none; neither provided a technically enforced isolation boundary. The raw wording and clarification remain in the independent assessment.

No controller was tested, no new engineering acceptance was granted, and the original response was not retrospectively upgraded to a passing assessment.

N-1 — review and proposed decision sheet

Keep N-1 open and withhold operational use pending an authorized decision supported by adequate evidence. The six supplied records do not establish compliance across the specified operating envelope. They are authored teaching fixtures; no hardware was available and no test was executed in this exercise.

Proposed rule

For observed elapsed time x, use the interval [x − U, x + U] ms, conditional on the supplier's assertion that U is a guaranteed symmetric error bound including clock alignment. This is a range of compatible true elapsed times, not additional observed readings or a statistical confidence interval. Confirm that assertion before actual use.

Apply the unchanged, inclusive requirement elapsed time ≤ 120 ms:

  • Compliance established for this observation: x + U ≤ 120 ms.
  • Noncompliance established for this observation: x − U > 120 ms.
  • Indeterminate: the interval includes both compliant and noncompliant times, so x − U ≤ 120 < x + U.

This rule is proposed, not adopted. The supplier's nominal-time rule does not establish compliance or noncompliance when the interval straddles the limit. No tolerance or margin is added to N-1.

Revised observation dispositions

All times are milliseconds. Input IDs, values, and supplier statuses are preserved.

ID Observed elapsed time U Supplier status Compatible elapsed-time interval Outcome under proposed rule and basis
OBS-1 111 3 pass [108, 114] Compliance established for this observation: upper bound 114 ≤ 120.
OBS-2 121 4 fail [117, 125] Indeterminate: interval spans 120; nominal exceedance does not establish noncompliance under the bound assumption.
OBS-3 130 2 fail [128, 132] Noncompliance established for this observation: lower bound 128 > 120.
OBS-4 120 0 pass [120, 120] Compliance established for this observation: equality is permitted, conditional on the asserted zero error bound.
OBS-5 116 4 pass [112, 120] Compliance established for this observation: upper bound equals the inclusive limit.
OBS-6 117 6 pass [111, 123] Indeterminate: interval spans 120; nominal compliance does not establish compliance under the bound assumption.

Acceptance status for every row and for N-1: no authorized acceptance decision is supplied. These are analytical dispositions of supplied fixtures, not new executed-test results, accepted evidence, or release authorization.

Closure and operational disposition

N-1 cannot now be closed. OBS-3 conflicts with the timing requirement under the supplied assumption; OBS-2 and OBS-6 remain unresolved. Even the three favorable dispositions establish only their individual timing claims. No argument connects six observations to coverage of the entire specified operating envelope.

For the operations lead's requested policy, any unresolved or established noncompliance means compliance is not established and use is withheld. Both conditions occur here. Record this as a recommendation; an indeterminate result is not a demonstrated violation, and withholding is not itself an authorized acceptance or rejection decision.

Before closure or use, the project needs to adopt and document the decision rule and identify the authorized decision owner; confirm U's guaranteed-bound meaning and applicability, including OBS-4's zero bound; establish the records' provenance, relevant configuration, operating conditions, valid-trip trigger, warning-assertion endpoint, and timing method; define and justify coverage of the specified envelope; and resolve OBS-3 plus the indeterminate records with traceable investigation and appropriate evidence. Any proposed additional verification remains planned until executed and recorded. Review and acceptance must identify their scope, conditions, owner, and disposition separately from the observation outcomes.

Source: evals/evidence/verification-tuning-20261113/revised-guidance/outputs/output.md

N-1 remains open. Recommend withholding operational use because compliance across the specified operating envelope is not established. The records are authored teaching fixtures; this review does not constitute hardware testing, executed verification, or an authorized acceptance decision.

The supplier's nominal-time rule ignores the supplied error bound. No project rule has been adopted, so the following is a proposal for review and adoption, conditional on confirming that U is a valid guaranteed symmetric bound, including clock alignment. It is not a statistical confidence interval.

For observed elapsed time t, the bound-derived interval of compatible elapsed times is [t − U, t + U]. N-1 permits elapsed times at or below 120 ms. Apply one mutually exclusive outcome per record:

  • Pass: t + U ≤ 120 ms; every compatible elapsed time meets the limit.
  • Fail: t − U > 120 ms; every compatible elapsed time exceeds the limit.
  • Inconclusive: t − U ≤ 120 ms < t + U; both compliant and noncompliant elapsed times remain possible.

These are conditional record-level conformity outcomes under the proposed rule. They neither adopt that rule nor authorize acceptance or use.

ID Observed elapsed time (ms) U (ms) Supplier status, preserved Bound-derived interval (ms) Proposed outcome Basis
OBS-1 111 3 pass [108, 114] Pass Upper bound 114 ≤ 120.
OBS-2 121 4 fail [117, 125] Inconclusive Interval includes values on both sides of 120; nominal exceedance alone does not establish noncompliance.
OBS-3 130 2 fail [128, 132] Fail Lower bound 128 > 120.
OBS-4 120 0 pass [120, 120] Pass Equality satisfies “no later than”; relies on the supplied zero-error assumption.
OBS-5 116 4 pass [112, 120] Pass Inclusive upper bound equals the permitted limit.
OBS-6 117 6 pass [111, 123] Inconclusive A nominal time below 120 does not exclude an actual time above 120.

The intervals are derived from the supplied observations and bounds, not additional observations. The preserved supplier statuses are historical inputs; the proposed outcomes show the consequences of a different, explicitly stated rule. No authorized acceptance decision is supplied for any record or for N-1.

Even if these were applicable executed measurements, OBS-3 would demonstrate an over-limit result under the supplied assumptions, OBS-2 and OBS-6 would remain unresolved, and the missing envelope-coverage argument would prevent whole-requirement closure. Three record-level passes cannot close N-1.

Before closure or use, the project needs to adopt a decision rule; confirm the bounds and their applicability to actual timing measurements; establish the operating envelope, relevant configuration, and a justified coverage plan; obtain traceable executed evidence; and resolve the represented failure and inconclusive cases. Evidence that distinguishes which side of 120 ms a crossing interval lies on could include a justified tighter bound or appropriately specified new measurements; no such evidence exists in this packet. Record review and an authorized acceptance decision with its owner and scope separately.

Withholding use follows the operations lead's stated preference whenever compliance is unestablished. It is an operational recommendation, not a claim that an inconclusive observation is a measurement failure, and no release or acceptance authority is exercised here.

Source: examples/aerospace/cubesat-constellation/README.md

CubeSat Constellation

Proposed teaching baseline. Physical performance and risk acceptance remain open. Source review identifies candidate citations and unresolved applicability; review status identifies the checked scope.

Overview

The CubeSat Constellation is a 12-unit low Earth orbit (LEO) formation providing multispectral Earth observation with 24-hour global revisit. Each 6U spacecraft carries an optical payload and a software-defined radio supporting intersatellite links (ISL) and CCSDS-compliant ground communication. The constellation operates autonomously between ground contacts, performing on-board orbit maintenance, data routing through the ISL mesh, and payload scheduling coordinated by a ground-based mission operations center.

The system is classified NASA Class C under NPR 7150.2 with mission assurance tailored per NPR 7123.1. Class C tailoring accepts higher risk for cost-constrained missions: formal independent verification is reduced, and heritage hardware with existing radiation characterization replaces full qualification testing for non-safety-critical components.

System Boundary

Inside the system boundary: - 12 spacecraft bus avionics (OBC, EPS, ADCS, propulsion) - Software-defined radio (ISL + ground link) - Optical payload instrument and on-board processing - Constellation management software (on-board and ground segment) - Intersatellite link mesh network

Outside the system boundary: - Ground segment infrastructure (antenna network, mission control center) - Launch vehicle and deployment system - Third-party relay satellites (if used for emergency communication) - End-user data distribution and processing systems - Space weather monitoring services (consumed data only)

Operational Environment

The constellation operates in a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit with an orbital lifetime target of 5 years. Each spacecraft experiences approximately 5,500 thermal cycles per year, total ionizing dose of approximately 10 krad(Si) over mission life, and single-event upset rates requiring EDAC on all critical memory. Ground contacts occur via polar ground stations with an average contact window of 8 minutes per pass, 4-6 passes per day per spacecraft.

Operating Modes

Mode ID Name Description Active Functions Constraints
MODE-001 Normal-Ops Nominal imaging, data relay, and orbit maintenance All FUN- functions active None
MODE-002 Safe-Hold Spacecraft-level safe mode after fault detection EPS, thermal, coarse attitude only Payload off; ISL beacon only; awaiting ground cmd
MODE-003 Constellation-Reconfig One or more spacecraft lost; mesh re-routing active ISL re-routing, revised scheduling Degraded revisit time; coverage gaps possible
MODE-004 Eclipse-Management Reduced operations during extended eclipse sequences Payload duty-cycled; ISL maintained Power-positive budget enforced; non-essential loads shed

Key Technical Challenges

  1. Radiation tolerance on COTS hardware. Class C tailoring permits commercial-grade processors with radiation characterization rather than full rad-hard parts. Demonstrating acceptable single-event effects mitigation through software FDIR and EDAC requires mission-specific radiation analysis and test data.

  2. Autonomous orbit maintenance. With limited ground contact windows, each spacecraft must execute autonomous station-keeping maneuvers to maintain the constellation geometry. Collision avoidance using TLE/CDM data must be performed on-board with ground override capability.

  3. ISL mesh routing under dynamic topology. The intersatellite link network topology changes as spacecraft enter and exit mutual visibility. The routing algorithm must converge within one orbit period and handle single-link failures without data loss.

  4. Ground segment interface standardization. CCSDS Space Link Extension (SLE) services must interface with multiple ground station providers, each with different SLE implementation profiles, requiring robust protocol negotiation and fallback mechanisms.

Stakeholders

Stakeholder Role
Mission operations center Constellation command, scheduling, orbit maintenance planning
Payload operations team Imaging campaign planning, data quality assessment
NASA mission assurance Class C mission assurance oversight, waiver authority
Launch services provider Deployment interface, orbit insertion accuracy
End-user community Earth observation data consumers; drive revisit and resolution needs

Standards Applicability

Standard Applicability
NPR 7123.1 Systems engineering processes; tailored for Class C mission risk posture
NPR 7150.2 Software engineering; Class C software classification drives V&V depth
CCSDS 133.0-B Space Packet Protocol for telemetry and telecommand framing
CCSDS 132.0-B TM Space Data Link Protocol for ground downlink
CCSDS 231.0-B TC Space Data Link Protocol for ground uplink
CCSDS 211.0-B Proximity-1 Space Link Protocol for intersatellite link
NASA-STD-8739.8 Software assurance and safety for Class C missions

Architecture

Proposed teaching baseline. Physical performance and risk acceptance remain open. Source review identifies candidate citations and unresolved applicability; review status identifies the checked scope.

System Context

The CubeSat Constellation operates as a distributed system of 12 spacecraft in LEO, coordinated by a ground-based mission operations center. Each spacecraft is an autonomous node that images, processes, stores, and relays data through the intersatellite link mesh. The ground segment provides orbit determination updates, imaging campaign commands, and constellation health monitoring.

Failure Containment / Partitioning

Spacecraft-Level FDIR

Each spacecraft implements a three-tier FDIR hierarchy: 1. Component-level: Hardware watchdog timers on OBC, SDR, and payload processors detect lockups and trigger local resets. 2. Subsystem-level: OBC flight software monitors health telemetry from each subsystem against predefined limits. Out-of-limit conditions trigger subsystem-level recovery (e.g., payload power cycle, ADCS mode reversion). 3. System-level: Persistent faults or multiple simultaneous anomalies trigger transition to MODE-002 (Safe-Hold), which powers off non-essential loads, maintains coarse sun-pointing for power-positive operation, and broadcasts a beacon on the ISL for ground notification.

Constellation-Level Fault Handling

The ground-based constellation manager (CMP-CON-01) monitors fleet health and detects spacecraft loss. Upon detecting a lost spacecraft (3 consecutive missed contacts per REQ-SAF-004), the constellation manager recalculates ISL mesh routes and imaging schedules for the remaining spacecraft, entering MODE-003 (Constellation-Reconfig). This reconfiguration accepts degraded revisit performance rather than risking constellation stability.

Radiation Mitigation (Class C Tailoring)

Class C tailoring accepts COTS processors with radiation characterization rather than full rad-hard qualification. Mitigation relies on: - EDAC (SECDED) on all OBC memory (REQ-FUN-006) - Periodic memory scrubbing (every 60 seconds) - Software-based watchdog and heartbeat monitoring - Safe-hold mode as the ultimate recovery for uncorrectable SEU accumulation

Architecture Decisions

AD-01: CCSDS Protocol Stack over Proprietary Protocols

Decision: Use the CCSDS protocol stack (Space Packet, TM/TC Data Link, Proximity-1) for all communication links rather than a proprietary protocol.

Rationale: CCSDS compliance enables ground station interoperability across the multi-provider polar ground station network without custom protocol adaptation at each site. The ISL uses CCSDS Proximity-1, which is designed for short-range spacecraft-to-spacecraft links and provides the store-and-forward capability needed for mesh routing.

Trade-off: CCSDS framing overhead is higher than a minimal proprietary protocol. Accepted because the interoperability benefit outweighs the bandwidth cost on the already-constrained S-band link.

AD-02: Ground-Based Constellation Management over Fully Autonomous

Decision: Place the constellation management function (scheduling, mesh routing coordination, orbit maintenance planning) in the ground segment rather than distributing it fully across the spacecraft.

Rationale: Ground-based management simplifies on-board software complexity, reduces OBC processing requirements, and keeps the human-in-the-loop for safety-relevant decisions (collision avoidance override, constellation reconfiguration). On-board autonomy is limited to safe-hold (MODE-002) and time-critical collision avoidance (REQ-SAF-002).

Trade-off: Requires sufficient ground contact for timely commanding. Mitigated by the ISL mesh, which allows ground commands to reach any spacecraft through relay even when only one spacecraft is in direct ground contact.

AD-03: Cold-Gas Propulsion over Electric Propulsion

Decision: Use cold-gas propulsion for orbit maintenance rather than electric propulsion.

Rationale: Cold-gas provides immediate thrust (no warm-up or duty cycle constraints), simplifying autonomous collision avoidance maneuver execution within the 4-hour timeline required by REQ-SAF-002. The delta-V budget for a 5-year mission in 500 km SSO is within cold-gas capability for a 6U form factor. Electric propulsion would provide higher specific impulse but requires extended thruster firing periods that complicate attitude control and imaging scheduling.

Trade-off: Lower Isp reduces total delta-V margin. Accepted because the operational simplicity and collision avoidance response time are higher priorities for a Class C mission.

REQ-FUN-001

Field Value

Field Value

REQ-FUN-003

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall establish and maintain intersatellite links with at least 2 neighboring spacecraft whenever line-of-sight geometry permits.
Rationale ISL mesh connectivity enables data relay to ground without requiring each spacecraft to have a direct ground contact.

Status Draft

REQ-FUN-004

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall transmit telemetry and receive telecommands using CCSDS Space Packet Protocol (CCSDS 133.0-B) over a TM/TC Space Data Link layer.
Rationale CCSDS protocol compliance ensures interoperability with the multi-provider ground station network.

Verification Test

REQ-FUN-005

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall perform autonomous orbit maintenance maneuvers to maintain the constellation phasing within +/-0.5 degrees of the nominal mean anomaly separation.
Rationale Constellation geometry maintenance ensures the revisit guarantee is met without requiring continuous ground commanding.
Source REQ-FUN-002; mission operations concept
Parent REQ-FUN-002
Verification Analysis, Demonstration
Allocation CMP-OBC-01, CMP-PROP-01
Status Draft

REQ-FUN-006

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft on-board computer shall implement error detection and correction (EDAC) on all critical memory, correcting single-bit errors and detecting double-bit errors.
Rationale Radiation-induced single-event upsets in LEO require memory protection to prevent silent data corruption on COTS processors.

Safety Requirements

REQ-SAF-001

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall comply with NASA-STD-8719.14 requirements for orbital debris mitigation, including a 25-year post-mission deorbit timeline.
Rationale Orbital debris mitigation is a mandatory compliance requirement for all NASA-affiliated LEO missions.
Source NASA-STD-8719.14; U.S. Government Orbital Debris Mitigation Standard Practices
Parent —
Verification Analysis

Status Draft

REQ-SAF-002

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall execute an autonomous collision avoidance maneuver within 4 hours of receiving a conjunction data message (CDM) indicating a probability of collision exceeding 1 x 10^-4, if ground confirmation is not received within 2 hours.
Rationale Limited ground contact windows require on-board collision avoidance capability to protect the constellation and the debris environment.
Source NASA Conjunction Assessment guidelines; stakeholder need (mission operations)
Parent —
Verification Test, Analysis
Allocation CMP-OBC-01, CMP-PROP-01
Status Draft

REQ-SAF-003

Field Value
Statement Each spacecraft shall transition to MODE-002 (Safe-Hold) within 60 seconds of detecting a fault condition that could result in uncontrolled attitude or unintended propulsive maneuver.
Rationale Safe-hold prevents a faulted spacecraft from becoming a collision hazard or depleting resources uncontrollably.
