Source: examples/historical/challenger/README.md

Challenger: make dissent reach the decision

HG-02 · 1986 · space · failure

Treat readiness as an evidence and communication process with identifiable decision authority.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-02-F1: The commission found that launch decision-makers lacked important information about O-ring problems, the initial contractor recommendation, and continuing engineering objections. HG-02-S1; Chapter V, pp. 82–83.
  • HG-02-F2: The formal readiness structure allowed concerns to bypass key managers despite review procedures having been followed. HG-02-S1; Chapter V, pp. 82–84.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. The readiness system includes contractors, engineering judgment, launch management, environmental conditions, and escalation paths.

Interfaces to examine

  • Engineering → launch authority: uncertainty and disagreement must survive management summarization.
  • Previous flight evidence → current decision: past operation is bounded by the conditions actually observed.

Decision. What should a readiness board receive when specialists and management disagree?

  • A single consolidated recommendation.
  • A recommendation plus unresolved dissent, its evidence, and the authority accepting the risk.

Teaching recommendation. Preserve the technical issue and its disposition as an explicit decision input.

Uncertainty. A new escalation form alone cannot establish that concerns will be heard or resolved.

HG-02-A1: Dissent disposition record

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Concern State mechanism, affected function, and disputed condition Underlying observations and missing-condition evidence
Disagreement Retain competing interpretations and named technical roles Direct review with decision authority
Disposition Record decision, rationale, owner, and reopening trigger Acknowledgment that dissent reached the deciding level

Practice engineering judgment

  1. What information would be lost in a red/amber/green readiness roll-up?
  2. When does previous success provide relevant evidence, and when does it fail to?
  3. Rewrite a vague concern into a decision request without overstating certainty.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Separates the absence of observed failure from demonstrated operating margin.
  • Retains dissent without treating every disagreement as equally supported.
  • Names who decides and what evidence would change the decision.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a launch-independent field deployment faces an environmental condition outside tested experience. Write the unresolved-issue paragraph for its readiness review.

Limits. This case does not infer outside political intervention or reduce the accident to one individual decision.

Sources and access

  • HG-02-S1: Rogers Commission Report, Volume I, Chapter V — 1986-06-06; original investigation. Locator: Chapter V, The Contributing Cause of the Accident, pp. 82–84. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/columbia/README.md

Columbia: keep anomalies visible across organizational boundaries

HG-06 · 2003 · space · failure

Successful previous operations do not resolve an unexplained hazard; information flow is part of system performance.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-06-F1: The board examined the physical damage from debris together with organizational conditions that shaped risk interpretation and decisions. HG-06-S1; Chapters 6–7.
  • HG-06-F2: It identified reliance on past success, communication barriers, inhibited dissent, and weak integration of safety information among organizational contributors. HG-06-S1; Chapter 7, introduction and sections 7.1–7.6.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Vehicle damage, imagery requests, analysis assumptions, mission management, technical authority, and possible response options define the in-flight assessment system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Observation → analysis: uncertainty about damage must remain visible through analytical approximations.
  • Analysis → management: the decision need includes what is unknown and what additional information could change.

Decision. How should repeated anomalies affect readiness and in-flight assessment?

  • Use the history of successful missions to close the concern.
  • Reassess the hazard, identify missing observations, and track assumptions to their decision consequence.

Teaching recommendation. Require a mechanism-based explanation before treating recurrence as acceptable.

Uncertainty. Better information does not guarantee a successful rescue or repair; feasibility needs separate evidence.

HG-06-A1: Anomaly-to-decision trace

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Observation Separate measured facts from inferred damage Image provenance, coverage, and resolution limits
Analysis assumption Connect each simplification to the affected conclusion Sensitivity or bounding evidence
Decision need State which response could change with new information Time window, feasibility assessment, and accountable authority

Practice engineering judgment

  1. What makes a previous anomaly informative about the next flight?
  2. How can a request for more data be translated into a concrete decision need?
  3. Write a status update that preserves technical uncertainty across management levels.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Avoids normalizing an unexplained event from favorable outcomes.
  • Separates obtaining information from proving a viable response.
  • Links communication structure to missing or distorted evidence.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: an autonomous vehicle reports recurring unexplained impact indications. Produce a one-page issue disposition with reopening criteria.

Limits. The gallery does not assert that a particular counterfactual intervention would have saved the crew.

Sources and access

  • HG-06-S1: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I — 2003-08; original investigation. Locator: Chapter 6, especially section 6.3; Chapter 7, sections 7.1–7.6. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/dns/README.md

DNS: distribute authority and manage stale information

HG-16 · 1987 · communications computing · design baseline

Scalability changes who owns data, how long others may reuse it, and what temporary disagreement means.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-16-F1: The design goals call for distributed maintenance and caching rather than collecting a continuously consistent copy of the entire database. HG-16-S1; Section 2.2.
  • HG-16-F2: The document places the trade among acquisition cost, update speed, and cache accuracy under control of the data source. HG-16-S1; Section 2.2.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Authoritative data owners, delegated zones, resolvers, caches, clients, and update operations form the naming system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Authority → cache: reuse reduces load while retaining information that may become stale.
  • Delegation → organization: a naming boundary is also an administrative responsibility boundary.

Decision. How should a team choose freshness behavior for a distributed lookup service?

  • Demand instant global consistency without considering cost or failures.
  • Choose an explicit reuse window and update plan consistent with the consumer’s tolerance for stale data.

Teaching recommendation. State authority, freshness, temporary-failure behavior, and rollback together.

Uncertainty. The acceptable window depends on the decision being supported; a historical design principle supplies no universal duration.

HG-16-A1: Authority and freshness contract

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Ownership Identify the authoritative owner and delegated scope Zone or dataset ownership record
Reuse State allowable age and conditions invalidating cached data Consumer tolerance and measured update path
Failure Distinguish unavailable answer from absent entity Fault scenario and recovery behavior

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why is cached information useful even when it is not current everywhere?
  2. Which organizational failure can defeat a technically valid delegation?
  3. Explain a stale answer without incorrectly calling it fabricated data.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Makes consistency, availability, and operating cost explicit.
  • Connects technical delegation to ownership and handover.
  • Distinguishes freshness, authority, and truth.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a fleet stores remote configuration locally during disconnection. Define who owns it, when it expires, and what operations remain allowed.

Limits. No live DNS changes or experiments were performed; security requirements for a present-day deployment require separate current evidence.

Sources and access

  • HG-16-S1: RFC 1034, Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities — 1987-11; original specification. Locator: Sections 2.2–2.4, 4.2, and 5.2.3. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. The historical document has many later updates. Its design rationale is used here; it is not a complete current DNS deployment or security specification.

      "Explain a stale answer without incorrectly calling it fabricated data."

Source: examples/historical/heathrow-terminal-5/README.md

Heathrow Terminal 5: opening a service is an integration test

HG-10 · 2008 · transport · transition failure

Operational readiness depends on people, logistics, software, facilities, and shared authority working together under representative conditions.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-10-F1: The committee found that building delays compressed staff familiarisation and questioned whether training and trials prepared staff for opening conditions. HG-10-S1; Paragraphs 8–14.
  • HG-10-F2: It examined communication failures between operator and airline and the treatment of concerns raised by staff. HG-10-S2; Paragraphs 15–19.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Passenger journey, staff access, baggage flow, facilities, airline processes, terminal operator, and disruption recovery form the service boundary.

Interfaces to examine

  • Facilities handover → staff training: incomplete spaces can invalidate planned familiarisation.
  • Airline → terminal operator: baggage and passenger exceptions require shared ownership and rapid coordination.

Decision. What evidence supports opening when subsystem completion reports are favorable?

  • Aggregate installation and training-attendance percentages.
  • Exercise end-to-end journeys and exceptions with representative staff, loads, and facilities.

Teaching recommendation. Use an integrated readiness decision with explicit exception handling and a staged transition option.

Uncertainty. The historical report does not prove which exact staging plan would have prevented the disruption.

HG-10-A1: Operational readiness slice

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Staff arrival Demonstrate access, orientation, and workstation readiness Representative shift exercise
Bag exception Follow a delayed or misrouted bag across organizational boundaries Timed exception recovery and accountable owner
Opening disruption Agree service reduction and recovery authority Joint rehearsal and decision log

Connected review exercise

  • Connected review task — A bounded review using multiple linked artifacts.
  • Source fact register — Attributed facts and exact report locators.
  • Editable interface register — New reconstruction with fact-level basis links.
  • Claim and evidence register — Supported observations separated from unexecuted checks.
  • Synthetic change request — A new transfer problem with affected teaching IDs.
  • Editable relation view — Information dependencies with teaching IDs.
  • Public review guide — Reasoning criteria and limitations for formative feedback.

New teaching relation view; arrows show information dependencies.

Source-derived logical flow · Editable SVG · Source graph

Practice engineering judgment

  1. How can all component owners report green while the service remains unready?
  2. What does attendance prove about training, and what does it not prove?
  3. Write a readiness recommendation that makes a phased opening decision reviewable.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Models handovers and exceptions, not only nominal flow.
  • Distinguishes activity completion from demonstrated performance.
  • Includes front-line knowledge and joint operational authority.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a hospital moves into a new building while its scheduling software also changes. Select three cross-team acceptance scenarios.

Limits. The proposed readiness slice is new teaching material, not a recovered airport acceptance plan.

Sources and access

  • HG-10-S1: House of Commons Transport Committee: The opening of Heathrow Terminal 5 — 2008-11-03; original investigation. Locator: Chapter 2, paragraphs 8–14. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Committee conclusions and witness accounts are distinguishable; trial participation alone does not establish trial representativeness.
  • HG-10-S2: The opening of Heathrow Terminal 5: communication and lessons — 2008-11-03; original investigation. Locator: Chapter 3, paragraphs 15–19. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. The committee explicitly avoided certainty that better cooperation would have prevented every problem.

Source: examples/historical/heathrow-terminal-5/review-guide.md

HG-10 review guide

This guide evaluates reasoning in the new exercise, not historical blame or a claim that a different decision would certainly have succeeded.

  • Preserve the distinction between completion of a briefing and demonstrated performance under representative conditions.
  • HG-10-C2 is unsupported because departmental readiness can coexist with missing handover and recovery capability.
  • HG-10-C3 cannot be promoted from proposed to executed merely by creating a rehearsal plan.
  • A useful fallback includes available resources, activation authority, customer consequences, and recovery criteria.
  • The original report supplies context; it does not prove that one proposed opening strategy would have prevented the historical disruption.

Source: examples/historical/heathrow-terminal-5/review-task.md

HG-10 connected review task

All IDs in this bundle are newly assigned teaching IDs. The source facts are attributed historical findings; the interfaces and claims are teaching reconstructions. The change request is synthetic and was never proposed to the original program. No test in this bundle has been executed.

Read source facts, interfaces, claim/evidence register, and change request together. Use the case sources and locators to challenge an assertion. The relation view is an editable information-flow aid, not a formal SysML model.

Decision to produce

Review HG-10-CH1 and identify the precise readiness claims that separate briefings could support. Identify the claims that require an integrated trial. Design one nominal journey and two exception scenarios that cross the airline/operator boundary. Specify roles, initial state, observable result, recovery authority, and the evidence record to retain.

Compare opening at full scope, opening at reduced scope, and delaying the affected service. Do not invent weights or throughput numbers: identify the missing information that would discriminate among the options.

Write a joint readiness note with unresolved issues, owners, service consequences, and a clear point for reopening the decision.

Review your result using the review guide. The guide is public formative material; this task is not a hidden performance benchmark.

Source: examples/historical/herald-free-enterprise/README.md

Herald of Free Enterprise: close the loop between physical state and permission

HG-14 · 1987 · maritime · failure

A safety-critical departure condition needs observable state, accountable confirmation, and a response to unknown or failed indication.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-14-F1: The court found that the ferry went to sea with its bow doors open and examined both individual duties and management failures. HG-14-S1; Paragraph 10; paragraphs 14–18.
  • HG-14-F2: Requests for bridge door indication preceded the accident; the report discussed fail-safe indication, procedures, and berth arrangements. HG-14-S1; Paragraph 18; paragraphs 28–30.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Doors, sensing, bridge display, crew responsibilities, berth geometry, departure authority, and shore management form the departure-control system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Door state → bridge: absence of a reported problem is not a positive closed-and-secured indication.
  • Crew improvement request → management: safety significance needs tracked disposition and feedback.

Decision. How should an unknown door state affect departure permission?

  • Assume completion unless a problem is reported.
  • Require positive confirmation and define the response to failed or contradictory indication.

Teaching recommendation. Review the physical condition, reporting loop, and harbor transition together.

Uncertainty. An indicator is also fallible; its diagnostic coverage and procedures need evidence rather than an assumption of perfection.

HG-14-A1: Departure condition contract

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Required condition Define closed and secured separately from command issued Physical confirmation and sensing basis
Unknown state Make failed indication visible and assign a response Fault injection and crew scenario evidence
Improvement request Record safety consequence, decision, and completion Owner acknowledgment and installation verification

Practice engineering judgment

  1. What is the difference between no alarm and confirmed readiness?
  2. How could a berth interface constrain a safe departure sequence?
  3. Write a technical response to a crew suggestion that makes its disposition accountable.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Models positive confirmation and loss of feedback.
  • Includes both vessel and port interfaces.
  • Treats reporting culture as part of the control process.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a loading system starts motion after a remote operator assumes a guard is closed. Draft its permission states and unknown-state response.

Limits. The proposed contract is not a recovered ship specification. No stability or flooding calculation is supplied.

Sources and access

  • HG-14-S1: Formal Investigation, mv Herald of Free Enterprise, Report of Court No. 8074 — 1987; original investigation. Locator: Front matter (publication and addendum); paragraphs 10, 14–18, and 28–30. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. The scanned copy states first published 1987 and third impression 1988. Its September 1987 addendum corrects attribution in paragraph 19.6; that addendum date is not the original publication date. Fatality counts vary between this contemporary report and later official summaries; no count is used here.

Source: examples/historical/hubble-optics/README.md

Hubble: verify the verifier

HG-03 · 1990 · space · failure and repair opportunity

Independence concerns the assumptions and physical references behind a test, not just the number of test results.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-03-F1: The board traced the primary-mirror figure error to an incorrectly assembled reflective null corrector used in manufacture and verification. HG-03-S1; Executive summary.
  • HG-03-F2: Other optical tests indicated an error, but their indications were discounted; the main corrector had not received an independent dimensional verification after assembly. HG-03-S1; Executive summary; null-corrector investigation.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Mirror, metrology fixture, fixture assembly, test interpretation, supplier oversight, and acceptance authority belong inside the optical acceptance boundary.

Interfaces to examine

  • Fixture geometry → optical result: an incorrect reference can make repeatable measurements misleading.
  • Anomalous test → acceptance decision: contradictory evidence needs a recorded resolution.

Decision. Should agreement with the production reference close an optical acceptance claim?

  • Accept repeated agreement with the same reference.
  • Require an independent check of the reference and disposition conflicting measurements.

Teaching recommendation. Choose evidence with a different failure mechanism and preserve unexplained disagreement.

Uncertainty. Independent measurement has its own uncertainty; two results are not a vote unless their error sources are understood.

HG-03-A1: Metrology evidence independence map

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Production measurement Record reference geometry and calibration chain As-assembled dimensions and uncertainty budget
Cross-check Use a different reference or physical principle Analysis of shared assumptions
Conflict Keep acceptance claim open until resolved Repeatable explanation of discrepant readings

Connected review exercise

  • Connected review task — A bounded review using multiple linked artifacts.
  • Source fact register — Attributed facts and exact report locators.
  • Editable interface register — New reconstruction with fact-level basis links.
  • Claim and evidence register — Supported observations separated from unexecuted checks.
  • Synthetic change request — A new transfer problem with affected teaching IDs.
  • Editable relation view — Information dependencies with teaching IDs.
  • Public review guide — Reasoning criteria and limitations for formative feedback.

New teaching relation view; arrows show information dependencies.

Source-derived logical flow · Editable SVG · Source graph

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Which dependencies make apparently separate tests correlated?
  2. How would you distinguish a bad test from a bad article?
  3. Write an acceptance statement that admits unresolved conflicting evidence.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Maps shared fixtures, calibration, software, and assumptions.
  • Proposes a discriminating check before discarding an inconvenient result.
  • Keeps measurement repeatability separate from accuracy.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: two inspection systems use the same generated geometry file. Draft a third check that can detect an error in that file.

Limits. This case concerns the 1990 investigation. It does not claim that the proposed artifact was used by the project or that a new optical analysis was executed.

Sources and access

  • HG-03-S1: The Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report, NASA-TM-103443 — 1990-11; original investigation. Locator: Executive summary; null-corrector investigation. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/hubble-optics/review-guide.md

HG-03 review guide

This guide evaluates reasoning in the new exercise, not historical blame or a claim that a different decision would certainly have succeeded.

  • Distinguish repeated measurement, independent computation, and an independent physical reference. They address different failure mechanisms.
  • HG-03-C2 is an unsupported independence claim even if both computers are functioning correctly.
  • HG-03-C3 remains unverified until the replacement fixture itself is checked; a drawing or calibration certificate for another configuration is insufficient.
  • Treat the auxiliary discrepancy as a question to resolve, not automatic proof that either instrument is correct.
  • A strong response chooses a check based on discriminating power and uncertainty, not the prestige or number of agreeing instruments.

Source: examples/historical/hubble-optics/review-task.md

HG-03 connected review task

All IDs in this bundle are newly assigned teaching IDs. The source facts are attributed historical findings; the interfaces and claims are teaching reconstructions. The change request is synthetic and was never proposed to the original program. No test in this bundle has been executed.

Read source facts, interfaces, claim/evidence register, and change request together. Use the case sources and locators to challenge an assertion. The relation view is an editable information-flow aid, not a formal SysML model.

Decision to produce

Review HG-03-CH1 using the interface and claim registers. Draw a dependency map for the two computers and the auxiliary instrument, including physical references and shared source data. Identify which dependencies make agreement weak evidence of accuracy.

Compare an independent dimensional check, a repeated measurement using the same reference, and a new physical measurement principle. State which uncertainty each option reduces and which it leaves untouched. Select a next check and explain what result would change your recommendation.

Write an acceptance statement with explicit open claims. Preserve the auxiliary result until a defensible explanation is available.

Review your result using the review guide. The guide is public formative material; this task is not a hidden performance benchmark.

Source: examples/historical/infusion-pump-initiative/README.md

Infusion Pump Improvement Initiative: design across the product lifecycle

HG-19 · 2010 · medical devices · improvement program

A device is used, maintained, and understood within a care system; design review must span that lifecycle.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-19-F1: The FDA describes pump problems that can cause over-infusion, under-infusion, or missed treatment. HG-19-S1; Overview.
  • HG-19-F2: The 2010 initiative combined stronger expectations for manufacturers, proactive design improvement, and increased user awareness across the lifecycle. HG-19-S1; Initiative goals.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Pump, drug library, programming, patient connection, clinicians, training, maintenance, incident reporting, and manufacturer response form the delivery system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Design → clinical use: interface behavior and alarms interact with workflow and interruptions.
  • Service history → design revision: field signals need configuration, reproducibility, and consequence context.

Decision. What should a design-improvement program evaluate beyond component reliability?

  • Concentrate exclusively on pump mechanism accuracy.
  • Evaluate programming, delivery, alarms, maintenance, and field feedback as connected activities.

Teaching recommendation. Trace each hazard to the lifecycle stages where it can be introduced, detected, or controlled.

Uncertainty. Program existence does not establish measured clinical benefit or the safety of an individual product.

HG-19-A1: Lifecycle hazard and feedback map

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Programming Connect intended therapy entry to device configuration Representative-use studies and input-error handling
Delivery interruption Specify detectable conditions and user response Alarm performance and recovery scenarios
Field signal Retain configuration, context, and action history Incident review with verified corrective closure

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why can technically accurate pumping still fail the clinical task?
  2. Which information makes a field incident useful for design learning?
  3. Explain what can and cannot be concluded from a regulator launching an improvement program.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Includes workflow, maintenance, and feedback beyond hardware.
  • Keeps historical program goals separate from proven outcomes.
  • Defines evidence for a product-specific claim.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: create an evidence plan for an alert redesign using a nonclinical bench setting and representative users. Keep clinical efficacy as a separate question.

Limits. No claim about present legal requirements, device approval, treatment settings, or patient outcomes is made.

Sources and access

  • HG-19-S1: FDA Infusion Pump Improvement Initiative — 2010 initiative; current official summary; official initiative summary. Locator: Initiative overview and three program goals. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. The page summarizes a historical program and links later guidance. It is not evidence that a particular pump was cleared, clinically effective, or corrected successfully.

Source: examples/historical/london-2012/README.md

London 2012: separate event readiness from legacy value

HG-20 · 2012 · public services · successful delivery with open legacy

A program can deliver its immediate service while long-term benefits remain separate claims with different owners and evidence.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-20-F1: The NAO described successful staging, intensive scenario testing, and changed governance as planning transitioned to operations. HG-20-S1; Summary paragraphs 5–6.
  • HG-20-F2: It reported effective contingency action for security staffing shortfalls while stating that the effectiveness of new legacy arrangements remained to be seen. HG-20-S1; Summary paragraphs 8–10.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Venues, transport, volunteers, security, delivery organizations, government decision bodies, and future venue operators span different lifecycle phases.

Interfaces to examine

  • Planning governance → operational command: decision speed and authority change at the event boundary.
  • Event delivery → legacy operation: assets, funding, obligations, and benefit measurement need a new owner.

Decision. What should a post-event success statement include?

  • Collapse delivery, cost forecasts, and future benefits into one success rating.
  • Report achieved service, residual liabilities, forecasts, and long-term benefits as separate claims.

Teaching recommendation. Keep a benefits register alive after the delivery organization winds down.

Uncertainty. Effective contingency may impose costs or dependencies elsewhere; successful staging does not settle every value-for-money question.

HG-20-A1: Delivery-to-legacy handover

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Event readiness Demonstrate integrated scenarios and response authority Observed exercises and issue closure
Contingency activation Name trigger, resource provider, and decision rights Availability and practical mobilization evidence
Legacy benefit Transfer owner, baseline, measure, and review date Post-event operating data and counterfactual assumptions

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Which measures expire when the event ends?
  2. What makes a contingency operationally credible?
  3. Write a success statement that is positive without claiming unrealized benefits.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Separates immediate outputs, operating outcomes, and later benefits.
  • Connects governance and resource readiness to contingencies.
  • Retains accountability after organizational transition.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a city completes an emergency-response facility before a major event. Draft separate opening and five-year benefit acceptance statements.

Limits. The case uses the 2012 audit’s knowledge state; it does not assert the eventual outcome of every legacy commitment.

Sources and access

  • HG-20-S1: National Audit Office, The London 2012 Olympic Games and Paralympic Games: post-Games review, HC 794 — 2012-12-05; original program audit. Locator: Summary paragraphs 5–10; Parts One, Two, and Four. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. A post-Games audit of delivery, then-current forecasts, and legacy arrangements. Future costs and benefits are not converted into realized outcomes.

Source: examples/historical/mars-climate-orbiter/README.md

Mars Climate Orbiter: own the meaning of an interface

HG-05 · 1999 · space · failure

An interface contract includes semantic meaning, producers, consumers, checks, and operational handover.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-05-F1: The board identified English-unit impulse data in a ground-software output where the interface specified metric units; navigation processing assumed the specified units. HG-05-S1; Executive summary; section 4.
  • HG-05-F2: Its contributing causes also included transition to operations, communication, staffing, training, and ground-software verification weaknesses. HG-05-S1; Executive summary; section 5.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Spacecraft events, ground data generation, navigation ingestion, trajectory review, and development-to-operations handover belong to one mission information flow.

Interfaces to examine

  • Producer → consumer: numerical values require units, reference frame, sign convention, timing, and version.
  • Predicted trajectory → operations team: persistent residuals need owned investigation and escalation.

Decision. What closes an interface verification claim?

  • Each team reports its own software test success.
  • Both teams demonstrate shared semantics with an independently checked end-to-end sample.

Teaching recommendation. Require a semantic contract and operational anomaly ownership together.

Uncertainty. A unit-tagged file alone does not verify the physical quantity, calibration, or trajectory model.

HG-05-A1: Interface acceptance contract

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Impulse field Declare quantity, units, frame, sign, and event interval Hand-checkable input/output sample agreed by both teams
Consumer check Reject invalid or unrecognized semantics Negative tests and observed error handling
Operational discrepancy Assign residual investigation and escalation owner Recorded threshold rationale and disposition history

Connected review exercise

  • Connected review task — A bounded review using multiple linked artifacts.
  • Source fact register — Attributed facts and exact report locators.
  • Editable interface register — New reconstruction with fact-level basis links.
  • Claim and evidence register — Supported observations separated from unexecuted checks.
  • Synthetic change request — A new transfer problem with affected teaching IDs.
  • Editable relation view — Information dependencies with teaching IDs.
  • Public review guide — Reasoning criteria and limitations for formative feedback.

New teaching relation view; arrows show information dependencies.

Source-derived logical flow · Editable SVG · Source graph

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why is adding unit conversion code an incomplete corrective action?
  2. Who owns acceptance when producer and consumer are different organizations?
  3. State what a persistent unexplained residual means without declaring a cause prematurely.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Separates schema conformance from physical meaning.
  • Includes end-to-end evidence and handover responsibility.
  • Keeps investigation open until discrepancies are explained.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a supplier delivers actuator impulse data to a fleet model. Draft a sample contract including one rejection case.

Limits. No reconstructed orbit or numerical failure simulation is provided. The original report describes multiple contributing conditions.

Sources and access

  • HG-05-S1: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report — 1999-11-10; original investigation. Locator: Executive summary pp. 6–8; sections 4–5, pp. 16–24. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/mars-climate-orbiter/review-guide.md

HG-05 review guide

This guide evaluates reasoning in the new exercise, not historical blame or a claim that a different decision would certainly have succeeded.

  • Preserve HG-05-C1 as a narrow attributed historical finding.
  • HG-05-C2 remains unsupported: new metadata cannot establish physical meaning or mission correctness by itself.
  • HG-05-C3 remains planned until an identified implementation is exercised and outputs are inspected. A plausible rejection policy is not a test result.
  • A credible disposition considers compatibility, explicit unknown states, quarantining disputed inputs, shared producer/consumer review, and the consequences of changing the format.
  • Do not claim that this exercise proves how the original mission would have behaved after the change.

Source: examples/historical/mars-climate-orbiter/review-task.md

HG-05 connected review task

All IDs in this bundle are newly assigned teaching IDs. The source facts are attributed historical findings; the interfaces and claims are teaching reconstructions. The change request is synthetic and was never proposed to the original program. No test in this bundle has been executed.

Read source facts, interfaces, claim/evidence register, and change request together. Use the case sources and locators to challenge an assertion. The relation view is an editable information-flow aid, not a formal SysML model.

Decision to produce

Write a disposition of HG-05-CH1 with a claim-by-claim evidence status. Revise HG-05-I1 to state how version and unit semantics are recognized, what happens to unknown inputs, and who owns the acceptance sample. Identify which existing files can support testing and which require provenance recovery.

Produce an acceptance matrix with at least a valid sample, an unrecognized unit, a missing unit, and a disagreement between metadata and an independently known quantity. State the oracle, expected disposition, and evidence still needed. Do not mark any row passed.

End with a short status message to an integration lead: decision, reason, remaining gap, owner, and the next review trigger.

Review your result using the review guide. The guide is public formative material; this task is not a hidden performance benchmark.

Source: examples/historical/mars-exploration-rovers/README.md

Mars Exploration Rovers: connect scientific intent to operational choices

HG-07 · 2004 · space · success with lifecycle adaptation

Turn a broad scientific question into a sequence of feasible observations, then manage the life of that capability.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-07-F1: The prelaunch concept balanced safe landing conditions with scientific value, using remote instruments to select targets for close-up examination. HG-07-S1; Landing-site and instrument-workflow paragraphs.
  • HG-07-F2: Opportunity operated beyond its primary 90-sol mission; NASA records a 2014 mission extension and flash-memory reformat responding to operational resets. HG-07-S2; In Depth, 2004 and September 2014 entries.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Science team, target selection, terrain, mobility, instruments, solar energy, communications, and software maintenance form an observation-producing system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Science question → target selection: a measurement must discriminate among scientific explanations.
  • Target priority → daily plan: traverse cost, power, hazards, and data return constrain achievable science.

Decision. How should a team compare a scientifically attractive target with a safer accessible one?

  • Rank targets only by expected scientific interest.
  • Compare information value with access cost, risk, energy, and remaining opportunities.

Teaching recommendation. Make the rejected option and its opportunity cost visible in the plan.

Uncertainty. Long life alone does not establish scientific effectiveness; compare returned observations with the scientific question.

HG-07-A1: Observation-to-operation trade

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Remote survey Select targets using discriminating features Images, spectral clues, and alternative explanations
Close examination Budget traverse, contact, power, and downlink together Terrain and instrument feasibility checks
Extended operations Reassess goals when capability changes Observed resets, updated constraints, and recoverability evidence

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Which scientific need is met by having both remote and contact instruments?
  2. How could a technically successful traverse be a poor mission decision?
  3. Write an extension recommendation with a condition that would reverse it.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Traces instruments to information needs rather than listing hardware.
  • Treats resources and opportunities as coupled.
  • Distinguishes design life, actual survival, and delivered mission value.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a survey robot has one day of battery remaining and three uncertain targets. Present a decision table without inventing probabilities.

Limits. The proposed trade is new. No rover science ranking, traverse model, or flight software experiment was executed here.

Sources and access

  • HG-07-S1: NASA Will Send Two Robotic Geologists to Roam on Mars — 2003-06-04; original project record. Locator: Paragraphs on landing-site selection and instrument workflow. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. This is a prelaunch statement: schedules and expected outcomes are plans, not flight evidence.
  • HG-07-S2: Opportunity mission history — current official retrospective; historical events through 2014 used; official retrospective. Locator: In Depth, 2004 mission and September 2014 extension entries. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Later history is used only to distinguish realized operation from the 2003 plans; post-2014 events are outside this case.

Structured case record · Gallery · Source register

Source: examples/historical/northeast-blackout/README.md

Northeast blackout: know whether the monitoring system is working

HG-12 · 2003 · energy · failure

Operators need evidence about both the physical system and the health of the tools used to observe it.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-12-F1: The task force grouped causes into inadequate system understanding, situational awareness, vegetation management, and reliability-coordinator diagnostic support. HG-12-S1; Chapter 3, pp. 17–19.
  • HG-12-F2: It found weaknesses in awareness of monitoring-tool condition, communication between computer support and operators, and checking functionality after repairs. HG-12-S1; Chapter 3, p. 18; Chapter 5, pp. 51–56.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Grid assets, vegetation, state estimation, alarm processing, operators, support teams, and neighboring reliability organizations form the coordinated system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Monitoring tool → operator: a quiet display may mean stability or loss of observation.
  • Control area → coordinator: missing or stale state can defeat analysis beyond one organization.

Decision. What should an operational display communicate when its data path is unhealthy?

  • Continue displaying the last known normal state.
  • Expose freshness and function status, trigger degraded monitoring, and coordinate restrictions.

Teaching recommendation. Treat loss of observability as an operational condition with owned responses.

Uncertainty. A heartbeat alone does not establish end-to-end alarm or state-estimation correctness.

HG-12-A1: Monitoring assurance contract

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Data freshness Expose age and failed updates Known stimulus observed through the full chain
Tool repair Restore function only after a bounded end-to-end check Recorded input, output, and operator acknowledgment
Coordination Notify affected neighbors of degraded visibility Shared degraded-operation protocol

Practice engineering judgment

  1. How can redundancy in servers fail to preserve situational awareness?
  2. Who should know that the monitoring tools are degraded?
  3. Draft a restoration message separating service availability from verified monitoring function.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Separates telemetry absence from a healthy physical state.
  • Includes organizational boundaries and fallback capability.
  • Uses a functional check rather than a process-up indicator alone.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a control dashboard keeps rendering cached values after an upstream outage. Define the operator-visible states and response owners.

Limits. No power-flow or blackout propagation model was executed. The report’s historical policy findings are not presented as current regulatory advice.

Sources and access

  • HG-12-S1: Final Report on the August 14, 2003 Blackout in the United States and Canada — 2004-04; original investigation. Locator: Chapter 3, printed pp. 17–19; Chapter 5, monitoring failures, pp. 51–56. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/san-bruno-pipeline/README.md

San Bruno: preserve the provenance of configuration data

HG-21 · 2010 · energy · failure

Digitizing a record does not validate the physical configuration it describes.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-21-F1: The pipeline GIS described the rupture segment as seamless pipe using information traced through a survey sheet to an accounting voucher with an erroneous material description. HG-21-S1; Section 1.7.2, pp. 26–27.
  • HG-21-F2: Investigators found welded short pipe sections with defects and configuration details that were not reflected in the GIS. HG-21-S1; Section 1.7.2, p. 27; section 1.8.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Physical asset, construction records, accounting records, survey sheets, GIS, integrity analysis, inspections, and operating decisions form the configuration-evidence chain.

Interfaces to examine

  • Legacy record → digital model: transformation must preserve origin and confidence instead of laundering uncertainty.
  • Model attribute → integrity decision: uncertain material identity changes which analyses are applicable.

Decision. What should happen when an important configuration field has weak provenance?

  • Treat a populated database field as authoritative.
  • Mark the uncertainty, bound its decision consequences, and seek suitable confirming evidence.

Teaching recommendation. Differentiate administrative records, engineering records, and observations of the installed asset.

Uncertainty. A missing record does not by itself prove a defect; it limits the claims that can be supported.

HG-21-A1: Configuration provenance ledger

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Material identity Retain source chain and conflicts Engineering record or suitable physical confirmation
Asset segmentation Represent actual changes in construction Inspection and as-built reconciliation
Decision applicability Flag analyses sensitive to uncertain fields Conservative bounds and owned resolution plan

Practice engineering judgment

  1. How can information become more convincing without becoming more accurate?
  2. What should a digital twin display when material identity is unresolved?
  3. Write an uncertainty statement that avoids both false assurance and unsupported failure claims.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Tracks the origin of each decision-critical attribute.
  • Propagates uncertainty into analysis applicability.
  • Separates absence of evidence from evidence of defect.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: migrate a legacy asset registry into a digital model. Define three provenance classes and rules preventing unsupported promotion to verified.

Limits. No pipeline integrity calculation or operating recommendation is made. All new ledger IDs are instructional.

  • HG-21-S1: NTSB Pipeline Accident Report PAR-11/01 — 2011-08-30; original investigation. Locator: Section 1.7.2, printed pp. 25–28; section 1.8. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/tcp/README.md

TCP: define what an acknowledgment means

HG-15 · 1981 · communications computing · design baseline

A useful interface states both the service it provides and the stronger claims it does not establish.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-15-F1: RFC 793 describes reliable ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and receive windows. HG-15-S1; Section 2.6, pp. 9–10.
  • HG-15-F2: It explicitly distinguishes receiving-TCP responsibility from delivery to the end user when describing acknowledgment semantics. HG-15-S1; Section 2.6, p. 10.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Application sender, transport endpoints, network, receiving application, and any durable business operation must be distinguished.

Interfaces to examine

  • Transport → application: receipt by a transport endpoint is weaker than application processing or durable commit.
  • Application retry → remote operation: retry semantics require an application-level decision.

Decision. Can a transport acknowledgment close a claim that a business operation completed?

  • Treat receipt as completion.
  • Define an application result and recovery protocol with separate durability and duplicate-handling claims.

Teaching recommendation. State the acceptance boundary in the vocabulary of the stakeholder’s operation.

Uncertainty. The historical protocol alone does not establish exactly-once processing, persistent storage, or operator acknowledgment.

HG-15-A1: Layered acknowledgment contract

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Transport receipt Bytes accepted by the receiving transport Protocol-level observation
Application acceptance Request parsed and accepted for a named operation Application response with request identity
Durable outcome Committed or explicitly unresolved after interruption Recovery query and duplicate-handling evidence

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Which stronger claims are often smuggled into the word delivered?
  2. What should a client do when an operation times out after possibly completing?
  3. Explain acknowledgment semantics to a non-network stakeholder in two sentences.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Separates receipt, processing, persistence, and business outcome.
  • Identifies ambiguity without promising exactly-once semantics.
  • Places evidence at the layer responsible for the claim.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: an industrial controller receives a command over a reliable connection. Define the acknowledgments needed before an operator can claim the physical action occurred.

Limits. No networking benchmark or current protocol compliance test was run. The artifact is an application-level teaching proposal.

Sources and access

  • HG-15-S1: RFC 793, Transmission Control Protocol — 1981-09; original specification. Locator: Sections 1.4–1.5, 2.4, and 2.6; section 3.9. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Historical specification, subsequently superseded. This case studies the 1981 service boundary, not current TCP implementation requirements.

Source: examples/historical/texas-city-refinery/README.md

Texas City refinery: measure the hazard you intend to control

HG-13 · 2005 · industrial · failure

Steady production and favorable injury statistics do not establish readiness for a hazardous startup.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-13-F1: The accident occurred during startup of the isomerization unit; a flooded distillation tower and atmospheric release exposed people near occupied trailers. HG-13-S1; Executive summary.
  • HG-13-F2: The CSB found that reliance on low personal-injury rates gave a misleading picture of process-safety performance. HG-13-S1; Executive summary; section 1.6; section 9.3.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Process equipment, startup state, instrumentation, staffing, temporary occupied buildings, maintenance, and management measures belong to the hazard boundary.

Interfaces to examine

  • Operating mode → protection: startup changes inventories and actions relative to normal production.
  • Management metric → resource decision: a convenient metric may omit the accident mechanism of concern.

Decision. Which evidence should support a startup readiness claim?

  • Use recent production availability and personal-injury performance.
  • Check mode-specific protection, instrumentation, procedures, staffing, and occupied-area exposure.

Teaching recommendation. Build measures around barriers to the major hazard and their observed condition.

Uncertainty. A barrier checklist still needs demonstrated functionality and authority to act on deficiencies.

HG-13-A1: Startup readiness and indicator slice

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Process state Confirm mode-specific limits and instrument validity Independent checks of inventory and protective functions
People in exposure area Review temporary occupancy against credible releases Siting and evacuation basis
Management measure Track unresolved barrier impairments with consequence Age, ownership, and verified closure of impairments

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why can a declining injury rate coexist with increasing major-accident risk?
  2. What changes when a plant enters a transient operating mode?
  3. Write a management brief that distinguishes output performance from protection health.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Links each measure to a mechanism and a decision.
  • Includes temporary facilities and contractors in the system boundary.
  • Avoids substituting completed paperwork for demonstrated protection.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a plant dashboard is green while three protective functions are bypassed. Redesign the decision-relevant portion of the dashboard.

Limits. The artifact is not a refinery operating procedure and does not establish safe staffing, siting distances, or protection settings.

Sources and access

  • HG-13-S1: CSB BP Texas City Final Investigation Report — 2007-03-20; original investigation. Locator: Executive summary; section 1.6 findings; sections 9.3–9.4 on management and indicators. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/therac-25/README.md

Therac-25: treat interaction timing and hazard communication as design concerns

HG-18 · 1987 · medical devices · failure

A credible safety argument must account for temporal interactions, operator feedback, and what users are told when a defect is found.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-18-F1: The authors describe a race condition involving rapid edits and interacting software tasks, not simply an incorrect static input value. HG-18-S2; Opening race-condition discussion.
  • HG-18-F2: They report that the FDA objected to an initial corrective notification because it failed to explain the defect, associated hazard, and urgency. HG-18-S2; Government and user response.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Treatment prescription, software tasks, beam configuration, interlocks, operator display, patient feedback, manufacturer, and clinical users form the safety system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Operator editing → control state: valid individual actions can form an unsafe temporal sequence.
  • Manufacturer → clinical user: corrective instructions need a truthful hazard explanation and clear scope.

Decision. What evidence supports a corrective release after a timing-dependent fault?

  • Patch the observed input sequence and send brief workaround instructions.
  • Reassess interacting states, independent protection, user feedback, and the complete corrective communication.

Teaching recommendation. Require mechanism-focused tests and a bounded safety claim for the changed system.

Uncertainty. A reproduced software fault does not establish all contributing conditions or prove the resulting clinical system safe.

HG-18-A1: Corrective-action evidence slice

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Interaction timing Exercise edits at relevant state boundaries Reproducible event traces and independent review
Protection Identify safeguards independent of the faulty path Failure-mode evidence and coverage limits
User notification Explain hazard, affected configuration, action, and urgency Readable instructions reviewed with representative users

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why do static input tests miss temporal hazards?
  2. What must a defect notice say beyond the workaround?
  3. How would you communicate uncertain accident details without dismissing a credible safety signal?

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Examines shared state, scheduling, and feedback.
  • Separates root-cause reproduction from overall safety acceptance.
  • Communicates hazard and uncertainty without minimizing either.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: a therapy-planning interface allows rapid mode edits while configuration is pending. Define a test plan and a hypothetical user notice; do not prescribe patient treatment.

Limits. No clinical advice, medical-device certification, or simulated radiation exposure is provided. The original authors’ uncertainty is retained.

Sources and access

  • HG-18-S1: Leveson and Turner, An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, Part I — 1993-07; original author investigation. Locator: Introduction and investigation limitations. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Original investigators’ article, reprinted with permission from IEEE Computer 26(7), pp. 18–41. It explicitly notes uncertain details and the absence of a single official commission report.
  • HG-18-S2: An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents, Part III — 1993-07; original author investigation. Locator: Race-condition discussion; Government and user response. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Same article as Part I; one underlying publication. Regulatory descriptions are historical and are not current regulatory guidance.

Source: examples/historical/united-232/README.md

United 232: functional redundancy is not physical independence

HG-09 · 1989 · aviation · failure with partial recovery

Test redundant architecture against shared physical hazards and the operational capability remaining after damage.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-09-F1: The FAA describes an uncontained tail-engine fan-disk failure whose debris damaged all three hydraulic systems. HG-09-S1; Accident Overview; Airplane.
  • HG-09-F2: The systems were functionally isolated but physically close in parts of the tail; the crew used wing-engine thrust to obtain limited control. HG-09-S1; Airplane; Flight Crew.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Engines, debris zones, hydraulic routing, flight controls, crew coordination, airport options, and emergency response define the damaged-aircraft system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Engine debris → multiple channels: a single event can cross logical redundancy boundaries.
  • Remaining propulsion → crew control: residual authority may be difficult to use and insufficient for stable flight.

Decision. How should a redundancy claim be challenged?

  • Count independent functional channels.
  • Trace shared locations, supplies, controls, maintenance, and external hazards.

Teaching recommendation. Pair functional decomposition with a physical dependency review and degraded-operation evidence.

Uncertainty. Physical separation is one design choice; effectiveness depends on the hazard envelope and achievable residual control.

HG-09-A1: Common-cause dependency review

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Three hydraulic channels Map proximity and common exposure Layout and credible debris-zone analysis
Residual control State achievable tasks after shared damage Representative handling evidence
Crew allocation Assign navigation, control, communication, and cabin coordination Observed workload and coordination evidence

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Which diagram would reveal a weakness hidden by a logical block diagram?
  2. What is the difference between having some control and meeting a landing requirement?
  3. Write a qualified redundancy claim for a new design.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Identifies shared hazard exposure instead of multiplying nominal reliabilities.
  • Defines residual capability in operational tasks.
  • Recognizes human adaptation without turning it into a guaranteed design control.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: three power channels share a service duct. Produce a common-cause review and compare relocation, shielding, and diverse backup.

Limits. No reliability probability, debris simulation, or claim that training alone would resolve the failure is made.

Sources and access

  • HG-09-S1: FAA Lessons Learned: United Airlines Flight 232, N1819U — official retrospective; date not stated; official retrospective. Locator: Accident Overview; Airplane; Flight Crew. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. The FAA account was inspected. The original NTSB report URL was unavailable during curation; this case does not represent direct access to that report.

Source: examples/historical/us-airways-1549/README.md

US Airways 1549: model the decision-maker’s time

HG-08 · 2009 · aviation · recovery

Validate scenarios against the time and information available to the operator, including recognition and decision delays.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-08-F1: The investigation examined the loss of thrust in both engines after a bird encounter and the subsequent Hudson River ditching. HG-08-S1; Executive summary.
  • HG-08-F2: Immediate-turn simulator attempts omitted recognition and decision time. The report describes one delayed return-to-LaGuardia attempt with a 35-second delay that did not succeed. HG-08-S1; Section 1.16.3, printed pp. 49–50; section 2.3.2; footnotes 88–89.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Aircraft energy, available landing areas, crew cognition, procedures, air traffic control, cabin preparation, and rescue response form the emergency system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Failure cues → crew action: detection, interpretation, decision, and execution consume time.
  • Flight deck → cabin: protective preparation must fit the remaining time and information.

Decision. What does a favorable simulator outcome establish about an actual emergency choice?

  • Treat the best trial as proof that a different choice was available.
  • Compare initial state, information, delays, training, and outcome variability before transferring a result.

Teaching recommendation. Report scenario applicability before judging the historical decision.

Uncertainty. One delayed failed trial does not estimate a general success probability or prove all alternative paths impossible.

HG-08-A1: Scenario applicability matrix

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Initial state Match position, energy, damage, and environment Validated reconstruction and uncertainty
Human timing Include recognition and decision tasks Observed timing or justified sensitivity range
Outcome claim State which tested conditions support the conclusion All attempts, failures, and exclusions

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why is immediate response a strong modeling assumption?
  2. What evidence would be needed to estimate success probability?
  3. Explain the difference between a possible trajectory and an available decision.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Includes information and action latency in the system model.
  • Avoids extrapolating one run into a universal conclusion.
  • Communicates the limits of counterfactual evidence.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: an emergency controller proposes a recovery action that succeeds only with zero delay. Specify a fair comparison protocol.

Limits. Simulation results are attributed to the NTSB. This repository did not rerun the flight or conduct new pilot trials.

Sources and access

  • HG-08-S1: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report AAR-10/03 — 2010-05-04; original investigation. Locator: Section 1.16.3, Operational Factors and Human Performance Simulations, printed pp. 49–50; section 2.3.2; footnotes 88–89. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Relevant sections inspected; this is not a reconstruction of every event or finding.

Source: examples/historical/world-wide-web-proposal/README.md

World Wide Web proposal: start with the organization’s information problem

HG-17 · 1989 · communications computing · concept baseline

A concept becomes credible when it explains the users, existing assets, adoption constraints, and deliberate scope boundaries.

All HG- identifiers are new teaching identifiers. Historical facts below are attributed to sources; the boundary, decisions, artifact, questions, and transfer exercise are newly authored. No local historical simulation was performed.

Source-grounded facts

  • HG-17-F1: The proposal addresses information loss and relationships across a changing organization, then calls for heterogeneous access, decentralization, and links to existing data. HG-17-S1; Losing Information at CERN; CERN Requirements.
  • HG-17-F2: It treats sophisticated authorization and accounting as outside the proposed local scope while discussing use of existing protection for protected data. HG-17-S1; Non requirements.

Retrospective systems analysis

Boundary. Researchers, institutional memory, existing databases, diverse computers, links, and local adoption form the proposed information system.

Interfaces to examine

  • Existing repository → new access layer: adoption depends on useful information being available early.
  • Local collaboration → broader deployment: a changed trust environment can invalidate deliberate scope exclusions.

Decision. How should a team assess a promising early concept?

  • Score it by the eventual market’s feature list.
  • Evaluate problem fit, adoption path, alternatives, and the assumptions that must hold in its initial context.

Teaching recommendation. Keep the initial scope coherent while recording conditions that trigger redesign.

Uncertainty. The later success of the Web does not prove each early design choice was inevitable or universally appropriate.

HG-17-A1: Concept and scope decision note

This proposed artifact is a compact starting point for review. Its evidence requests are unexecuted; its rows are not recovered project requirements.

Item Proposed disposition Evidence to seek
Stakeholder problem Preserve relationships across people, projects, and repositories Observed retrieval and handover difficulties
Adoption path Expose useful existing material before requiring migration Pilot access to representative repositories
Boundary change Reopen protection and governance when access expands New users, threats, obligations, and ownership

Practice engineering judgment

  1. Why is access to existing information an architectural requirement rather than only a convenience?
  2. When is a non-requirement responsible scoping, and when does it become a dangerous inherited assumption?
  3. Pitch a small pilot without using eventual success as evidence available in 1989.

Reasoning signals for a formative review

  • Frames the problem in organizational work rather than a technology label.
  • Recognizes adoption and compatibility as system constraints.
  • Keeps historical context distinct from present-day security needs.

Transfer exercise. Synthetic: propose a shared engineering knowledge service for three teams using incompatible repositories. Include one deliberate exclusion and its reopening trigger.

Limits. This is analysis of the original proposal, not a claim about all subsequent Web standards or a current security recommendation.

Sources and access

  • HG-17-S1: Tim Berners-Lee, Information Management: A Proposal — 1989-03; recirculated 1990-05; original project proposal. Locator: Losing Information at CERN; CERN Requirements; Non requirements; A Practical Project. Relevant content inspected 2026-11-13. Author-hosted HTML transcription of the original proposal. It is evidence of intent, not proof that every proposed feature was implemented or widely adopted.
